choices.text: It is a hyalinized calcification marking a healed infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an Aschoff body diagnostic of rheumatic carditis

explanation.summary: Asteroid bodies, star-shaped inclusions in histiocytes within a cleared circle, may be seen in sarcoidosis but are not specific for it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The end result of the idiopathic inflammation of sarcoidosis is the formation of non-necrotizing granulomas, and, while not specific, asteroid bodies, a histologic finding in histiocytes resembling a star in a cleared circle, may be seen. Their presence supports but does not confirm the diagnosis, which remains one of exclusion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Talc appears as white, jagged flake-like material that is bright under polarized light, not a star-shaped inclusion, and would indicate a foreign body granuloma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Asteroid bodies are not organisms; a fungal organism would produce a necrotizing granuloma and require special stains to identify.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyalinized, calcified old granulomas are markers of a resolved infection and are not intracellular star-shaped inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aschoff bodies are nodules of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages in the heart during acute rheumatic fever, not histiocyte inclusions in a sarcoid lymph node.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman hospitalized for pneumonia is treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. One week later she develops profuse watery diarrhea and crampy abdominal pain. Colonoscopy reveals yellow-white plaques overlying the colonic mucosa. Which of the following best explains why the responsible organism was able to establish this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Loss of the gastric acid barrier

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depletion of the normal gut microbiota

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired mucociliary clearance in the airways

explanation.summary: The normal gut microbiota competes with incoming organisms, and antibiotics disrupt it, permitting Clostridioides difficile overgrowth and pseudomembranous colitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The resident gut flora competes with newly arriving organisms for resources and limits colonization. Antibiotics disrupt this microbiota, allowing C. difficile to proliferate and release toxins A and B, which drive cytokine release, neutrophil recruitment, and the pseudomembrane of inflammatory cells and debris.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastric acid is a defense against ingested organisms, but the plaques and antibiotic history point to microbiota disruption, not achlorhydria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mucociliary clearance is a respiratory tract defense and is unrelated to colonic infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgA deficiency is not the mechanism the brick attributes to antibiotic-associated C. difficile colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinary obstruction predisposes to urogenital infection, not to pseudomembranous colitis.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man develops nausea, crampy abdominal pain, and watery diarrhea two days after a picnic where he ate ham sandwiches and potato salad. Which of the following is the most likely route by which the causative organism entered his body?

explanation.summary: Most gastrointestinal pathogens enter with food or drink contaminated by fecal matter, known as fecal-oral transmission.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that most GI pathogens enter with food or drink contaminated by fecal matter (fecal-oral transmission), producing symptoms through toxin production or direct mucosal damage. Foodborne diarrheal illness after a shared meal fits this route.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhalation is the entry route for respiratory pathogens, not for foodborne gastroenteritis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sexual contact transmits pathogens such as HIV and N. gonorrhoeae, not foodborne diarrheal organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Percutaneous inoculation involves breaks in the skin, such as bites or needle sticks, not ingestion of food.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retrograde axonal transport moves certain viruses along nerves to the CNS and does not cause food-related diarrhea.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is bitten on the leg by a raccoon while camping. Several weeks later he develops agitation, difficulty swallowing, and a rapidly fatal encephalitis. By which mechanism did the responsible pathogen most likely reach the central nervous system?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Direct extension across the intact skin

explanation.summary: Some viruses spread along nerves to the CNS by retrograde axonal transport, as seen with rabies.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that viruses may spread along nerves to the central nervous system by retrograde axonal transport, listing rabies virus, poliovirus, varicella-zoster virus, and HSV. A fatal encephalitis after an animal bite reflects this neural route.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hematogenous seeding spreads organisms via blood to sites such as heart valves, not the described neural route to the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphatic spread carries pathogens to lymph nodes before the bloodstream and is not how these neurotropic viruses reach the CNS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pathogen does not extend across intact skin; it enters at the bite wound and travels up nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transplacental transmission passes organisms from mother to fetus and is irrelevant to an animal bite.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man who injects heroin presents with fever and a new heart murmur. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci, and echocardiography shows a vegetation on the tricuspid valve. Which of the following best describes how the organism reached the heart valve?

explanation.summary: Intravenous drug use can introduce skin bacteria into the bloodstream, which then seed a heart valve, producing endocarditis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that bloodborne dissemination lets pathogens seed distant sites and that endocarditis is a consequence of septicemia. Intravenous drug use with a hypodermic needle introduces bacteria from the skin into the blood, where they lodge on a valve and form a vegetation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Retrograde axonal transport carries certain viruses along nerves to the CNS, not bacteria to heart valves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mucociliary mechanisms clear the airways and do not deliver organisms to the endocardium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fecal-oral ingestion is a route for gastrointestinal pathogens, not for valve seeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ascending urethral spread causes urinary tract infection, not endocarditis.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A newborn is found to have cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and a patent ductus arteriosus. The mother recalls a febrile rash illness during the first trimester. Transmission of the responsible pathogen most likely occurred by which route?

explanation.summary: Placental (transplacental) transmission of TORCH agents such as rubella during pregnancy causes congenital developmental abnormalities.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes placenta-fetal (vertical) transmission of TORCH infections, which include rubella, and states these cause developmental abnormalities, eye damage, and skin manifestations, often with mild maternal symptoms. First-trimester maternal infection with congenital anomalies fits transplacental spread.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Breast milk transmits viruses such as CMV, HIV, and HBV to the newborn but does not explain first-trimester congenital malformations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Birth canal exposure causes neonatal infections such as gonococcal or chlamydial conjunctivitis, not the congenital triad described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Respiratory droplet spread is a person-to-person mode and does not account for prenatal organ malformation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fecal-oral ingestion causes gastrointestinal infection and is unrelated to congenital anomalies.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A tissue biopsy shows aggregates of epithelioid macrophages, some fused into multinucleated giant cells, surrounded by a rim of lymphocytes. Which histologic pattern of reaction to injury does this represent?

explanation.summary: Granulomatous inflammation is defined by activated epithelioid macrophages and multinucleated giant cells gathered around an insult.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines granulomatous inflammation as a special type of mononuclear inflammation in which activated macrophages gather around an infectious insult, some fusing into multinucleated giant cells; the accumulation is called a granuloma. This matches the described histology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Suppurative inflammation is neutrophil-rich pus, not epithelioid macrophages and giant cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytopathic-cytoproliferative reactions involve single-cell viral changes or cell proliferation, not organized macrophage aggregates.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic scarring is dominated by fibrosis, not by epithelioid macrophages and giant cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Coagulative infarction reflects ischemic necrosis and is not the granulomatous pattern described.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: Autopsy of a patient with pneumonia reveals multiple localized areas of liquefactive necrosis rich in neutrophils, each surrounded by a fibrotic rim. Which type of organism most characteristically produces this pattern of reaction?

explanation.summary: Suppurative inflammation with abscess formation is the hallmark reaction to pyogenic (pus-forming) bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes suppurative (purulent) inflammation as neutrophil-dominated, most commonly caused by pyogenic bacteria, with an abscess defined as localized liquefactive necrosis surrounded by a peripheral fibrotic deposit. This matches the described lung findings.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Viruses typically produce cytopathic-cytoproliferative or mononuclear reactions, not neutrophilic abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spirochetes such as T. pallidum elicit mononuclear (lymphocytic) inflammation, not suppuration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Helminths characteristically drive mononuclear and eosinophil-rich responses rather than pyogenic abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An autoimmune process would not typically produce this classic pyogenic abscess pattern of infection.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man develops rough, cauliflower-like verrucous growths on his hands. Biopsy shows proliferation of epithelial cells with cytopathic changes. This lesion is an example of which pattern of tissue reaction to infection?

explanation.summary: The cytopathic-cytoproliferative pattern includes viral cell injury and virus-driven cell proliferation, such as HPV warts.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the cytopathic-cytoproliferative reaction as involving single cells or small aggregates with cytopathic changes, and notes that some viruses cause cells to proliferate, such as the verrucous warts of human papillomavirus (HPV). The described warty proliferation fits this pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Suppurative inflammation is neutrophilic pus formation, not verrucous epithelial proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulomatous inflammation forms epithelioid macrophage aggregates, not virus-induced warts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Caseating necrosis is central cheese-like death seen in tuberculosis granulomas, not proliferative warts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chronic inflammation with scarring produces fibrosis, not the proliferative warty lesion described.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: An unvaccinated child develops a thick gray membrane over the pharynx and, several days later, cardiac arrhythmia. The toxin responsible for this illness damages host cells primarily by which mechanism?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acting as a superantigen to trigger cytokine release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Being recognized by macrophages via its Lipid A

explanation.summary: Diphtheria toxin is an A-B toxin whose A subunit inhibits protein synthesis, causing the pharyngeal pseudomembrane and myocarditis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that in diphtheria toxin the B component mediates entry by endocytosis and the A component inhibits protein synthesis in the ribosome, leading to cell death; local injury forms the pseudomembrane, and toxin entering the bloodstream can damage myocardial cells to cause acute myocarditis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cleavage of desmoglein-1 is the mechanism of staphylococcal exfoliative toxin, not diphtheria toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Superantigen activity is characteristic of staphylococcal enterotoxin and TSST, not diphtheria toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Disruption of the enterocyte cytoskeleton describes Clostridioides difficile toxins A and B.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lipid A recognition describes gram-negative endotoxin, not the A-B diphtheria exotoxin.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child develops widespread superficial blistering and peeling of the skin following a staphylococcal infection. The toxin responsible for this presentation acts by which mechanism?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Forming membrane pores via Lipid A

explanation.summary: Staphylococcal exfoliative toxins cleave desmoglein-1, detaching keratinocytes and causing scalded-skin syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that exfoliative A and B toxins produced by S. aureus cleave desmoglein-1, a desmosome protein important for keratinocyte adherence. The resulting detachment compromises the skin barrier, producing staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome with blistering and exfoliation, primarily in pediatric patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhibition of protein synthesis is the action of diphtheria toxin, not exfoliative toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipid A pore/immune activation describes gram-negative endotoxin, not the skin-cleaving toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ciliary immobility is associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae, not staphylococcal skin disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blocking neurotransmitter release describes clostridial neurotoxins, not exfoliative toxin.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A young woman develops high fever, hypotension, a diffuse macular rash, and later desquamation of the palms. Cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus from an infected nasal packing. The toxin responsible produces disease by which mechanism?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Signaling through the Lipid A of lipopolysaccharide

explanation.summary: Superantigen toxins cause toxic shock syndrome by driving nonspecific T-cell activation and a massive cytokine release.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes enterotoxin and TSST as superantigens that stimulate a robust immune response with release of massive amounts of cytokines, and it links toxic shock syndrome to massive cytokine release, including cases from infected nasal packing or postoperative wound materials.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Protein synthesis inhibition is the diphtheria toxin mechanism, not superantigen action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cleavage of desmosomal proteins describes exfoliative toxin causing scalded-skin syndrome, not TSS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cytoskeletal disruption of enterocytes is the mechanism of C. difficile toxins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lipid A signaling is the mechanism of gram-negative endotoxin, not a staphylococcal superantigen.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A patient with gram-negative bacteremia develops fever and hypotension. The outer membrane component of the bacterium primarily responsible for triggering this systemic response is detected by macrophages through which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Lipid A portion of lipopolysaccharide

explanation.summary: Endotoxin (LPS), particularly its Lipid A portion, is sensed by macrophages and drives fever and cytokine-induced hypotension.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies lipopolysaccharide (LPS), also called endotoxin, as an outer membrane component of gram-negative bacteria; its Lipid A portion is detected by immune cells such as macrophages, provoking pro-inflammatory cytokines and complement activation that cause fever and cytokine-induced hypotension.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Peptidoglycan is a cell wall component, but the brick attributes the gram-negative endotoxin response specifically to Lipid A of LPS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Teichoic acid is a gram-positive cell wall component and is not the gram-negative endotoxin described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A-B exotoxins are secreted toxins such as diphtheria toxin, not the outer membrane endotoxin sensed here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Desmoglein-1 is a host desmosomal protein targeted by exfoliative toxin, not a bacterial sensing component.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has a history of recurrent pneumonia, a liver abscess, and osteomyelitis caused by catalase-positive organisms. Biopsy of an infected lymph node shows granulomatous inflammation. Which of the following best explains this child's recurrent infections?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deficiency of myeloperoxidase in neutrophil granules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mutation in the LYST lysosomal trafficking regulator gene

explanation.summary: Chronic granulomatous disease results from defective NADPH oxidase, crippling reactive-oxygen-species-dependent intracellular killing.
explanation.whyCorrect: In chronic granulomatous disease, phagocytes cannot generate reactive oxygen species in the phagolysosome because NADPH oxidase is defective. Intracellular killing by macrophages and neutrophils fails, so patients suffer recurrent pneumonia, abscesses, lymphadenitis, skin infections, and osteomyelitis, and the defective macrophages accumulate as granulomatous inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Myeloperoxidase deficiency prevents conversion of hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid but is usually asymptomatic and does not classically produce granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency impairs integrin-mediated migration and produces infections with absent pus, not reactive-oxygen-species failure with granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Severe congenital neutropenia is defined by too few neutrophils; here the problem is defective killing by phagocytes that are present, as evidenced by granuloma formation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A LYST mutation causes Chediak-Higashi syndrome, which adds partial albinism, neurologic defects, and bleeding rather than isolated granulomatous infection.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child has partial albinism of the skin and hair, recurrent pyogenic infections, easy bruising, and progressive neurologic dysfunction. A peripheral blood smear shows leukocytes containing abnormally large cytoplasmic granules. A defect in which of the following is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Chediak-Higashi syndrome arises from a defect in the LYST lysosomal trafficking regulator, producing giant granules that cannot release their contents.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by mutations in the LYST gene encoding a lysosomal trafficking regulator protein. Neutrophils, natural killer cells, and cytotoxic T lymphocytes cannot release toxic granule contents, so patients are vulnerable to infection. Melanosomes cannot release pigment (partial albinism), platelet dense granules cannot be released (bleeding), and lysosomal dysfunction in neurons and glia produces neurologic defects; the giant granules are the diagnostic clue.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An NADPH oxidase defect causes chronic granulomatous disease with granulomas, not albinism, giant granules, and bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Integrin adhesion defects cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency with impaired pus formation, not pigment and platelet-granule abnormalities.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Complement deficiency impairs opsonization and lysis but does not cause giant leukocyte granules or albinism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myeloperoxidase deficiency is typically asymptomatic and does not produce albinism, neurologic disease, or giant granules.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A newborn is diagnosed with an inherited disorder detected at birth and develops rapidly spreading soft-tissue bacterial infections. Despite severe infection, the involved tissues characteristically show no pus. Which of the following abnormalities best explains these findings?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of oxidative burst within phagolysosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inability to release cytotoxic granule contents

explanation.summary: Severe congenital neutropenia is defined by a dramatic reduction in neutrophils, so pus is absent even during serious infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Severe congenital neutropenia is a group of inherited disorders with markedly impaired neutrophil counts, usually diagnosed at birth. Because neutrophils are the key cellular component of a purulent inflammatory response, pus is characteristically absent, and bacteria can spread quickly through soft tissue into the bloodstream.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A defective oxidative burst describes chronic granulomatous disease; those neutrophils are present and form granulomas rather than being absent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inability to release granule contents describes Chediak-Higashi syndrome, which also features albinism and neurologic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Deficient hypochlorous acid generation is myeloperoxidase deficiency, which is usually asymptomatic and does not abolish pus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Absent membrane attack complex is a complement defect affecting lysis and opsonization, not neutrophil numbers or pus formation.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus develops a severe Candida albicans infection. Laboratory testing reveals an inherited deficiency of a heme-containing enzyme normally present in neutrophil granules; the patient has otherwise been asymptomatic throughout life. Which enzymatic reaction is most likely impaired?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduction of molecular oxygen to superoxide by NADPH oxidase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Digestion of bacterial cell walls by lysozyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cleavage of complement C3 into C3b

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polymerization of actin filaments during phagocytosis

explanation.summary: Myeloperoxidase deficiency prevents conversion of hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid, usually asymptomatic but linked to Candida infection in diabetics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myeloperoxidase is a heme-containing enzyme in neutrophil granules that converts hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid. Without it, affected cells compensate with other antimicrobial substances, so most patients are asymptomatic; however, severe Candida albicans infections are reported, particularly in the setting of diabetes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Impaired superoxide generation by NADPH oxidase defines chronic granulomatous disease, which is not usually asymptomatic and produces granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lysozyme digests bacterial cell walls and is not the heme-containing granule enzyme described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C3 cleavage is a complement function; its deficiency impairs opsonization broadly rather than presenting as isolated Candida infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Actin polymerization supports phagocytic engulfment and is not a heme-dependent oxidative killing step.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A virus infecting a host epithelial cell downregulates expression of MHC class I molecules to avoid recognition by cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Despite this, the infected cell is still killed. Which of the following cells is most likely responsible, and by what mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Natural killer cells detecting absent MHC class I

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neutrophils generating hypochlorous acid within phagolysosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plasma cells secreting neutralizing antibodies against the viral capsid

choices.label: D
choices.text: CD4-positive helper T cells directly lysing the infected cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Eosinophils releasing major basic protein onto the cell surface

explanation.summary: Natural killer cells sense loss of MHC class I and kill virus-infected cells non-specifically via perforin and granzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: A common viral evasion strategy is downregulation of class I MHC to escape cytotoxic T cells. Natural killer cells sense the lack of class I MHC and kill the virus-infected cell non-specifically by secreting perforins and proteolytic granzymes, driving the cell into apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutrophil oxidative killing targets phagocytosed microbes, not host cells that have lost surface MHC class I.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibodies neutralize extracellular virus and opsonize, but they do not exploit the absence of MHC class I to kill an infected cell.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD4-positive helper T cells coordinate responses through cytokines; they are not the direct cytolytic effectors that respond to missing MHC class I.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Eosinophils act mainly against helminths and are not the effectors that kill MHC-class-I-negative virus-infected cells.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: During replication, a virus generates double-stranded RNA within an infected cell. In response, the cell produces and releases interferons that act on neighboring cells to establish an antiviral state. Which of the following best describes how these interferons block viral protein synthesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They activate enzymes that degrade mRNA and inhibit eIF-2

choices.label: B
choices.text: They bind viral gp120 and prevent attachment to CD4 receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: They insert a membrane attack complex into the viral envelope

choices.label: D
choices.text: They opsonize virions to enhance phagocytosis by macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: They cross-link viral capsid proteins to prevent uncoating

explanation.summary: Interferons induce enzymes that, in the presence of double-stranded RNA, halt protein synthesis and thereby block viral replication.
explanation.whyCorrect: Interferons are released from infected cells in response to double-stranded RNA present during viral replication. They activate 2'-5' oligoadenylate synthetase, which induces a ribonuclease that degrades mRNA, and they activate protein kinase R, which inhibits the initiation factor eIF-2. Both actions stop protein synthesis and prevent production of new virus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking gp120-CD4 binding is a mechanism relevant to HIV entry, not the antiviral action of interferons.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The membrane attack complex is a complement structure that lyses cells and microbes; it is not how interferons work.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Opsonization is a complement- and antibody-mediated process, not an interferon-induced block of protein synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Interferons do not cross-link capsid proteins; they act intracellularly to shut down translation.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A pregnant woman develops a febrile illness after eating unpasteurized dairy products, and her neonate is subsequently born with disseminated infection and meningitis. The responsible gram-positive bacillus survives inside host cells and spreads directly from one cell to the next without re-entering the extracellular space. Which of the following mechanisms best accounts for this intracellular survival and spread?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Listeriolysin O ruptures the phagosome and actin polymerization propels the organism between cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: A polysaccharide capsule blocks complement deposition on the bacterial surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protein A binds the Fc portion of IgG to prevent opsonization

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antigenic variation of surface pili avoids antibody recognition

choices.label: E
choices.text: Downregulation of MHC class I prevents cytotoxic T-cell killing

explanation.summary: Listeria monocytogenes escapes the phagosome via listeriolysin O and uses actin-based motility to spread cell-to-cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Listeria monocytogenes is a gram-positive bacillus acquired from dairy and milk products that can cross the placenta and cause disseminated neonatal infection and meningitis. After being taken up, it escapes the phagosome using listeriolysin O, a pore-forming toxin, before phagolysosomal killing occurs. It then propels itself through the cell by polymerizing actin filaments (ActA), protruding into and entering the next cell, so it spreads without re-entering the extracellular space.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A polysaccharide capsule resists phagocytosis extracellularly and does not explain cytoplasmic escape and actin-based spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protein A is a Staphylococcus aureus mechanism that blocks opsonization, not intracellular motility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antigenic variation of pili is a Neisseria strategy against antibodies, unrelated to phagosomal escape.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MHC class I downregulation is a viral evasion tactic, not the mechanism used by this intracellular bacterium.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A strain of Staphylococcus aureus expresses a surface protein that binds the Fc portion of IgG antibodies. As a result, IgG bound to the bacterium can no longer engage Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages. Which of the following is the most direct consequence of this mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Impaired antibody-mediated phagocytosis of the bacterium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of natural killer cell recognition of infected host cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of interferon-induced antiviral protein synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of phagolysosome formation within macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Antigenic variation of the bacterial surface proteins

explanation.summary: Staphylococcal Protein A binds IgG by its Fc region, preventing the antibody from directing phagocytes to the bacterium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Staphylococcus aureus expresses Protein A, which binds the Fc portion of IgG. Because the Fc region is what normally engages Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages, this binding prevents the bound IgG from triggering phagocytosis, so antibody-mediated (opsonic) clearance of the bacterium is impaired.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Natural killer cell recognition depends on MHC class I status of host cells, not on IgG binding to a bacterial surface protein.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interferon-induced antiviral responses are unrelated to this antibody-blocking mechanism used against a bacterium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting phagolysosome formation is a strategy of intracellular organisms such as mycobacteria, not the effect of Protein A.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antigenic variation involves changing surface antigens; Protein A instead blocks the antibody's effector function directly.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A patient develops repeated infections with Neisseria despite generating antibodies against the organism during each episode. Analysis shows that the bacterium expresses new pilin surface proteins over time by placing different pilin coding sequences next to a single promoter. Which of the following best describes the mechanism responsible for this immune evasion?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Secretion of a polysaccharide capsule that blocks phagocytosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Binding of the Fc portion of IgG by a surface protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Escape from the phagosome using a pore-forming toxin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Downregulation of host MHC class I molecules

explanation.summary: Neisseria evades adaptive immunity by antigenic variation, using homologous recombination to swap pilin variants next to its promoter.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neisseria carries 10-15 silent pilin protein variants and expresses only the one situated next to the promoter. Through homologous recombination, a new pilin coding sequence is placed next to the promoter, so a new pilin protein is expressed that antibodies raised against the previous variant no longer recognize. This antigenic variation allows the organism to escape the antibody response.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A polysaccharide capsule resists phagocytosis but does not explain the sequential change in pilin antigens described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Binding the Fc portion of IgG is the Protein A mechanism of Staphylococcus aureus, not pilin antigenic variation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pore-forming phagosomal escape is used by Listeria; it does not change surface antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MHC class I downregulation is a viral strategy against T cells, not a bacterial antibody-evasion mechanism.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A virus uses its surface glycoprotein gp120, together with the chemokine co-receptors CCR5 and CXCR4, to bind and enter a specific population of host cells. Over time, destruction of these cells leaves the patient in an immunosuppressed state and vulnerable to opportunistic infections. Which host cells does this virus preferentially infect?

explanation.summary: HIV shows tropism for CD4-positive helper T cells because gp120 binds CD4 with the co-receptors CCR5 and CXCR4.
explanation.whyCorrect: Human immunodeficiency virus utilizes gp120 to bind CD4 and the chemokine co-receptors CCR5 and CXCR4 to enter and infect the cell. This gives the virus tropism for CD4-positive cells, known as helper T cells. Their infection and destruction leaves the patient immunosuppressed and vulnerable to other infections.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Natural killer cells lack the CD4-based entry receptor and are not the target population defined by gp120 tropism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils are not CD4-positive helper T cells and are not preferentially infected via gp120-CD4 binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mature B lymphocytes are not the CD4-positive helper T cells targeted by gp120 and its co-receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although macrophages can be infected, the specific tropism described by gp120 binding to CD4 with CCR5/CXCR4 defines helper T cells, not macrophages exclusively.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A pathogenic fungus proliferating in a patient's tissues secretes abundant capsular material, and a co-infecting bacterium is likewise surrounded by a thick polysaccharide coat. Neither organism is efficiently cleared by neutrophils or macrophages. Which of the following best explains how the capsule promotes immune evasion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It interferes with complement deposition and phagocytosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: It degrades host mRNA to block protein synthesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: It binds the Fc portion of IgG to block Fc receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits interferon release from infected cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It downregulates MHC class I on host cells

explanation.summary: Polysaccharide capsules interfere with complement deposition and phagocytosis, letting encapsulated microbes evade professional phagocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Polysaccharide capsules interfere with complement deposition and phagocytosis. Encapsulated bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae and certain fungi like Cryptococcus neoformans exploit this; Cryptococcus even secretes capsule material to inhibit immune attack, allowing the organisms to resist engulfment by neutrophils and macrophages.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Degrading host mRNA describes an interferon-induced antiviral action, not the function of a microbial capsule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Binding the Fc portion of IgG is the staphylococcal Protein A mechanism, not a property of the polysaccharide capsule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting interferon release is a viral tactic and does not explain capsule-mediated resistance to phagocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MHC class I downregulation is a strategy of viruses, not of encapsulated bacteria and fungi.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A child has recurrent bacterial infections in which the affected sites conspicuously fail to form pus, and neutrophils are found to remain within the bloodstream rather than migrating into infected tissues. Which of the following defects best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Impaired integrin-mediated adhesion of leukocytes to endothelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defective NADPH oxidase in the phagolysosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inability to release cytotoxic granules due to a LYST mutation

explanation.summary: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency impairs integrin-mediated adhesion, so leukocytes cannot migrate into tissue and pus fails to form.
explanation.whyCorrect: For leukocytes to leave the bloodstream and migrate into tissues, integrins are needed for adhesion to endothelial cells. In leukocyte adhesion deficiency, impaired integrin function prevents this adhesion and migration, so infections recur and the affected sites fail to form pus despite serious infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A defective oxidative burst causes chronic granulomatous disease; those neutrophils reach tissue and form granulomas rather than failing to migrate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myeloperoxidase deficiency impairs hypochlorous acid generation and is usually asymptomatic, not a defect of leukocyte migration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A LYST mutation causes Chediak-Higashi syndrome with giant granules, albinism, and bleeding, not an isolated adhesion/migration defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Absent complement opsonization reduces microbial coating and lysis but does not trap neutrophils in the bloodstream.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to sort host defenses into innate and adaptive categories. Which of the following is a component of adaptive rather than innate immunity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cilia that expel pathogens from the airway

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lysozyme that digests bacterial cell walls

explanation.summary: Innate immunity is non-specific (barriers, antimicrobial substances, phagocytosis, complement); antibodies are the specific weapons of adaptive humoral immunity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Innate, or natural, immunity is non-specific and includes physical barriers such as skin, mucus, and cilia; antimicrobial substances such as lysozyme and defensins; phagocytosis with intracellular killing; and the complement system. Adaptive immunity is acquired and uses specific attacks against antigens, including antibodies produced by B cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cilia are a physical barrier of innate immunity that mechanically expel pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lysozyme is an innate antimicrobial substance that digests bacterial walls.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phagocytosis and intracellular killing are core innate functions of neutrophils and macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Complement-mediated opsonization is an innate function, although complement also participates in adaptive immunity.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman develops fever and hypotension from a bloodstream infection with a gram-negative bacillus. Endotoxin from the outer membrane of the organism triggers a surge of cytokines and chemokines. Which of the following host structures initiates this response by recognizing the endotoxin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fc receptors on circulating neutrophils and macrophages

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4 and CCR5 co-receptors on helper T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Integrins on leukocytes migrating from the bloodstream

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toll-like receptors on phagocytes and dendritic cells

explanation.summary: Lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) is a pathogen-associated molecular pattern recognized by toll-like receptors, whose activation leads to cytokine and chemokine release.
explanation.whyCorrect: The innate immune system reacts to pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), including peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls and lipopolysaccharide (LPS, endotoxin) in the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria. PAMPs are recognized by toll-like receptors (TLR) on phagocytic and dendritic cells, and activation of these receptors leads to cytokine and chemokine release.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fc receptors engage the Fc portion of bound IgG to trigger phagocytosis; they do not recognize LPS directly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 with CCR5 is the entry receptor complex that HIV gp120 exploits, not a pattern-recognition receptor for endotoxin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epitope-specific lymphocyte receptors belong to adaptive immunity and recognize specific antigenic sites, not conserved molecular patterns.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Integrins mediate leukocyte adhesion to endothelium for migration into tissue; they do not sense endotoxin.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A researcher studying innate antimicrobial substances at an epithelial surface isolates a class of small peptides that kill bacteria by disrupting their membranes. Which of the following is the substance most likely isolated?

explanation.summary: Defensins are innate antimicrobial substances that disrupt bacterial membranes, in contrast to lysozyme, which digests bacterial walls.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the antimicrobial substances of innate immunity, lysozyme digests bacterial walls and defensins disrupt bacterial membranes. A membrane-disrupting antibacterial peptide therefore corresponds to defensins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lysozyme acts by digesting bacterial cell walls rather than disrupting membranes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Myeloperoxidase is a heme-containing neutrophil granule enzyme that converts hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interferons are cytokines released by virus-infected cells that block viral protein synthesis; they are not antibacterial membrane-disrupting peptides.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Perforin is secreted by natural killer cells to kill virus-infected host cells, not an epithelial antibacterial substance.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent bacterial infections. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates an inherited deficiency of complement component C3, while neutrophil counts, neutrophil oxidative burst, and leukocyte migration are all normal. Which of the following innate processes is most directly impaired in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Generation of hypochlorous acid in neutrophil granules

choices.label: B
choices.text: Integrin-mediated adhesion of leukocytes to endothelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recognition of molecular patterns by toll-like receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Non-specific coating of pathogens to enhance phagocytosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of toxic granule contents by cytotoxic lymphocytes

explanation.summary: Complement deficiency impairs opsonization, the non-specific coating of pathogens in complement (specifically C3b) that enhances phagocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phagocytosis is enhanced with the aid of the complement system through opsonization, in which certain pathogens are non-specifically coated in complement. Complement, specifically C3b, is critical for opsonization, so complement deficiency is characterized by impaired opsonization.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hypochlorous acid generation depends on myeloperoxidase, not complement, and is intact here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Integrin-mediated adhesion is the defect of leukocyte adhesion deficiency; leukocyte migration is normal in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Toll-like receptor recognition of PAMPs is independent of complement components.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Release of granule contents by cytotoxic lymphocytes depends on the lysosomal trafficking regulator protein, not on C3.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man develops a pulmonary infection with Histoplasma capsulatum. Biopsy shows the fungus living within the phagolysosomes of macrophages, where it modulates its local environment in order to survive. Which of the following host killing mechanisms does this fungus most directly counteract?

explanation.summary: Histoplasma capsulatum survives inside phagocytes by modulating phagolysosomal pH, neutralizing the acidic environment that normally contributes to intracellular killing.
explanation.whyCorrect: After phagocytosis, intracellular killing is accomplished with reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, lysosomal enzymes, and acidic pH. Interference with phagolysosomal killing is a pathogen survival strategy, and Histoplasma capsulatum, a fungus, modulates phagolysosomal pH to survive.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Nitric oxide is one of the intracellular killing tools, but pH modulation is the specific strategy described for Histoplasma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reactive oxygen species generation by NADPH oxidase is the target of chronic granulomatous disease, not the mechanism countered by Histoplasma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lysosomal enzymes participate in killing, but Histoplasma is described as altering pH rather than degrading enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypochlorous acid formation by myeloperoxidase is a neutrophil granule reaction and is not the mechanism Histoplasma modulates.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has a chronic cough with an apical cavitary lung lesion. Acid-fast bacilli are found alive within alveolar macrophages that have engulfed them. Which of the following best explains how these organisms survive after being phagocytosed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Escape from the phagosome with a pore-forming toxin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Binding of the Fc portion of IgG on the cell surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secretion of capsular material into the tissue

explanation.summary: Mycobacteria survive in macrophages by inhibiting phagolysosome formation, one of several strategies for interfering with phagolysosomal killing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Interference with phagolysosomal killing is a strategy employed by pathogens to survive. Mycobacteria inhibit phagolysosome formation, whereas Histoplasma capsulatum modulates phagolysosomal pH and Listeria monocytogenes escapes the phagosome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phagosomal escape with a pore-forming toxin (listeriolysin O) is the strategy of Listeria monocytogenes, not mycobacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Modulating phagolysosomal pH is the survival strategy of the fungus Histoplasma capsulatum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Binding the Fc portion of IgG is the Protein A mechanism of Staphylococcus aureus, which blocks phagocytosis rather than allowing intracellular survival.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Secretion of capsular material is a Cryptococcus neoformans strategy that interferes with phagocytosis before engulfment.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A fungal pathogen engulfed by macrophages survives and proliferates slowly inside the non-activated cells. Intracellular killing begins only after the macrophages are stimulated by a cytokine released from helper T cells. Which of the following is that cytokine?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interferon gamma from helper T cells

explanation.summary: Helper T cells activate macrophages with interferon gamma, an adaptive contribution that initiates intracellular killing of organisms surviving in non-activated macrophages.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once engulfed, many bacteria and fungi can survive and proliferate slowly in non-activated macrophages. Cytokine-mediated activation of macrophages by helper T cells, a contribution from adaptive immunity, helps to initiate intracellular killing; the cytokine named is interferon gamma (IFN-gamma).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chemokines attract the migration of inflammatory cells rather than activating macrophage killing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Perforin is secreted by natural killer cells to kill virus-infected host cells; it is not a helper T-cell activating cytokine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granzymes are proteolytic enzymes delivered by natural killer cells to induce apoptosis, not macrophage activators.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Listeriolysin O is a bacterial pore-forming toxin used by Listeria to escape the phagosome.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man develops gastrointestinal distress after eating soft cheese, and Listeria monocytogenes is subsequently cultured from his blood. The organism is able to induce its own uptake into non-immune enterocytes as an endocytic vacuole. Which of the following bacterial proteins mediates this entry?

explanation.summary: Listeria monocytogenes uses internalin to induce its uptake by both phagocytes and non-immune cells such as enterocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. monocytogenes is an intracellular pathogen able to induce uptake by phagocytic cells, such as macrophages, and non-immune cells, such as enterocytes, using internalin. It enters as an endocytic vacuole and only afterward uses other proteins to escape and spread.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Listeriolysin O is the pore-forming toxin used to escape the endocytic vacuole after entry, not to enter the cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Act A drives actin polymerization that propels the bacterium through the cytosol and into the next cell after it has already entered.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protein A is a Staphylococcus aureus surface protein that binds the Fc portion of IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pilin is the Neisseria pilus protein subject to antigenic variation, not a Listeria entry protein.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student has an inherited deficiency of the terminal complement components (C5b through C9) and develops recurrent bloodstream infections. Which of the following complement functions is lost in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Opsonization of bacteria for enhanced phagocytosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attraction of inflammatory cells by chemokines

choices.label: D
choices.text: Formation of a pore that lyses the bacterium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Presentation of peptides on MHC class I

explanation.summary: The terminal complement components assemble the membrane attack complex, a transmembrane pore through bacterial membranes that lyses the target microbe.
explanation.whyCorrect: The complement system, in addition to opsonization, forms the membrane attack complex, a transmembrane pore through bacterial membranes that functions to lyse the target microbe. The pore is assembled from C5b, C6, C7, C8, and C9, so loss of these terminal components abolishes complement-mediated lysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Opsonization depends on C3b coating the pathogen and is not carried out by the terminal components that form the pore.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Attraction of inflammatory cells is the function of chemokines, not of the membrane attack complex.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Degradation of mRNA is an interferon-induced antiviral action via ribonuclease, unrelated to complement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peptide presentation on MHC class I is a host-cell antigen presentation function, not a complement activity.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: IgG antibodies bind to the surface of a bacterium in the bloodstream. Complement is then activated on the bacterial surface, leading to enhanced phagocytosis, leukocyte activation, and lysis of the organism. Through which of the following pathways do the antibodies activate complement?

explanation.summary: Antibodies activate complement through the classical pathway, which is how complement, though non-specific itself, interacts with adaptive immunity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibodies activate complement through the classical pathway. This leads to downstream effects such as enhanced phagocytosis, leukocyte activation, and formation of the membrane attack complex for bacterial lysis, so complement, though non-specific in itself, also interacts with adaptive immunity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The alternative pathway is not the antibody-triggered route of complement activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The lectin pathway is not initiated by bound antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interferons act on neighboring cells to block viral protein synthesis; they are not a complement activation pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toll-like receptors recognize PAMPs and trigger cytokine release; they do not activate the complement cascade via antibody.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A large foreign protein entering the body has many different recognizable sites on its surface, but a given antibody binds only one small portion of it. Which of the following terms describes that specific binding site?

explanation.summary: The epitope is the smaller recognizable portion of an antigen where the antibody or lymphocyte receptor binds.
explanation.whyCorrect: Humoral immunity utilizes specific antibodies produced by B cells. The smaller, recognizable portion of the antigen, the place where the antibody binds, is known as the epitope. An antigen may have many recognizable sites, but a particular lymphocyte receptor recognizes only the epitope it is programmed to bind.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The antigen is the whole foreign molecule; the question asks for the specific site on it that is bound.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adhesins are pathogen surface molecules that bind host cell receptors for attachment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An opsonin (such as complement) coats a pathogen to enhance phagocytosis; it is not a site on the antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pathogen-associated molecular patterns are conserved microbial structures recognized non-specifically by toll-like receptors.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A pathogenic bacterium uses adhesins located on its pili to attach to the surface of human epithelial cells as the first major step in establishing infection. Which of the following host molecules are the most common receptors for these pili?

choices.label: D
choices.text: MHC class I and MHC class II

explanation.summary: Mannose and fibronectin are widely expressed on human epithelial cells and serve as common receptors for pathogenic pili.
explanation.whyCorrect: For bacteria and fungi, adherence depends on adhesins on the pathogen and receptors on host cells. Pili are appendages that feature adhesins and are used by the microbe to stick to the host, and mannose and fibronectin are widely expressed on human epithelial cells and are common receptors for pathogenic pili.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4 with the chemokine co-receptor CXCR4 is the entry receptor for HIV gp120, not a receptor for bacterial pili.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peptidoglycan and lipopolysaccharide are bacterial components (PAMPs), not host epithelial receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MHC molecules present peptides to T cells and are not the epithelial receptors targeted by pili.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lysozyme and defensins are host antimicrobial substances that attack bacteria rather than serving as attachment receptors.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man who injects drugs presents with fever and a new heart murmur. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus, and echocardiography shows a bulky vegetation on a valve. The organism initially attached at a site of endothelial injury using adhesin surface receptors. Which of the following host proteins deposited at the injured site do these adhesins bind?

explanation.summary: S. aureus adhesins bind fibrinogen and fibronectin deposited at sites of endothelial injury, initiating the vegetation of endocarditis.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. aureus uses adhesin surface receptors against fibrinogen and fibronectin. In endocarditis, these bind deposited proteins at a site of endothelial injury within the heart; bacterial binding and proliferation then lead to increased cytokine signaling, an inflammatory response, and deposition of thrombotic material, producing the bulky vegetation. Parts of the vegetation can embolize into the bloodstream, causing further dissemination and even infarcts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mannose is an epithelial receptor for pathogenic pili, and MHC class I presents peptides to T cells; neither is the deposited protein bound by staphylococcal adhesins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Peptidoglycan and lipopolysaccharide are bacterial cell-wall components, not host proteins at an injury site.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C3b and IgG are opsonins that coat the bacterium; they are not the adhesin targets that anchor it to injured endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CD4 and CCR5 are the receptors HIV uses to enter helper T cells, unrelated to bacterial adherence in endocarditis.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: In a cell culture experiment, interferon released by virus-infected cells reaches neighboring uninfected cells. The infected cells stop synthesizing protein and die, yet the uninfected cells exposed to the same interferon continue normal protein synthesis unharmed. Which of the following best explains why the uninfected cells are spared?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Interferon receptors are expressed only on infected cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interferon is degraded before it reaches uninfected cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The interferon-induced enzymes require dsRNA to function

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uninfected cells lack the initiation factor eIF-2

explanation.summary: The downstream interferon-induced enzymes must have double-stranded RNA to function, so only virus-infected cells shut down protein synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Interferons activate 2'-5' oligosynthetase, which induces a ribonuclease in the presence of dsRNA, and protein kinases, which inhibit eIF-2 in the presence of dsRNA. Without protein synthesis the virus cannot replicate but the infected cell also dies. Because these downstream enzymes must have dsRNA, which is present only during viral replication, non-infected cells are protected from destruction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Interferons act on neighboring cells generally; the selectivity comes from the dsRNA requirement, not from restricted receptor expression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Uninfected cells can be induced to make the enzymes; the enzymes simply remain inactive without dsRNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interferon does reach and act on neighboring cells; degradation is not the explanation for sparing them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: eIF-2 is a normal protein synthesis initiation factor in all cells; it is inhibited only when protein kinase is activated by dsRNA.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A poxvirus is found to secrete soluble proteins that mimic host cytokines and cytokine receptors, sequestering host cytokines and chemokines and blunting complement-mediated defense while infected cells continue to proliferate. Which of the following terms describes these viral products?

explanation.summary: Poxviruses produce decoy proteins and receptors called virokines and viroreceptors that interfere with cytokine, chemokine, and complement-mediated host defense.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytokines are important to defense against viruses, but some viruses produce proteins that interfere with cytokine, chemokine, and complement-mediated host defense. Poxviruses, for example, produce decoy proteins and receptors, known as virokines and viroreceptors, that can cause cells to proliferate while avoiding host defenses.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Adhesins and pili are bacterial and fungal attachment structures, not viral decoy proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Perforins and granzymes are host natural killer cell products that kill virus-infected cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Opsonins coat pathogens for phagocytosis and epitopes are antigen binding sites; neither is a viral decoy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Internalin and listeriolysin O are Listeria monocytogenes proteins for cell entry and phagosomal escape.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: Cells infected with adenovirus are observed to resist apoptosis, allowing the virus to continue replicating. The viral protein E1B-19K is responsible for this effect. Which of the following host proteins does E1B-19K mimic?

explanation.summary: Adenovirus E1B-19K mimics BCL-2, an important anti-apoptotic protein, allowing infected cells to resist cell death.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some viruses resist cell death of the infected cell. Adenovirus produces E1B-19K, which mimics BCL-2, an important anti-apoptotic protein, so the infected cell does not undergo apoptosis and viral production can continue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: eIF-2 is the protein synthesis initiation factor inhibited by interferon-activated protein kinases; mimicking it would not block apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 2'-5' oligosynthetase is an interferon-induced enzyme that leads to mRNA degradation; it is not anti-apoptotic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Granzymes are proteolytic enzymes from natural killer cells that drive apoptosis, the opposite of the effect described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interferon gamma is a cytokine that activates macrophages; it is not the anti-apoptotic protein mimicked by E1B-19K.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A Neisseria isolate from a patient with a recurrent infection is found to express several different OPA surface proteins at once, some sufficiently altered that antibodies from the prior episode no longer recognize them. Sequencing of the OPA gene shows many repeats of a five-nucleotide sequence. Which of the following mechanisms best accounts for this antigenic variation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recombination of a silent pilin variant next to the promoter

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deletions and duplications within the repetitive sequence

choices.label: C
choices.text: Escape from the phagosome using a pore-forming toxin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secretion of capsular material into surrounding tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blockade of peptide loading onto MHC class I

explanation.summary: The second Neisseria antigenic-variation strategy relies on the repetitive OPA gene, whose five-nucleotide repeats make it vulnerable to deletions and duplications that alter the expressed proteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Besides homologous recombination of the pilin gene, Neisseria spp. achieve antigenic variance through mutations of the OPA gene. The OPA gene has many repeats of a five-nucleotide sequence, making it vulnerable to genetic deletions and duplications. These mutational changes can lead to expression of altered proteins or even multiple OPA proteins at once, some sufficiently different from previous epitopes to avoid antibody detection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Placing a silent pilin coding sequence next to the promoter describes pilin antigenic variation, not the OPA repeat-driven mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phagosomal escape with a pore-forming toxin is the Listeria monocytogenes strategy against phagolysosomal killing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Capsule secretion is a Cryptococcus neoformans strategy that interferes with phagocytosis, not a mechanism of changing surface antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blocking peptide loading onto MHC class I is a herpes simplex virus tactic against T cells, not a bacterial mutational mechanism.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman receiving immunosuppressive treatment following a kidney transplant develops a disseminated fungal infection. Antigen presentation by dendritic cells and macrophages and the helper cell responses that normally combat such infections are blunted by her medications. Which of the following arms of host defense is most critically compromised?

explanation.summary: T-cell mediated responses are critical to combating many fungal infections, so immunosuppressive states such as post-transplant therapy are permissive to fungal disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: T-cell mediated responses are critical to combatting many fungal infections, including antigen presentation by dendritic cells and macrophages for the stimulation of antifungal antibodies as well as helper T-cell mediated actions. Immunosuppressive states are permissive to fungal and other infections and include corticosteroids, immunosuppressive treatments following transplantation, and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement opsonization is an innate function and is not the T-cell dependent arm highlighted as critical against fungi.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypochlorous acid production by myeloperoxidase is a neutrophil granule function; its isolated deficiency is usually asymptomatic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgE antibodies are the humoral response characteristic of parasitic infections, not the key antifungal defense.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Interferon-induced blockade of protein synthesis is an innate antiviral mechanism rather than an antifungal defense.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy who recently traveled abroad has abdominal pain, and stool examination reveals a parasitic worm infection. A complete blood count shows a markedly increased eosinophil count. Which of the following antibody classes is characteristically produced in the humoral response to this type of infection?

explanation.summary: The humoral response to parasites is characterized by IgE antibodies, and eosinophils are commonly seen in parasitic infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: The humoral response to parasites includes the production of IgE antibodies, and eosinophils are commonly seen in parasitic infections. A helminth infection with eosinophilia therefore points to an IgE-dominated humoral response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgG is the antibody whose Fc portion is bound by staphylococcal Protein A; it is not the class characteristic of the anti-parasite response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgA is not the antibody class the brick associates with parasitic infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgM is not the antibody class characteristically linked with parasites and eosinophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgD is not the class associated with the anti-parasite humoral response.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man returning from sub-Saharan Africa develops fever, lymphadenopathy, and progressive daytime somnolence; Trypanosoma brucei is identified on a blood smear. Serum studies show a large quantity of immunoglobulins that fail to neutralize the parasite. Which of the following best describes how this organism evades adaptive immunity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Polyclonal B-cell activation yielding non-specific antibody

choices.label: B
choices.text: Homologous recombination among silent pilin gene variants

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surface protein binding to the Fc portion of host IgG

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blockade of peptide loading onto MHC class I molecules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretion of polysaccharide capsule material into tissue

explanation.summary: Trypanosoma brucei, the cause of African sleeping sickness, exhausts the humoral response by inducing polyclonal B cells to produce non-specific immunoglobulins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Trypanosoma brucei, the cause of African sleeping sickness, activates polyclonal B-cells to produce non-specific antibodies. This exhausts the immune system through the induction of polyclonal B-cells producing non-specific immunoglobulins, so abundant antibody is made yet the parasite is not effectively targeted.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Homologous recombination of pilin variants is the antigenic variation strategy of Neisseria spp., not a trypanosome mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Binding the Fc portion of IgG is the Protein A mechanism of Staphylococcus aureus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking peptide loading onto MHC class I is the herpes simplex virus tactic against T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Secreting capsule material is a Cryptococcus neoformans strategy against phagocytosis, unrelated to B-cell exhaustion.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: Examination of a parasite recovered from a patient shows that its surface is coated with the patient's own antigens and immunoglobulins, and the host immune system fails to mount an effective attack against it. This finding best represents which of the following evasion strategies?

explanation.summary: Some parasites camouflage themselves with host antigens and immunoglobulins so that they are not detected as foreign.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some parasites are able to camouflage themselves with host antigens and immunoglobulins to avoid detection. Because the parasite surface appears to be self, the adaptive immune system does not recognize and attack it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antigenic variation involves switching the parasite's own surface antigens, as Neisseria does with pilin and OPA, rather than borrowing host molecules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Exhaustion of polyclonal B cells is the Trypanosoma brucei strategy of inducing non-specific antibody production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interference with complement deposition is the function of polysaccharide capsules on bacteria and fungi.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting phagolysosome formation is the intracellular survival tactic of mycobacteria.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has recurrent herpes simplex virus type 1 lesions. Studies of her infected cells show that although viral peptides are produced, the cells display very little MHC class I on their surface and are poorly recognized by cytotoxic CD8+ T cells. Which of the following steps does HSV-1 block to achieve this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Presentation of peptides on MHC class II

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loading of peptides onto MHC class I

choices.label: C
choices.text: Production of interferon by the infected cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release of perforin by natural killer cells

explanation.summary: HSV-1 evades T cells by blocking peptide loading onto MHC-I and preventing MHC-I from reaching the cell surface.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some DNA viruses can alter major histocompatibility complexes to avoid destruction by T-cells. HSV-1 can block peptide loading onto MHC-I and also prevent it from getting to the surface, helping the infected cell evade detection by circulating immune cells such as cytotoxic CD8+ T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MHC class II presentation is not the pathway HSV-1 is described as blocking; the evasion targets MHC-I recognized by CD8+ T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV-1's described strategy is interference with antigen presentation, not suppression of interferon production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Natural killer cells are triggered by absent MHC class I; HSV-1 does not act by blocking perforin release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Complement opsonization of virions is not the step described in HSV-1 evasion of T-cell detection.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has had clusters of painful vesicles on the same area of his lip about three times a year for several years, typically during periods of stress. Between episodes he is entirely well and the lesions resolve completely. Which of the following best explains the recurrent episodes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: New infection from a different exposure each time

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antigenic variation of the viral surface proteins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reactivation of virus from a latent state

choices.label: D
choices.text: Exhaustion of polyclonal B cells by the virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Continuous viral replication in the bloodstream

explanation.summary: Herpes labialis recurs because the virus persists in a latent state, lying dormant, with intermittent reactivation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some viruses persist in a latent state, or lying dormant, and later reactivate. Recurrent herpes labialis reflects this intermittent sequence of latency and reactivation of herpes simplex virus at the same site, rather than a new infection each time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Recurrence at the identical site with complete resolution between episodes reflects reactivation of a persistent virus, not repeated new exposures.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antigenic variation is a Neisseria strategy for escaping antibodies; it does not explain periodic lesions from a dormant virus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polyclonal B-cell exhaustion is the mechanism of Trypanosoma brucei, not of recurrent herpes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The patient is well between episodes, which is inconsistent with continuous replication; the virus is dormant until reactivation.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl with recurrent pyogenic infections has light-blonde hair with a metallic sheen and numerous bruises on her arms and legs. Genetic testing confirms a mutation in the LYST gene. Which of the following best explains her bleeding tendency?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired release of granules by neutrophils

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of platelets to release dense granules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of melanosome release by melanocytes

explanation.summary: In Chediak-Higashi syndrome, platelets cannot release their dense granules, which aid coagulation, so patients bleed and bruise easily.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chediak-Higashi syndrome results from a defective lysosomal trafficking regulator protein due to LYST mutations. Beyond granulocytes, other cells are affected: platelets are unable to release platelet dense granules, which aid in coagulation, leading to increased bleeding. The same trafficking defect explains the hypopigmented hair with a metallic sheen and the recurrent infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The defect is in granule release, not platelet number; thrombocytopenia is not the described mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulation factor deficiency is not part of the syndrome; the problem is the platelet dense granules that aid coagulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Impaired release of neutrophil granules explains the recurrent infections, not the bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Failure of melanosome release explains the hypopigmentation of skin, eyes, and hair, not the bruising.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with several months of cough and weight loss undergoes lung biopsy. When the tissue is stained and then treated with acid-alcohol, slender rod-shaped organisms retain the stain and appear pink. Which structural feature is most responsible for this staining property?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A waxy cell wall containing mycolic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ability to form dormant endospores

explanation.summary: M. tuberculosis is acid-fast because of mycolic acid in its cell wall.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. tuberculosis is an aerobic rod with a waxy cell wall that includes mycolic acid. This feature causes the organism to retain stain after treatment with acid-alcohol, which is why it is called acid-fast and is highlighted by the acid-fast bacilli (AFB) special stain.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A polysaccharide capsule is a virulence feature of other bacteria and does not account for acid-fastness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A lipopolysaccharide outer membrane characterizes gram-negative bacteria, not the acid-fast mycobacterial wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Corkscrew morphology describes the spirochete Treponema pallidum, not M. tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: M. tuberculosis does not form endospores; its stain retention is due to mycolic acid.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: M. tuberculosis is phagocytosed by a nonactivated alveolar macrophage but is not destroyed and instead replicates inside the cell. Which mechanism best explains how the organism avoids intracytoplasmic killing?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It secretes an IgA protease that cleaves mucosal antibody

choices.label: C
choices.text: It integrates its genome into the host cell DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: It forms spores that resist lysosomal enzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: It uses corkscrew motility to escape into the cytoplasm

explanation.summary: M. tuberculosis survives in macrophages by blocking phagolysosome maturation.
explanation.whyCorrect: After entering nonactivated macrophages via mannose-binding lectin and CR3, M. tuberculosis avoids intracytoplasmic killing by preventing phagolysosomal formation and by halting acidification and reactive oxygen species production. It is then left to replicate within the protection of the intracellular vesicle.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IgA protease is a mucosal evasion strategy of other pathogens and is not the mechanism described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Genome integration is characteristic of certain viruses, not of M. tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M. tuberculosis does not form spores; it blocks phagolysosome function instead.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Corkscrew motility describes Treponema pallidum, not intracellular mycobacterial survival.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with active pulmonary tuberculosis has a lung lesion resected. On gross examination the lesion is friable, cheesy, and white; microscopically there is central necrosis surrounded by epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells. Which term best describes this classic histologic feature of active tuberculosis?

explanation.summary: Caseating granulomas are the classic histologic finding of active tuberculosis.
