explanation.whyCorrect: The ongoing immune attack against M. tuberculosis within granulomas produces necrosis, manifesting as caseating granulomas. These are friable, cheesy, and white grossly, and show central necrosis with epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells microscopically.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythema nodosum refers to painful red nodules of the lower extremities that may rarely accompany primary tuberculosis, not the granuloma itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrosis is a nonspecific reparative change seen in many processes, including healing mycobacterial disease, but it is not the classic active lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gummas are granulomatous nodules of tertiary syphilis, not tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Condylomata lata are elevated plaques of secondary syphilis, unrelated to tuberculosis.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A healthcare worker receives an intradermal injection of tuberculin. Because she was exposed to tuberculosis in the past, an erythematous, indurated reaction develops at the injection site 48 to 72 hours later. This reaction is mediated by which type of hypersensitivity?

explanation.summary: The tuberculin (PPD) skin test reflects a Type IV, Th1 cell-mediated response.
explanation.whyCorrect: If a person has been exposed to tuberculosis, injecting tuberculin triggers a cell-mediated Th1-cell response, a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction, producing an erythematous reaction at the injection site within 48 to 72 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Type I reactions are immediate and IgE-mediated, occurring within minutes, not over 48 to 72 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type II involves antibody directed against cell-surface antigens, which is not the basis of the delayed skin test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type III involves immune complex deposition and does not explain the delayed T-cell reaction to tuberculin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reaction is an adaptive T-cell response, not a purely innate complement-mediated one.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: After tuberculosis antigens drain into lymph nodes, a pro-inflammatory cytokine stimulates naive T-cells to differentiate into T helper type 1 (Th1) cells, which then coordinate the antimycobacterial response. Which cytokine drives this Th1 differentiation?

explanation.summary: IL-12 promotes differentiation of naive T-cells into Th1 cells in tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tuberculosis antigens draining into lymph nodes trigger production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-12, which stimulates naive T-cells to differentiate into Th1 cells. Th1 cells then produce IFN-gamma to activate macrophages.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-4 drives Th2 differentiation, which is not the protective response emphasized against M. tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-5 supports eosinophil responses, not Th1 differentiation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-10 is generally immunosuppressive and dampens, rather than drives, the Th1 response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta has regulatory and fibrotic roles and does not promote Th1 differentiation here.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with HIV develops fever, night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis years after a resolved primary tuberculosis infection. Chest imaging shows cavitary disease. In this reactivation (secondary) tuberculosis, the lesions most characteristically involve which location?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The upper apices of the lungs

choices.label: B
choices.text: The right hilar lymph nodes only

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pleural space without lung involvement

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lung bases with a peripheral wedge shape

choices.label: E
choices.text: The vertebral bodies of the spine

explanation.summary: Secondary (reactivation) tuberculosis characteristically involves the upper lung apices.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary pulmonary tuberculosis tends to manifest in the upper apices of the lungs. Because the immune system is already primed, it prompts a robust response with erosion and cavitation of lung parenchyma and fibrosis, and symptoms include night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Right hilar lymphadenopathy is a feature of primary tuberculosis, not the apical cavitary lesions of reactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pleural effusions can occur, but secondary disease characteristically involves the upper lung apices, not isolated pleura.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A basilar wedge-shaped lesion is not the classic pattern of secondary tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vertebral involvement describes Pott disease, an extrapulmonary form, not the typical apical reactivation site.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 60-year-old immunocompromised man dies of an overwhelming infection. At autopsy the spleen, liver, and bone marrow are studded with numerous small tan-white tubercles resembling scattered millet seeds. Which process best explains these findings?

explanation.summary: Widespread millet-seed-like tubercles across multiple organs indicate miliary tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The term miliary refers to the resemblance to millet seeds and describes unchecked tuberculosis that accesses the lymphatic and venous blood supplies, seeding organs such as the lung, liver, bone marrow, spleen, adrenal glands, or kidneys. Progressive dissemination throughout the bloodstream to multiple organs is termed systemic miliary tuberculosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Latent tuberculosis is asymptomatic and contained, without widespread organ seeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary tuberculosis is the first, often unrecognized infection and does not usually produce disseminated millet-seed nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pott disease is isolated vertebral tuberculosis, not multiorgan seeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Erythema nodosum refers to tender skin nodules, not disseminated organ tubercles.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with a single genital lesion that appeared about three weeks after unprotected intercourse. The lesion is solitary, painless, erythematous, and has a sharp border with an ulcerative base. Which finding is most suggestive of primary syphilis?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A maculopapular rash of the palms and soles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Raised, moist tan-white plaques of intertriginous areas

explanation.summary: The chancre, a solitary painless ulcer, is the key finding of primary syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The chancre is the key clinical finding in primary syphilis. It is usually solitary, occurs at the site of the original infection (often the genitals), and is painless and erythematous, typically with a sharp border and an ulcerative base, appearing about three weeks after infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A maculopapular rash of the palms and soles is characteristic of secondary syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multiple painful vesicles suggest herpes simplex virus infection, not the painless syphilitic chancre.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Annular plaques of the face are described in secondary syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Raised moist plaques of intertriginous areas are condylomata lata, a feature of secondary syphilis.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman develops a symmetric maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles, along with moist elevated plaques in the anogenital region and mild fever, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy. Her genital ulcer resolved several weeks earlier. Which stage of syphilis does this presentation represent?

explanation.summary: A palm-and-sole rash with condylomata lata and constitutional symptoms marks secondary syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary syphilis manifests 2 to 8 weeks after the chancre and is characterized by multiple lesions, including maculopapular rashes often of the palms and soles, and condylomata lata (elevated plaques of intertriginous areas). Constitutional signs include sore throat, lymphadenopathy, mild fever, and malaise.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Primary syphilis is defined by a single painless chancre, which had already resolved in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Latent syphilis is continued infection in the absence of clinical symptoms, not an active rash.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tertiary syphilis appears years later with gummas, cardiovascular, or neurologic disease, not an acute rash.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Congenital syphilis results from vertical transmission to a fetus, not this adult presentation.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a remote history of untreated syphilis is found to have a new diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation and imaging showing dilation of the aortic root and an ascending aortic aneurysm. Which process best accounts for these cardiovascular findings?

explanation.summary: Cardiovascular tertiary syphilis causes aortitis with root dilation, regurgitation, and aneurysm.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cardiovascular syphilis accounts for most cases of tertiary syphilis. Inflammation of the aorta leads to dilation of the aortic root and arch, resulting in valvular insufficiency and aortic regurgitation, and aneurysms can form in the aorta, predisposing to dissection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mitral stenosis from rheumatic disease is a distinct valvular process not caused by syphilitic aortitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Although coronary ostial stenosis can occur in syphilis, atherosclerotic plaque rupture is a separate mechanism and does not explain the aortic root dilation and regurgitation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pulmonary arterial hypertension does not produce aortic root dilation or aortic regurgitation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral pericarditis causes an effusion, not aortic root dilation, aneurysm, and regurgitation.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is brought in for progressive memory and judgment decline. On exam his pupils are small and, although they constrict when he focuses on a finger held near his nose, they do not react to light. He also has red-purple facial nodules containing friable tan-yellow material. Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?

explanation.summary: Argyll Robertson pupils, dementia, and facial gummas point to tertiary neurosyphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Argyll Robertson pupil accommodates to near objects but does not react to light and is a classic sign of advanced (tertiary) syphilis. Paretic neurosyphilis follows T. pallidum invasion of the brain with progressive cognitive decline, and the friable facial nodules are gummas of tertiary syphilis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Primary syphilis presents with a painless chancre, not dementia and pupillary abnormalities.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Secondary syphilis features rashes and constitutional symptoms, not Argyll Robertson pupils and gummas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Latent syphilis is asymptomatic by definition, so it cannot explain these active neurologic findings.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tuberculous meningitis does not produce Argyll Robertson pupils or cutaneous gummas.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child born to a mother with untreated syphilis has notched, peg-shaped teeth, clouding of the cornea from interstitial keratitis, and progressive hearing loss. Which finding is characteristic of congenital syphilis rather than acquired adult syphilis?

explanation.summary: Hutchinson (notched) teeth are a late finding specific to congenital syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Late congenital syphilis may manifest as interstitial keratitis, eighth cranial nerve deafness, and bone or teeth abnormalities. Notched or peg-shaped teeth, called Hutchinson teeth, are characteristic of congenital syphilis and are not a feature of acquired adult syphilis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Condylomata lata may be seen in secondary syphilis or congenital syphilis, so they are not specific to congenital disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A painless chancre is the hallmark of acquired primary syphilis in adults.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gummas occur in tertiary (adult) syphilis and can also occur congenitally, so they are not specific to the congenital form.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A maculopapular rash occurs in both secondary and congenital syphilis and is therefore not distinguishing.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A public health nurse investigates a cluster of tuberculosis cases among residents of a long-term care facility who share a common dayroom. Which feature of Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmission best explains why people living in close quarters are at increased risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It spreads by direct contact with infected skin lesions

choices.label: B
choices.text: It spreads in small droplets that remain airborne for hours

choices.label: C
choices.text: It spreads by ingestion of contaminated food or water

choices.label: D
choices.text: It spreads through shared needles and blood products

choices.label: E
choices.text: It spreads across the placenta from mother to fetus

explanation.summary: M. tuberculosis spreads by small bacteria-containing droplets that can stay airborne for hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. tuberculosis spreads through small, bacteria-containing droplets that can remain airborne for hours. This is why risk is increased in close quarters such as prisons, shelters for unhoused individuals, and long-term care, as well as in people with immunosuppressing disease states.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Contact with skin lesions is not the route of M. tuberculosis spread; the organism is inhaled in droplets and reaches the alveoli.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ingestion is not the route described for M. tuberculosis; airborne droplets reach the lungs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blood-borne transmission between people is not the mechanism; inhaled droplets initiate infection in the alveoli.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vertical transmission to a fetus describes congenital syphilis caused by T. pallidum, not tuberculosis spread in a care facility.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: After inhalation, a small number of M. tuberculosis organisms reach the alveoli, where they are phagocytosed by nonactivated alveolar macrophages. Interaction with which pair of host molecules mediates this phagocytic entry?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Toll-like receptor 4 and the CD14 coreceptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fc-gamma receptors and the C5a complement receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD4 and the CCR5 chemokine receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mannose-binding lectin and type 3 complement receptor (CR3)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Class II MHC and the alpha-beta T-cell receptor

explanation.summary: M. tuberculosis enters nonactivated macrophages through mannose-binding lectin and CR3.
explanation.whyCorrect: Upon exposure, M. tuberculosis in droplets reaches the alveoli and enters nonactivated macrophages via phagocytosis through interactions between mannose-binding lectin and type 3 complement receptor (CR3). Once inside, it prevents phagolysosomal formation and replicates within the protection of the intracellular vesicle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: TLR4 and CD14 recognize lipopolysaccharide of gram-negative bacteria and are not the entry interaction described for M. tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fc receptors and C5a receptor are not the receptors through which the bacillus is phagocytosed in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD4 and CCR5 are the entry receptors for HIV, not for M. tuberculosis uptake by macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Class II MHC and the T-cell receptor mediate antigen presentation to T cells later in the response, not phagocytic entry into the macrophage.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: In a patient mounting an effective response to M. tuberculosis, Th1 cells release interferon gamma (IFN-gamma), which activates infected macrophages. In addition to stimulating phagolysosomes, producing nitric oxide, and mobilizing defensins, IFN-gamma triggers which additional process that aids in killing intracellular bacteria?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autophagy of the cell's own contents

explanation.summary: IFN-gamma triggers macrophage autophagy, which helps kill intracellular M. tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Th1 cells produce IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages to attack M. tuberculosis through stimulation of the phagolysosomes, production of nitric oxide (NO), and mobilization of defensins, a type of antimicrobial peptide. Autophagy, the eating of a cell's own contents, is also triggered by IFN-gamma and aids in killing intracellular bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Class switching to IgA is a B-cell process and is not the macrophage killing mechanism activated by IFN-gamma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Histamine release from mast cells is an allergic (Type I) mechanism, not an IFN-gamma-driven antimycobacterial effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M. tuberculosis does not form endospores; this is not a host killing mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Complement lysis is not the IFN-gamma-triggered intracellular killing mechanism described; the bacillus resides inside macrophages.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with secondary pulmonary tuberculosis reports several weeks of malaise, anorexia, weight loss, fever, and night sweats. These constitutional symptoms are primarily attributed to the release of which mediator?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycolic acid from the bacillary cell wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor necrosis factor from activated macrophages

explanation.summary: The systemic symptoms of secondary tuberculosis are due to cytokine release, such as TNF from activated macrophages.
explanation.whyCorrect: Symptoms of secondary tuberculosis are due to cytokine release, such as TNF from activated macrophages, and include malaise, anorexia, weight loss, fever, and night sweats. Hemoptysis and pleuritic chest pain may also be experienced in secondary pulmonary tuberculosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Histamine mediates immediate allergic responses, not the constitutional symptoms of tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-4 drives Th2 responses; the tuberculosis response is Th1-driven and the symptoms are attributed to TNF.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgE is involved in Type I hypersensitivity and does not produce the systemic symptoms of tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mycolic acid accounts for acid-fast staining of the organism, not for the cytokine-mediated constitutional symptoms.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman who emigrated from a country where BCG vaccination is routine has a firm, erythematous, indurated reaction 48 to 72 hours after intradermal placement of tuberculin. She is asymptomatic and her chest x-ray is normal. Which statement best characterizes the interpretation of this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The reaction may reflect prior BCG vaccination rather than infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reaction confirms active pulmonary tuberculosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reaction indicates an IgE-mediated allergy to tuberculin

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reaction proves the infection is latent rather than active

choices.label: E
choices.text: The reaction indicates a Type III immune complex response

explanation.summary: The tuberculin skin test cannot distinguish active from latent infection and is also triggered by prior BCG vaccination.
explanation.whyCorrect: The tuberculosis skin test (PPD) injects tuberculin under the skin and, in a previously exposed person, produces a cell-mediated Th1 (Type IV) reaction within 48 to 72 hours. Because of this, the test cannot distinguish active or latent TB infection and is also triggered by previous BCG vaccinations that use attenuated mycobacterial strains.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A positive PPD does not confirm active disease; it only indicates prior sensitization, and this patient is asymptomatic with a normal chest x-ray.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The reaction is a delayed Type IV cell-mediated response, not an IgE-mediated (Type I) allergy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The skin test cannot distinguish latent from active infection, so it cannot prove latency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The PPD reaction is a Th1 cell-mediated Type IV hypersensitivity, not an immune complex (Type III) response.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 22-year-old college student with no prior tuberculosis exposure develops a low-grade fever, shortness of breath, and a non-productive cough after a roommate is diagnosed with tuberculosis. Which chest radiograph finding is most characteristic of this primary infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cavitation of both upper lung apices

choices.label: B
choices.text: Collapse of a thoracic vertebral body

explanation.summary: Primary tuberculosis characteristically shows unilateral (right) hilar lymphadenopathy on chest imaging.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many primary tuberculosis cases go clinically unrecognized, though some patients develop fever, shortness of breath, and a non-productive cough. Chest imaging may show lymphadenopathy that is unilateral and of the right hilar nodes; other findings include patchy opacities and pleural effusions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Apical cavitation is the pattern of secondary (reactivation) tuberculosis in a previously sensitized host, not primary infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vertebral collapse describes Pott disease, an extrapulmonary manifestation, not the typical primary chest finding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ascending aortic dilation is a feature of cardiovascular tertiary syphilis, not tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Calcified pleural plaques are not the described imaging finding of primary tuberculosis.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman recently diagnosed with primary tuberculosis develops several painful, red nodules on the front of both lower legs. Which term best describes this finding?

explanation.summary: Erythema nodosum, painful red nodules of the lower extremities, may rarely accompany primary tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Erythema nodosum refers to painful, red nodules of the lower extremities that can rarely be seen in the context of primary tuberculosis, alongside fever, shortness of breath, and non-productive cough.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Condylomata lata are elevated moist plaques of intertriginous areas in secondary syphilis, not painful shin nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A gumma is a granulomatous nodule of tertiary syphilis affecting bone, skin, and upper respiratory mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Saber shin refers to anterior bowing of the tibia in late congenital syphilis, not tender inflammatory nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A chancre is the solitary painless ulcer of primary syphilis at the site of infection.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 55-year-old asymptomatic man has a chest x-ray for an unrelated reason that shows a small, calcified granuloma in the lung. His tuberculin skin test is negative. Besides a healed mycobacterial infection, infection with which organism is the most likely alternative explanation for this finding?

explanation.summary: Old calcified granulomas may result from other granuloma-forming infections such as the fungus Histoplasma capsulatum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because granulomatous inflammation is damaging, resolution of a tuberculosis infection typically leaves a scar that may calcify over time. Old, calcified granulomas and scarring visualized on chest imaging could also be due to other granuloma-forming infections, such as Histoplasma capsulatum, a fungus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: T. pallidum causes syphilis; it is not the alternative cause of a calcified pulmonary granuloma described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: S. pneumoniae causes acute pneumonia and is not described as a granuloma-forming infection that leaves calcified lung scars.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Influenza is a viral respiratory infection that does not produce calcified granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Candida is not the granuloma-forming fungus described as a mimic of healed tuberculosis on chest imaging.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man had primary tuberculosis 10 years ago that resolved without symptoms. After volunteering in a shelter where several residents had active tuberculosis, he develops night sweats and hemoptysis, and imaging shows cavitation and fibrosis of the upper lobes. His physician notes the disease could represent either reactivation or reinfection. Which host feature best explains the cavitary, destructive tissue response in this episode compared with his initial infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prior sensitization of the immune system to mycobacterial antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of Th1 cell function acquired during the interval

choices.label: C
choices.text: Absence of IFN-gamma production by his T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of his macrophages to form granulomas

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased mycolic acid content of the new bacilli

explanation.summary: Secondary tuberculosis occurs in a previously sensitized host, whose primed immune system mounts a robust, cavitating tissue response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary infections refer to any time tuberculosis arises in a previously sensitized host, either from reactivation of latent mycobacteria or from reinfection with new mycobacteria from an external source. Because the immune system is already primed to attack the infection, secondary tuberculosis typically prompts a robust tissue response with erosion and cavitation of lung parenchyma and fibrosis, usually in the upper apices.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of Th1 function would weaken, not intensify, the tissue-destructive response; the cavitation reflects a primed immune response.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IFN-gamma drives the macrophage activation and granuloma formation responsible for the response; its absence does not explain cavitation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granuloma formation with necrosis is exactly what produces the destructive lesions; failure to form granulomas is not the explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The bacterial cell wall composition does not differ; the difference is the host's prior sensitization.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy has months of fever, back pain, and a progressive deformity of his spine. Imaging shows destruction of adjacent thoracic vertebral bodies, and biopsy demonstrates caseating granulomas containing acid-fast bacilli. Which term best describes this isolated manifestation of tuberculosis?

explanation.summary: Pott disease is vertebral involvement by tuberculosis and can cause spinal deformity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tuberculosis may manifest in isolated organs or regions. Pott disease refers to vertebral involvement by tuberculosis, a possible consequence of advanced infection affecting the spine that can produce spinal deformity, as in an 8-year-old child.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Miliary tuberculosis is widespread seeding of many organs via the bloodstream, not isolated vertebral disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythema nodosum refers to painful red nodules of the lower extremities, a skin finding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The primary complex refers to the localized lung lesion and its draining lymph node in primary infection, not spinal disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Latent tuberculosis is asymptomatic contained infection, not active destructive disease of bone.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A biopsy of a painless genital ulcer is examined with a special stain, which reveals slender, corkscrew-shaped organisms that appear black against the surrounding tissue. Which stain was most likely used?

explanation.summary: T. pallidum, a spirochete with corkscrew morphology, is highlighted as black on silver special stain.
explanation.whyCorrect: T. pallidum is a spirochete with a spiral or corkscrew-like morphology and is the causative agent of syphilis. On special staining with a silver stain, the organisms are seen as black, corkscrew-shaped forms in tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain highlights M. tuberculosis as pink rods, not black spirochetes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PAS is used for fungi and glycogen, not for demonstrating spirochetes as black.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gram stain does not adequately show T. pallidum; special silver staining or immunohistochemistry is used.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Congo red is used for amyloid, not for spirochetes.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man undergoes biopsy of a solitary, painless, sharply bordered ulcer on the penis that appeared 3 weeks after unprotected intercourse. Which histologic pattern is most likely to be seen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Caseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lymphocytes and plasma cells clustered around blood vessels

explanation.summary: The chancre of primary syphilis shows lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, particularly around blood vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once in the submucosa, T. pallidum multiplies slowly until a cell-mediated response with T lymphocytes and activated macrophages produces a chancre about 3 weeks after infection. Histologically, the chancre shows lymphocytes and plasma cells (lymphoplasmacytic inflammation), particularly around blood vessels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseating granulomas are the classic finding of active tuberculosis, not the primary chancre.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutrophilic microabscesses are not the described inflammatory pattern of a chancre.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An eosinophil-rich infiltrate is not characteristic; the chancre is lymphoplasmacytic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intranuclear inclusions suggest herpes simplex virus, which causes multiple painful vesicles rather than a single painless ulcer.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man noticed a single painless ulcer on his penis that disappeared on its own after about 4 weeks. He did not seek care and now believes the problem has resolved. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling regarding his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Resolution of the ulcer indicates the spirochete has been eliminated

choices.label: B
choices.text: Resolution indicates the lesion was a gumma rather than a chancre

choices.label: C
choices.text: Resolution indicates a herpes vesicle rather than a syphilitic lesion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Resolution indicates the infection has already reached the tertiary stage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resolution occurs with or without treatment, and dissemination may follow

explanation.summary: The chancre resolves with or without treatment, but T. pallidum may persist and disseminate to cause secondary syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The chancre of primary syphilis resolves with or without treatment. Despite the immune attack against it, T. pallidum may persist and disseminate throughout the body, and secondary syphilis manifests 2 to 8 weeks following the chancre in a subset of patients with untreated infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Spontaneous healing of the chancre does not mean the organism is gone; untreated infection can progress to secondary and later stages.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gummas are granulomatous nodules of tertiary syphilis occurring years later, not a single early genital ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A solitary painless ulcer is the chancre of primary syphilis; herpes causes multiple painful vesicles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tertiary syphilis occurs at least 5 years and often 15 to 20 years after infection, not within weeks of a chancre.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man presents with patchy hair loss, ring-shaped plaques around his nose and mouth, gray patches on the tongue, a sore throat, and generalized lymphadenopathy. He recalls a painless genital sore that healed 6 weeks earlier. If he remains untreated, what is the expected course of these findings over the next several weeks?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Progression to a solitary painless ulcer at the site of infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Resolution of the lesions with entry into an asymptomatic latent stage

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immediate development of gummas of the bone and skin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Development of aortic root dilation and valvular insufficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Persistence of the mucocutaneous lesions indefinitely until treated

explanation.summary: Secondary syphilis lasts a couple of weeks before the patient enters a latent stage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patchy alopecia, annular plaques of the mouth and nose, lesions of the tongue and oral cavity, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy are manifestations of secondary syphilis. This stage lasts for a couple of weeks before the patient enters a latent stage, defined as continued infection in the absence of clinical symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A solitary painless ulcer (chancre) is the primary stage, which this patient has already passed through.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gummas belong to benign tertiary syphilis, which occurs years after infection, not immediately after secondary disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cardiovascular syphilis is a tertiary manifestation occurring at least 5 years and often 15 to 20 years later.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Secondary lesions do not persist indefinitely; the stage resolves into latency after a couple of weeks even without treatment.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with a scaling papulosquamous rash of the trunk, palms, and soles undergoes skin biopsy. The pathologist sees granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and initially considers a mycobacterial process. Which additional histologic feature most supports a late-secondary syphilitic lesion rather than tuberculosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Central necrosis with a cheesy gross appearance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rod-shaped organisms retained on acid-alcohol staining

choices.label: C
choices.text: Multinucleated giant cells within the granulomas

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endarteritis of small vessels with abundant plasma cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Epithelioid histiocytes arranged in a nodule

explanation.summary: Secondary syphilitic lesions show endarteritis of small vessels and increased plasma cells, sometimes with a granulomatous pattern in late-secondary lesions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Under the microscope, secondary syphilitic lesions commonly demonstrate endarteritis of small vessels and increased plasma cells, and can also manifest as a granulomatous pattern, particularly in late-secondary lesions. Lymphoplasmacytic inflammation surrounding a small artery is the vascular clue, and T. pallidum can then be confirmed with special stains or immunohistochemistry.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseous (cheesy) necrosis is the classic feature of active tuberculosis, not of secondary syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acid-fast rods would indicate M. tuberculosis; T. pallidum is a spirochete shown with silver stain or immunohistochemistry.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Giant cells occur in the granulomas of both tuberculosis and late-secondary syphilis, so they do not discriminate between the two.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Epithelioid histiocytes are a feature of granulomas in general, including tuberculous granulomas, so they are not distinguishing.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant has positive syphilis serologies on routine prenatal screening. She is asymptomatic now but recalls an untreated rash of the palms and soles about a year ago. Which outcome of her current stage of infection is of greatest concern for this pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Transplacental transmission of T. pallidum to the fetus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Development of a new chancre at the original site

choices.label: C
choices.text: Spontaneous eradication of the spirochete without therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Onset of an aortic aneurysm during the pregnancy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conversion of treponemal antibodies to negative

explanation.summary: Latent syphilis can transmit T. pallidum to the fetus, causing congenital syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Latent syphilis is continued infection in the absence of clinical symptoms. Its outcomes include relapse to secondary syphilis, transmission of T. pallidum to the fetus resulting in congenital syphilis, continued latency, or progression to tertiary syphilis. Congenital syphilis follows vertical (placenta-fetal) transmission, and intrauterine or perinatal death occurs in up to a fourth of cases.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A chancre is the primary lesion; latent infection does not regenerate a chancre at the original site.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Latent syphilis is continued infection; spontaneous eradication is not among its described outcomes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aneurysms belong to cardiovascular tertiary syphilis, which occurs at least 5 years and often 15 to 20 years after infection, not within this pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Treponemal antibodies persist after exposure, even after successful treatment, so they do not convert to negative.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with untreated syphilis decades ago develops exertional chest pain. Angiography shows narrowing confined to the origins of both coronary arteries arising from a dilated aortic root, with the distal coronary vessels appearing widely patent. Which process best explains the coronary narrowing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lipid-rich atherosclerotic plaque of the distal vessels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vasospasm of the epicardial coronary arteries

choices.label: C
choices.text: Septic embolism from a valvular vegetation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gummatous infiltration of the ventricular myocardium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ostial stenosis from inflammation of the aortic root

explanation.summary: Cardiovascular syphilis can cause coronary ostial stenosis that compromises blood supply to the heart.
explanation.whyCorrect: In cardiovascular syphilis, inflammation of the aorta leads to dilation of the aortic root and arch. Additionally, coronary ostial stenosis, narrowing of these critical arteries at their origins, can affect the blood supply to the heart, explaining ischemic chest pain with disease localized to the coronary ostia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atherosclerosis would affect the vessels themselves; here the distal vessels are patent and narrowing is confined to the ostia at the inflamed aortic root.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vasospasm is not the mechanism described in tertiary syphilis and would not produce fixed ostial narrowing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Embolism from a vegetation is a complication of endocarditis, not of syphilitic aortitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gummas occur in bone, skin, and upper respiratory mucosa; myocardial gummatous infiltration does not explain ostial narrowing.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with a known aortic aneurysm attributed to tertiary syphilis develops sudden, tearing chest pain and dies. At autopsy, an elastin-stained section of the aorta shows blood within the aortic wall, creating a channel between its layers. Which process best describes this finding?

explanation.summary: Syphilitic aneurysms predispose to dissection, in which blood enters the vessel wall and creates a channel with possible rupture.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aneurysms, the weakening and dilation of a vessel, can be seen in the aorta in tertiary syphilis. Aneurysms predispose patients to dissections, which occur when blood enters the vessel wall and creates a channel with possible rupture; on elastin special stain, blood can be seen entering the elastin-rich aortic wall.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aortic regurgitation is valvular insufficiency from root dilation, not blood tracking within the vessel wall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coronary ostial stenosis is narrowing of the coronary origins, not intramural blood in the aorta.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A gumma is a granulomatous nodule of benign tertiary syphilis in bone, skin, or mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Miliary dissemination describes hematogenous seeding of organs in tuberculosis, not an aortic wall process.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with untreated syphilis has several months of headache and neck stiffness. Cerebrospinal fluid shows chronic inflammation, and meningeal biopsy demonstrates lymphocytes and plasma cells surrounding small blood vessels. Which form of neurosyphilis, and the most common presentation of neurosyphilis, does this represent?

explanation.summary: Neurosyphilis most often presents as meningovascular neurosyphilis, a chronic meningitis with perivascular lymphoplasmacytic inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neurosyphilis occurs in a small subset of patients and most often presents as meningovascular neurosyphilis, a chronic meningitis with perivascular lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, matching the chronic meningeal symptoms and biopsy findings here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Paretic neurosyphilis is invasion of the brain parenchyma causing progressive cognitive decline and dementia, not primarily meningitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tabes dorsalis is damage to sensory axons of the dorsal roots with posterior column loss, producing ataxia and shooting pains.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Benign tertiary syphilis refers to gummas of bone, skin, and upper respiratory mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cardiovascular syphilis involves aortitis with aortic root dilation and aneurysm, not the meninges.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with untreated syphilis many years ago reports shooting, stabbing pains in his legs, tingling of the feet, an unsteady gait that worsens in the dark, and difficulty emptying his bladder. Examination shows loss of joint position sense in the lower limbs. Syphilitic damage to which structure best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sensory axons of the dorsal roots and posterior columns

choices.label: B
choices.text: Motor neurons of the anterior horns of the cord

choices.label: C
choices.text: Descending axons of the lateral corticospinal tracts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Purkinje cells of the cerebellar cortex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ascending axons of the spinothalamic tracts

explanation.summary: Tabes dorsalis results from syphilitic damage to dorsal root sensory axons with loss of axons and myelin in the posterior columns.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tabes dorsalis is the result of syphilitic damage to the sensory axons in the dorsal roots of spinal nerves and results in impaired joint position sense and ataxia, as well as paresthesias, shooting and stabbing pains, and bladder dysfunction. On pathology examination, loss of axons and myelin is seen in the posterior columns.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anterior horn motor neuron loss causes weakness and atrophy, not the sensory ataxia and position-sense loss described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Corticospinal tract damage produces upper motor neuron weakness and spasticity rather than lost proprioception and lancinating pains.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cerebellar disease causes ataxia but does not explain lost joint position sense, paresthesias, and bladder dysfunction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spinothalamic tracts carry pain and temperature; the posterior columns carry position sense, which is what is lost in tabes dorsalis.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with tertiary syphilis has bilaterally small, irregular pupils that constrict briskly when he focuses on a near object but fail to constrict when a bright light is shone into either eye. Which mechanism is thought to underlie this pupillary finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Demyelination of the optic nerve anterior to the chiasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of all parasympathetic fibers within the oculomotor nerve

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impairment of the light reflex pathway in the dorsal midbrain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interruption of sympathetic fibers to the pupillary dilator

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fibrosis of the ciliary muscle within the globe

explanation.summary: The Argyll Robertson pupil is thought to result from impairment of the pupillary light reflex pathway in the dorsal midbrain with sparing of the accommodation pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the Argyll Robertson pupil, pupils that are already abnormally small (miotic) at baseline constrict in response to near objects (accommodation) but not in response to light. Though the exact mechanism is unknown, the finding is thought to be due to impairment of the pupillary light reflex pathway in the dorsal midbrain with sparing of the pathway responsible for near-object accommodation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Optic nerve disease would impair vision and the afferent limb, but the finding is attributed to a dorsal midbrain lesion sparing accommodation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of all parasympathetic output would abolish constriction to near objects as well; here accommodation is preserved.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sympathetic interruption produces a miotic pupil that still reacts to light, unlike the light-near dissociation described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ciliary muscle fibrosis would impair accommodation, which is intact in this patient.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is treated for secondary syphilis. Her physician wants a serologic test to follow over the coming months to confirm response to therapy, choosing one that tends to revert to a negative result after successful treatment. Which test is most appropriate for this purpose?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Silver stain of a skin biopsy

explanation.summary: Nontreponemal tests (RPR, VDRL) tend to slowly revert to negative after successful therapy, making them useful for following treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Non-treponemal tests include rapid plasma reagin (RPR) and VDRL and measure antibodies to a cardiolipin-cholesterol-lecithin antigen present in both T. pallidum and the host. They are low-cost, easy to perform, useful for initial screening, and tend to slowly revert to a negative result after successful therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Treponemal tests remain positive after exposure even after successful treatment, so they cannot distinguish active from resolved infection or track response to therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Silver staining of tissue identifies organisms in a lesion but is not a serologic test for monitoring treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The tuberculin skin test evaluates prior exposure to tuberculosis, not syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immunohistochemistry identifies T. pallidum in affected tissue and is not used to serially monitor therapy.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man who was adequately treated for syphilis 8 years ago undergoes routine screening. His RPR is nonreactive, but a treponemal-specific antibody test is reactive. He has no symptoms and no new sexual exposures. Which is the most likely interpretation of these results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Active secondary syphilis requiring immediate retreatment

choices.label: B
choices.text: A biologic false-positive result of the nontreponemal test

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recent reinfection with T. pallidum during the past year

choices.label: D
choices.text: Previously treated infection with persistent treponemal antibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progression to tertiary syphilis with neurologic involvement

explanation.summary: Treponemal tests cannot distinguish active from resolved infection because antibodies to T. pallidum persist after exposure, even after successful treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treponemal tests measure antibodies specific to T. pallidum and are more specific than non-treponemal tests, so they are often used to confirm a positive screen. However, they cannot distinguish between an active or resolved infection, since a person will have antibodies to T. pallidum after exposure even after successful treatment. A nonreactive RPR, which reverts to negative after successful therapy, fits a treated past infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Active secondary syphilis would produce a reactive nontreponemal test and clinical findings; his RPR is nonreactive and he is asymptomatic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A false-positive would apply to a reactive nontreponemal test; here the nontreponemal test is negative and the specific treponemal test is positive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reinfection would be expected to produce a reactive nontreponemal test, and he reports no new exposures.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tertiary syphilis is a clinical diagnosis with gummas, cardiovascular, or neurologic disease, none of which is present.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 6-week-old infant born to a mother who received no prenatal care has persistent nasal discharge and congestion, hepatosplenomegaly, a maculopapular rash, and moist raised plaques around the anus. Radiographs of the long bones show inflammation of the periosteum and of the bone-cartilage junctions. Which diagnosis best explains these findings?

explanation.summary: Snuffles, mucocutaneous lesions, condylomata lata, hepatosplenomegaly, osteochondritis, and periostitis are early manifestations of congenital syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Congenital syphilis follows vertical (placenta-fetal) transmission, and its manifestations may occur early (within 2 years but often within months) or late (after two years). Early manifestations include nasal discharge and congestion (snuffles), mucocutaneous lesions, condylomata lata, hepatosplenomegaly, and osteochondritis (inflammation of bone and cartilage of a joint) and periostitis (inflammation of the periosteum surrounding a bone).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Late congenital syphilis occurs after two years and manifests as interstitial keratitis, eighth cranial nerve deafness, recurrent arthropathy, Hutchinson teeth, saddle nose, and saber shins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Miliary tuberculosis is hematogenous seeding of organs by M. tuberculosis and does not produce snuffles, condylomata lata, or periostitis in a neonate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary syphilis is the adult stage marked by a solitary painless chancre after sexual transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Benign tertiary syphilis refers to gummas in bone, skin, and upper respiratory mucosa in adults years after infection.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 24-year-old hiker in Connecticut develops a single, slowly expanding annular red skin lesion with central clearing on the thigh about one week after a tick bite. The lesion resembles a bullseye. Which of the following is the most likely dermatologic finding?

explanation.summary: Erythema migrans is the classic skin finding of early localized Lyme disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted by the Ixodes deer tick, produces an annular erythematous rash with a pale center that resembles a bullseye, known as erythema migrans. It appears in the early localized stage and usually resolves within 4-12 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythema marginatum is the serpiginous rash of acute rheumatic fever following Group A streptococcal infection, not Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythema nodosum is nonspecific tender red nodules on the lower extremities seen in conditions such as tuberculosis and sarcoidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erythema multiforme presents with targetoid lesions typically triggered by infections such as HSV or by drugs, not by B. burgdorferi.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Necrolytic migratory erythema is associated with glucagonoma, an unrelated endocrine tumor.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: Despite the generation of specific antibodies over several weeks, Borrelia burgdorferi persists in an infected host. The organism shuttles different sequences of an outer surface lipoprotein (VlsE) next to a single gene promoter for expression. This strategy best illustrates which of the following mechanisms of immune evasion?

explanation.summary: B. burgdorferi escapes antibody-mediated attack by antigenic variation of its VlsE lipoprotein.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes that B. burgdorferi possesses multiple alternate sequences of the surface lipoprotein VlsE next to a single promoter. Only the sequence adjacent to the promoter is expressed, so different variants can be shuttled in to express alternate VlsE proteins and escape immune recognition. This is antigenic variance (variation).

whyWrongByChoice.B: The described mechanism involves changing a surface protein while extracellular, not hiding inside host cells as a latent form.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Molecular mimicry means resembling host antigens; here the organism actively changes its own antigen rather than imitating the host.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Superantigens nonspecifically activate large numbers of T cells and are not the mechanism of VlsE switching.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgA protease cleaves mucosal IgA and is a feature of certain respiratory pathogens, not the VlsE variation described.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man reports several weeks of migratory joint pain, palpitations, and a stiff neck. He recalls a bullseye rash that faded a few weeks earlier. Physical exam reveals lymphadenopathy and an irregular heart rhythm. These findings are most consistent with which stage of Lyme disease?

explanation.summary: Cardiac arrhythmias, lymphocytic meningitis, and multisystem signs days to weeks after erythema migrans define early disseminated Lyme disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Early disseminated disease follows hematogenous spread of B. burgdorferi days to weeks after erythema migrans. The brick lists constitutional symptoms, multiple erythema migrans, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, migratory joint/muscle pain, cardiac arrhythmias, and nervous system involvement such as lymphocytic meningitis and nerve dysfunction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Early localized disease is characterized by a solitary erythema migrans lesion without dissemination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Late disseminated disease occurs months later and is dominated by large-joint arthritis, not this acute multisystem picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Late localized disease is not a recognized stage of Lyme disease and serves as a distractor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Congenital Lyme disease is not the entity described; this is an adult with recent tick exposure and dissemination.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man who never received treatment for a tick-borne illness months earlier now presents with swelling and pain of both knees. Arthrocentesis shows inflammatory fluid, and there is ongoing synovial inflammation. Which stage of Lyme disease does this presentation most likely represent?

explanation.summary: Large-joint arthritis from synovial inflammation months after untreated infection marks late disseminated Lyme disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that months after infection, untreated patients may progress to late disseminated (persistent) disease, which is usually dominated by large-joint arthritis due to ongoing synovial inflammation and damage. Chronic neurologic changes may rarely occur.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Early localized disease features a solitary erythema migrans lesion days after the bite, not chronic arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Early disseminated disease occurs days to weeks after erythema migrans and features migratory pains, carditis, and meningitis rather than persistent large-joint arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acute retroviral syndrome is an HIV entity, not a Lyme stage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Primary infection with viremia describes HIV dissemination, unrelated to Borrelia joint disease.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A researcher studies the virus responsible for AIDS and notes that its genome consists of two RNA molecules and that it synthesizes DNA from viral RNA within the cells it infects. This enzymatic activity is the reason the virus is classified in which of the following groups?

explanation.summary: HIV is a retrovirus because it uses reverse transcriptase to make DNA from its RNA genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes HIV as a virus with a genome of two (diploid) RNA molecules, a capsid, and an envelope. It is referred to as a retrovirus because it uses reverse transcriptase to synthesize DNA from viral RNA within the infected cell.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HIV is an RNA virus; it only produces DNA secondarily through reverse transcription and is not itself a double-stranded DNA virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prions are misfolded proteins with no nucleic acid genome, unlike HIV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV is enveloped, not a non-enveloped virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bacteriophages infect bacteria, whereas HIV infects human CD4+ T cells.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with known HIV infection is being staged. His most recent CD4+ T-cell count is 150 cells/microL. Which of the following best explains why he now meets criteria for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4+ T-cell count less than 200 cells/microL

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD4+ T-cell count of 500 cells/microL or greater

choices.label: D
choices.text: Detectable HIV-1 RNA in the blood

explanation.summary: For adults, AIDS is defined as a CD4+ T-cell count below 200 cells/microL.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that AIDS is defined as a CD4+ T-cell count of less than 200/microL and corresponds to HIV Stage 3. This profound immunosuppression leaves the patient vulnerable to opportunistic infections, secondary neoplasms, and neurologic disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A count of 200-499 cells/microL corresponds to HIV Stage 2, which does not meet AIDS criteria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A count of 500 or more cells/microL corresponds to HIV Stage 1, the earliest stage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Detectable HIV-1 RNA marks active viral replication and is useful for monitoring but does not by itself define AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-HIV antibodies indicate infection but do not define the AIDS stage; the CD4 count does.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man develops sore throat, myalgia, fever, and fatigue about 3 weeks after a high-risk sexual exposure. Symptoms resolve spontaneously over the next few weeks. Around this time, virus-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T cells appear and detectable viral titers fall. This clinical picture is most consistent with which phase of HIV infection?

explanation.summary: A self-limited mononucleosis-like illness weeks after exposure, coinciding with rising CD8+ CTLs, is the acute retroviral syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that virus-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T cells appear within 3-7 weeks of exposure, corresponding to a drop in viral titers (the first equilibrium point). Acute retroviral syndrome is the initial, usually nonspecific presentation with sore throat, myalgia, fever, weight loss, and fatigue that resolves in 2-4 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The chronic phase is clinically latent and largely asymptomatic, following the acute syndrome rather than presenting as an acute febrile illness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clinical AIDS reflects profound immunosuppression with opportunistic infections and neoplasms, not a transient early illness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Late disseminated disease is a stage of Lyme disease, not HIV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is a late neurologic complication of advanced AIDS, not the acute seroconversion illness.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with a CD4+ T-cell count of 90 cells/microL presents with progressive dyspnea and a nonproductive cough. CT of the chest shows diffuse ground-glass opacities. Bronchoalveolar lavage is performed, and a Gomori methenamine silver stain highlights cyst walls as dark gray organisms. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?

explanation.summary: Ground-glass opacities plus GMS-positive cysts on BAL in an AIDS patient indicate Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes Pneumocystis jirovecii as a ubiquitous fungus that is asymptomatic in immunocompetent hosts but causes pneumonia in AIDS, with dyspnea and nonproductive cough, bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray, and diffuse ground-glass opacities on CT. Bronchoalveolar lavage with GMS staining highlights the cyst walls, confirming the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CMV in AIDS classically causes retinitis, colitis, and meningoencephalitis rather than GMS-positive cystic organisms on lavage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tuberculosis is a bacterial opportunistic infection and would not show silver-staining cyst walls on BAL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toxoplasma gondii causes ring-enhancing brain lesions, not this pulmonary cyst picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HSV in AIDS typically produces mucocutaneous or perirectal ulceration, not diffuse ground-glass pneumonia with cysts.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with untreated AIDS develops progressive vision loss in one eye. Ophthalmoscopic examination reveals retinal hemorrhage and inflammation. Which of the following opportunistic pathogens is the most likely cause of her blindness?

explanation.summary: CMV retinitis is an important cause of blindness in AIDS, with retinal hemorrhage and inflammation on fundoscopy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that CMV reactivation in immunosuppressed patients can cause severe infections including CMV colitis, meningoencephalitis, and retinitis, the last being an important cause of blindness with inflammation and hemorrhage seen on ophthalmoscopic examination.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pneumocystis jirovecii causes pneumonia, not retinitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Human herpesvirus-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma, not retinal infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, a white matter disease, not retinitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Candida albicans typically causes oral or vaginal candidiasis in this setting rather than hemorrhagic retinitis.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with AIDS presents with headache and focal neurologic deficits. MRI of the brain shows multiple enhancing, ring-like lesions. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible for these findings?

explanation.summary: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in AIDS classically indicate toxoplasmic encephalitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that although primary Toxoplasma gondii infection is usually asymptomatic in immunocompetent hosts, in AIDS patients it can cause toxoplasmic encephalitis with multiple enhancing, ring-like lesions on MRI. These correspond to multiple abscesses and necrotic foci on neuropathologic examination.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CMV in AIDS causes retinitis, colitis, and meningoencephalitis rather than the classic multiple ring-enhancing lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pneumocystis jirovecii causes pneumonia, not focal brain lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with B-cell lymphomas, which would appear as mass lesions but are not the classic toxoplasmosis ring-enhancing picture described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease, not ring-enhancing brain abscesses in AIDS.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man with advanced HIV infection develops multiple violaceous patches and plaques on the chest and oral mucosa. Biopsy shows a proliferation of bland, ovoid-to-spindled endothelial cells. This vascular neoplasm is most strongly associated with which of the following viruses?

explanation.summary: Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular endothelial tumor, is associated with human herpesvirus-8 (HHV8).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that HHV8 infection is associated with Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular neoplasm that manifests as multiple cutaneous, mucosal, or visceral lesions and is composed of proliferating endothelial cells (bland, ovoid-to-spindled cells on microscopy).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with B-cell lymphomas such as a subset of diffuse large B-cell and Hodgkin lymphoma, not the vascular endothelial tumor described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytomegalovirus causes retinitis, colitis, and encephalitis, not Kaposi sarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HSV-1 causes mucocutaneous ulcerations, not an endothelial neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, not a vascular tumor.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with AIDS develops progressive weakness and cognitive decline. MRI shows white matter lesions, and brain tissue demonstrates demyelination with enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei in infected glial cells. The responsible virus preferentially infects which cell type to produce this demyelinating disease?

explanation.summary: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy results from JC virus infection of oligodendrocytes, causing demyelination.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes JC virus-induced progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy as an AIDS-associated demyelinating disease. The JC virus infects oligodendrocytes, which are responsible for the production and maintenance of myelin, so their infection leads to loss of myelin (white matter lesions) with enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HIV itself infects CD4+ T lymphocytes, but the demyelinating JC virus targets oligodendrocytes, not T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endothelial cells are the target in Kaposi sarcoma, not in progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Retinal photoreceptors are affected in CMV retinitis, not in JC virus disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type II pneumocytes are lung cells and are not the target of the JC virus.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A public health officer investigates a cluster of cases of an annular rash and arthritis in a wooded region of New England. The causative organism is identified in a patient's skin biopsy. Which of the following best describes the organism and its mode of transmission?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spirochete transmitted by the Ixodes deer tick

choices.label: B
choices.text: Spirochete transmitted by the human body louse

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gram-negative coccobacillus transmitted by the Dermacentor dog tick

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obligate intracellular bacterium transmitted by the Dermacentor dog tick

choices.label: E
choices.text: Protozoan transmitted by the Anopheles mosquito

explanation.summary: Borrelia burgdorferi is a spirochete carried by the Ixodes deer tick and causes Lyme disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes B. burgdorferi as a spirochete transmitted by the Ixodes deer tick (adult and nymph forms shown in Figure 1) and responsible for Lyme disease, which is named after a town in Connecticut. The combination of an annular rash and arthritis in a wooded northeastern region points to this organism and vector.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lyme disease is tick-borne; the body louse is not the vector of B. burgdorferi.
whyWrongByChoice.C: B. burgdorferi is a spirochete, not a gram-negative coccobacillus, and the vector is the Ixodes tick rather than Dermacentor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: B. burgdorferi is an extracellular spirochete rather than an obligate intracellular bacterium, and Dermacentor is not its vector.
whyWrongByChoice.E: B. burgdorferi is a bacterium (spirochete), not a protozoan, and mosquitoes do not transmit it.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A microbiologist studies how Borrelia burgdorferi moves from an attached, feeding Ixodes tick into a human. Which of the following best describes the step that allows the spirochete to pass into the human host?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A secreted exotoxin triggers its regurgitation from the tick midgut into the wound

choices.label: B
choices.text: A switched outer surface protein lets it migrate to and bind the tick salivary gland

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is deposited in tick feces on the skin and scratched into the bite wound

choices.label: D
choices.text: It forms a resistant spore that is injected through the tick mouthparts

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is carried into the wound inside infected circulating tick hemocytes

explanation.summary: During tick feeding, B. burgdorferi switches its outer surface protein so it can migrate to the tick salivary gland and bind a salivary protein, enabling passage into the human.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that during feeding by the tick, B. burgdorferi changes its outer surface protein to allow migration to the tick salivary gland, where it binds to a salivary protein, allowing its passage into the human host. The spirochetes then multiply and spread throughout the dermis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick describes active migration to the salivary gland, not exotoxin-driven regurgitation from the midgut.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fecal deposition and scratching is not the route described for B. burgdorferi; transmission occurs through the tick's saliva.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spirochetes do not form spores; the organism migrates as a live, motile bacterium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transmission is via the salivary gland and saliva, not via tick blood cells.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman develops an expanding red annular lesion at a tick bite site. Within the dermis, macrophages begin releasing IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor in response to the spirochete. Which of the following interactions initiates this innate cytokine release?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial lipopolysaccharide binding to Toll-like receptor 4

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacterial double-stranded RNA binding to Toll-like receptor 3

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bacterial lipoproteins binding to Toll-like receptor 2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bacterial peptidoglycan binding to the CD4 receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bacterial flagellin binding to the Fc receptor

explanation.summary: The innate response to B. burgdorferi begins with bacterial lipoproteins engaging TLR2 on macrophages, which then release IL-6 and TNF.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the immune system mounts both an innate and adaptive response: bacterial lipoproteins bind to Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) on macrophages, which in turn release pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor (TNF). Antibodies against the spirochete are generated later, over weeks to months.

whyWrongByChoice.A: TLR4 recognizes lipopolysaccharide; the brick specifies that lipoproteins of B. burgdorferi bind TLR2.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TLR3 senses double-stranded RNA, a viral pattern, and is not the receptor described for this spirochete.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD4 is a T-cell coreceptor (and the receptor HIV uses), not a macrophage pattern-recognition receptor for bacterial lipoproteins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fc receptors bind antibody, which is not yet present in the first days of early localized disease; the innate response uses TLR2.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is found to have a single annular erythematous lesion with a pale center on his calf after camping. He declines treatment and asks what will happen to the rash if it is left alone. Which of the following is the expected course of this skin lesion?

explanation.summary: Erythema migrans usually resolves within 4-12 weeks even without treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that erythema migrans, the annular erythematous rash with a pale center of early localized disease, is often compared to a bullseye and usually resolves within 4-12 weeks. Resolution of the rash does not mean the infection has cleared; the spirochete may still disseminate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A few days is too short; the rash persists for weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 2-4 weeks is the duration of the acute retroviral syndrome of HIV, not the course of erythema migrans.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 3-7 weeks is the time frame in which virus-specific CD8+ T cells appear after HIV exposure, not the course of the Lyme rash.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The rash resolves spontaneously; it does not persist indefinitely without treatment.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man develops palpitations, an irregular heart rhythm, migratory joint pain, and fatigue 3 weeks after a bullseye rash. The signs and symptoms of this stage of Lyme disease are thought to arise predominantly through which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct cytolytic damage by the multiplying spirochete

choices.label: B
choices.text: A secreted exotoxin acting on cardiac and synovial tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: The host immune response to the spirochete

explanation.summary: Early disseminated Lyme manifestations are thought to be immune-mediated rather than caused by direct microbial damage.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that the exact mechanism of Lyme disease-associated signs and symptoms is unknown but is thought to be the host's immune response to the spirochete rather than direct damage from the microbe itself. Cardiac arrhythmias and migratory joint pain days to weeks after erythema migrans are features of early disseminated disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick specifically contrasts the immune-mediated mechanism with direct damage from the microbe.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No exotoxin is described for B. burgdorferi; its pathology is attributed to the host response.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endotoxin-driven shock is not part of Lyme disease pathogenesis as the brick describes it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hematogenous spread occurs, but the manifestations reflect immune response rather than suppurative abscesses.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with headache, stiff neck, and low-grade fever 4 weeks after an untreated bullseye rash acquired while hiking. Lumbar puncture is performed. Which of the following cerebrospinal fluid findings is most consistent with the nervous system involvement of this stage of Lyme disease?

explanation.summary: Nervous system involvement in early disseminated Lyme disease presents as stiff neck from lymphocytic meningitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 in the brick lists nervous system findings of early disseminated B. burgdorferi infection as stiff neck (lymphocytic meningitis) and nerve dysfunction. Meningeal inflammation weeks after erythema migrans therefore yields a lymphocyte-predominant CSF.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A neutrophilic predominance suggests acute bacterial (pyogenic) meningitis, not the lymphocytic meningitis of Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bloody CSF with xanthochromia indicates subarachnoid hemorrhage, not Lyme meningitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acid-fast bacilli indicate tuberculous meningitis; B. burgdorferi is a spirochete.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stiff neck in this setting reflects true meningeal inflammation, so the CSF is not expected to be normal.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A physician compares the neurologic features of the different stages of Lyme disease in a patient who was never treated. Which of the following manifestations is characteristic of late disseminated disease rather than early disseminated disease?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Distal paresthesias and spinal radicular pain

explanation.summary: Late disseminated Lyme disease can rarely produce chronic neuropathic findings such as distal paresthesias and spinal radicular pain, along with alterations of memory, mood, or sleep.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that in late disseminated (persistent) disease, patients rarely experience chronic neurological repercussions such as alterations of memory, mood, or sleep, and that neuropathic signs and symptoms include distal paresthesias (tingling or burning sensations) and spinal radicular pain. These are distinct from the lymphocytic meningitis and nerve dysfunction of the early disseminated stage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Stiff neck from lymphocytic meningitis is the nervous system finding listed for early disseminated disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cardiac arrhythmias are an early disseminated (heart) manifestation in Table 1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Multiple erythema migrans is the skin finding of early disseminated disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Migratory joint and muscle pain is the musculoskeletal feature of early disseminated disease; the late stage features persistent large-joint arthritis instead.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS
