questions.stem: An epidemiologist reviews the routes by which HIV is acquired. Which of the following routes of transmission has become extremely rare today because of rigorous screening?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sexual contact across a mucosal surface

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sharing of needles during intravenous drug use

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ingestion of breast milk by an infant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage through the birth canal during delivery

explanation.summary: Transmission of HIV through blood products is now extremely rare because of the rigor of blood and plasma screening.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists HIV entry through mucosal infection such as sexual contact, direct inoculation from trauma, intravenous drug use, and receipt of blood products, noting that the last is extremely rare today due to the rigor of blood and plasma screening. Vertical transmission (transplacental, birth canal, breast milk) has been decreased by antiretroviral therapy but is not attributed to screening.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mucosal infection through sexual contact is described as the usual route of HIV entry, not a rare one.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intravenous drug use remains a described route of direct inoculation and is not prevented by product screening.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Breast milk ingestion is a route of vertical transmission that antiretroviral therapy, not screening, has reduced.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Delivery through the birth canal is a vertical transmission route that antiretroviral therapy has reduced; it is not the route eliminated by screening.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman acquires HIV through mucosal exposure. Shortly afterward, the virus is established in her regional lymph nodes, where large numbers of CD4+ T cells become infected before viremia develops. Which of the following cells is responsible for carrying the virus from the mucosa to the lymph nodes?

explanation.summary: Infected dendritic cells migrate from the mucosa to lymph nodes, where they transmit HIV to more CD4+ T cells; replication there spills into the blood as viremia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that HIV infects mucosal CD4+ T cells and other immune cells such as dendritic cells once it gains access to the host. The infected dendritic cells migrate to lymph nodes, where they transmit the infection to more CD4+ T cells, and viral replication in the lymph nodes spills into the bloodstream, resulting in viremia (Figure 4).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neutrophils are not described as carriers of HIV to lymphoid tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: B lymphocytes are later affected by HIV-related lymphomagenesis but are not the vehicle that transports virus to the lymph node.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Platelets are anucleate fragments and play no role in HIV dissemination in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Erythrocytes do not carry HIV to lymph nodes.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with HIV infection returns for follow-up. His physician wants to assign him to one of the three clinical stages of HIV infection that reflect declining immune function. Which of the following laboratory measures is used for this purpose?

explanation.summary: Declining immune function is best reflected by the CD4+ T-cell count, which divides HIV infection into Stages 1, 2, and 3.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical reasoning box states that although HIV-1 RNA levels are detectable in blood and useful for monitoring and management, declining immune function is best associated with CD4+ T-cell counts, which are used clinically to divide patients into HIV Stage 1 (500 or more cells/microL), Stage 2 (200-499), and Stage 3 or AIDS (less than 200).

whyWrongByChoice.A: HIV-1 RNA is a useful marker for monitoring and management but is not the measure that defines the three immune stages.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody titers indicate infection, not the degree of immune decline.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells rise in the acute response, but the staging system is based on CD4+ counts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Total lymphocyte count is not the staging measure described; the specific CD4+ T-cell count is.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 36-year-old asymptomatic woman with known HIV infection has a CD4+ T-cell count of 350 cells/microL. Which of the following best describes her current classification?

explanation.summary: A CD4+ T-cell count of 200-499 cells/microL corresponds to HIV Stage 2.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick divides HIV infection by CD4+ T-cell count into Stage 1 (500 or more cells/microL), Stage 2 (200-499 cells/microL), and Stage 3, also known as AIDS (less than 200 cells/microL). A count of 350 falls within the Stage 2 range.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Stage 1 requires a CD4+ count of 500 or more cells/microL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stage 3 requires a CD4+ count below 200 cells/microL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acute retroviral syndrome is the symptomatic initial illness weeks after exposure, not a CD4-based stage; this patient is asymptomatic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: AIDS is synonymous with Stage 3 and requires a CD4+ count below 200 cells/microL.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man in the chronic, clinically latent phase of untreated HIV infection develops a bacterial pneumonia. Over the following months his HIV-1 RNA level rises and his CD4+ T-cell count falls more rapidly than before. Which of the following best explains the effect of the intercurrent infection on the course of his HIV disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotic therapy directly inhibits reverse transcriptase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytokines released during other microbial infections increase HIV replication

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bacterial superantigens delete HIV-specific cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bacteria transfer plasmid-encoded resistance genes to the virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neutrophil recruitment clears latently infected lymphoid tissue

explanation.summary: During clinical latency, other microbial infections and their cytokines drive increased viral replication, accelerating destruction of lymphoid tissue and CD4+ depletion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Figure 4 in the brick shows that after establishment of chronic infection (virus concentrated in lymphoid tissues with low-level virus production), other microbial infections and cytokines lead to increased viral replication, followed by destruction of lymphoid tissues and depletion of CD4+ T cells, culminating in AIDS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics do not act on reverse transcriptase, and the observed change is a rise in replication, not a fall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick attributes the accelerated course to cytokine-driven viral replication, not to superantigen deletion of CTLs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bacteria cannot transfer plasmids to a virus; this is not a described mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The progression involves destruction of lymphoid tissue by increased viral replication, not clearance of latently infected tissue by neutrophils.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with untreated HIV infection and a CD4+ T-cell count of 380 cells/microL has been largely asymptomatic for several years. Which of the following infections is the brick's example of an opportunistic infection that may develop during this chronic phase, before the onset of AIDS?

explanation.summary: During the chronic phase, patients may remain asymptomatic or develop infections such as vaginal or oral candidiasis, herpes zoster, and tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that during the chronic phase of infection, while CD4+ T cells are slowly destroyed and the immune system progressively deteriorates, patients may continue to be asymptomatic or develop some opportunistic infections, such as vaginal or oral candidiasis (Figure 3), herpes zoster infections, and tuberculosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pneumocystis pneumonia is presented as an opportunistic infection of AIDS, the stage of profound immunosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Toxoplasmic encephalitis is described in the context of AIDS, not the clinically latent chronic phase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CMV retinitis is a severe reactivation infection of AIDS patients and other profoundly immunosuppressed hosts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is an AIDS-associated demyelinating disease, not a chronic-phase infection.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV infection during the chronic phase. He declines antiretroviral therapy and asks how long it typically takes for untreated infection to progress to AIDS. Which of the following is the most accurate estimate?

explanation.summary: Without treatment, most patients with HIV progress to AIDS after a chronic phase of approximately 7-10 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that in the absence of treatment, most patients with HIV progress to AIDS after a chronic phase of approximately 7-10 years, during which CD4+ T cells are progressively destroyed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2-4 weeks is the duration of the acute retroviral syndrome, not the time to AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 3-7 weeks is the interval after exposure at which virus-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T cells appear.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 4-12 weeks is the time in which erythema migrans of Lyme disease usually resolves.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 20-30 years is far longer than the approximately 7-10 year untreated chronic phase described.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with AIDS presents with a widespread inflammatory rash. The scalp, eyebrows, and skin folds of the face show red, flaky patches covered with greasy yellow scales. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Widespread and unusually severe seborrheic dermatitis, an inflammatory rash with red, flaky, greasy scales, is encountered in HIV and AIDS.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that rashes and other dermatologic conditions may be encountered in HIV and AIDS, such as widespread seborrheic dermatitis, an inflammatory rash with red, flaky, and greasy scales. Seborrheic dermatitis begins on the scalp and face and in skin folds where sebaceous glands are active.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Kaposi sarcoma produces violaceous patches, plaques, or nodules of a vascular neoplasm, not flaky greasy scales.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythema migrans is the annular bullseye rash of early Lyme disease, not a scaly facial eruption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV in AIDS causes severe mucocutaneous or perirectal ulcerations rather than a scaly rash.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral candidiasis presents as white patches in the mouth, not scaling of the scalp and face.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with a CD4+ T-cell count of 60 cells/microL develops a malignancy. Her oncologist explains that the loss of a particular immune function makes patients with AIDS vulnerable to secondary neoplasms. Which of the following best describes this mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Loss of T-cell-mediated immune surveillance against transformed cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insertion of HIV oncogenes into the host genome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase-induced mutation of tumor suppressor genes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chronic antibody-mediated stimulation of epithelial growth

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of neutrophil killing of tumor cells

explanation.summary: Immune surveillance helps prevent cancer, and the lack of functioning T cells in AIDS contributes to neoplasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the three major consequences of advanced HIV (opportunistic infections, secondary neoplasms, neurologic disease) result from the impaired immune system. Immune surveillance helps to prevent cancer, and the lack of functioning T cells contributes to neoplasia, which is why secondary neoplasms such as Kaposi sarcoma and B-cell lymphomas occur at higher rates.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick does not attribute AIDS-related tumors to HIV oncogenes; it attributes them to the loss of T-cell immune surveillance and to virus-induced transformation by HHV8 and EBV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from viral RNA; it is not described as mutating host tumor suppressor genes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibody-driven epithelial growth is not a described mechanism; the defect is in T-cell function.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The neoplasia risk stems from loss of functioning T cells, not neutrophils.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with advanced HIV infection and profound CD4+ T-cell depletion develops an EBV-positive large B-cell lymphoma. Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this tumor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Germinal center hypermutation producing a MYC translocation in B cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Unchecked EBV reactivation in latently infected B cells after T-cell loss

choices.label: C
choices.text: HHV8-driven transformation of endothelial cells into a vascular tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Direct integration of HIV provirus into the DNA of germinal center B cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased follicular T helper cell stimulation of germinal center B cells

explanation.summary: In advanced HIV, T-cell depletion permits unchecked EBV/KSHV reactivation in latently infected B cells, producing virus-associated B-cell lymphomas.
explanation.whyCorrect: Figure 14 in the brick shows that in advanced infection, T-cell depletion leads to unchecked EBV/KSHV reactivation in latently infected B cells, which gives rise to virus-associated B-cell lymphomas: EBV+ large cell lymphoma, HHV8+ primary effusion lymphoma, and EBV+ Hodgkin lymphoma. The brick also notes EBV is implicated in a subset of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and classic Hodgkin lymphoma cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Germinal center hypermutation with MYC translocation is the separate, non-viral pathway of B-cell hyperplasia leading to lymphoma; it does not explain an EBV-positive tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HHV8 transformation of endothelial cells produces Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular neoplasm, not a B-cell lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick does not describe HIV integration into B cells as the cause of lymphoma; lymphomas arise from viral reactivation and germinal center hypermutation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increased follicular T helper cells are depicted as a feature of early infection in Figure 14, not the mechanism in advanced infection with T-cell depletion.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with chronic HIV infection develops a rapidly growing B-cell lymphoma. Molecular testing demonstrates a translocation of the MYC gene, and the tumor cells are negative for EBV and HHV8. Which of the following best describes how this lymphoma arose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reactivation of latent virus in B cells after loss of T-cell control

choices.label: C
choices.text: B-cell hyperplasia in germinal centers causing DNA breaks and hypermutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: JC virus infection of lymphoid follicles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of myelin-producing cells with secondary lymphoid proliferation

explanation.summary: In HIV infection, B-cell hyperplasia in germinal centers can lead to DNA breaks and hypermutation that progress to lymphoma, including tumors driven by MYC translocation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that, in addition to viral-induced transformation, B-cell hyperplasia in germinal centers within the context of HIV infection can lead to DNA breaks and hypermutation that may then progress to lymphoma. Its examples include a lymphoma driven by translocation of the MYC gene and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with BCL6 alterations. A virus-negative MYC-translocated tumor fits this non-viral pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Viral reactivation in latently infected B cells produces EBV+ or HHV8+ lymphomas; this tumor is negative for both viruses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HHV8 causes Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma; the tumor here is HHV8 negative.
whyWrongByChoice.D: JC virus infects oligodendrocytes and causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, not lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myelin breakdown relates to HIV neurocognitive disease and PML, not to lymphomagenesis.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with AIDS presents with dyspnea. Imaging shows a large pleural effusion without an associated mass. Cytologic examination of the fluid shows sheets of malignant lymphocytes with enlarged nuclei and intermixed apoptotic bodies. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Primary effusion lymphoma is an HHV8-associated hematologic malignancy that grows within body cavity effusions in AIDS patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that HHV8 is also associated with primary effusion lymphoma, a hematologic malignancy that grows within effusions. Figure 13 shows that malignant lymphocytes with enlarged nuclei and intermixed apoptotic bodies constitute an effusion fluid in primary effusion lymphoma in the context of AIDS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm of proliferating endothelial cells, not malignant lymphocytes in an effusion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma is an EBV-associated lymphoma occurring in a subset of AIDS patients but is not the lymphoma defined by growth within an effusion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The cells are malignant with enlarged nuclei and apoptotic bodies, which is not a reactive process.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pneumocystis pneumonia produces ground-glass opacities and frothy casts on lavage, not malignant lymphocytes in pleural fluid.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with AIDS develops cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows classic Hodgkin lymphoma. Which of the following viruses is implicated in this AIDS-associated neoplasm?

explanation.summary: Epstein-Barr virus is implicated in a subset of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and classic Hodgkin lymphoma cases in AIDS.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that viral-induced transformation can lead to lymphoma, such as HHV8+ primary effusion lymphoma and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), the latter of which is implicated in a subset of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and classic Hodgkin lymphoma cases. Figure 14 likewise lists EBV+ Hodgkin lymphoma among the virus-associated B-cell lymphomas of advanced HIV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HHV8 is associated with Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma, not classic Hodgkin lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CMV causes colitis, meningoencephalitis, and retinitis in AIDS; it is not linked to Hodgkin lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, a demyelinating disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HSV causes severe mucocutaneous and perirectal ulcerations, not lymphoma.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man with AIDS presents with severe pain on defecation. Examination reveals a large, deep, confluent perirectal ulceration. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: HSV infection or reactivation in AIDS can produce severe mucocutaneous and perirectal ulcerations.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that HSV infection (or reactivation) in AIDS patients may cause severe mucocutaneous or perirectal ulcerations (Figure 6) and can also involve the esophagus, liver, and lung. HSV is one of the pathogens that can reactivate from latent infection and present atypically in the absence of a normal immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CMV reactivation in AIDS causes colitis, meningoencephalitis, and retinitis rather than deep perirectal ulceration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HHV8 causes Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma, not ulcerative perirectal lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Candida in HIV typically causes oral or vaginal candidiasis with white patches.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxoplasma causes encephalitis with ring-enhancing brain lesions in AIDS, not mucocutaneous ulcers.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A neuropathologist examines the brain of a patient who died with HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder. HIV is detected directly within resident CNS cells, and there is evidence of cytokine release and astrocyte activation. Which of the following CNS cell types, described as the resident monocytes of the central nervous system, is directly infected by HIV?

explanation.summary: HIV infects microglia, the resident monocytes of the CNS, as well as astrocytes, contributing to neurocognitive dysfunction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that HIV infects microglia, the resident monocytes of the central nervous system, as well as astrocytes, which are important supportive glial cells. Direct cellular damage, neurotoxic effects of certain HIV-associated proteins, and downstream effects of cytokine release and astrocyte activation result in parenchymal damage and cellular depletion, and HIV also contributes to myelin breakdown.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oligodendrocytes are the target of JC virus in progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, not the cell HIV directly infects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neurons suffer parenchymal damage downstream of cytokines and neurotoxic proteins, but the brick identifies microglia and astrocytes as the infected cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ependymal cells are not described as HIV targets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerves and are not the resident monocytes of the CNS.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with no known medical history presents to the emergency department with slowly progressive shortness of breath. CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities, and cytopathologic examination of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid shows frothy casts with organisms consistent with Pneumocystis jirovecii. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

explanation.summary: Pneumocystis pneumonia in an apparently healthy adult should prompt HIV testing, because P. jirovecii causes disease only in immunosuppressed hosts.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case connection explains that P. jirovecii is asymptomatic in immunocompetent patients, but a progressive pulmonary infection may occur in immunosuppressed patients such as those with AIDS. Because CD4+ cells are needed to control the organism, HIV testing should be performed in this patient to investigate this possibility.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphocytic meningitis is a feature of early disseminated Lyme disease and is not suggested by pneumocystis pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lyme disease does not predispose to Pneumocystis infection; the underlying concern is immunosuppression from HIV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Kaposi sarcoma is a possible AIDS-associated neoplasm, but establishing the underlying HIV infection is the appropriate next step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxoplasmic encephalitis is evaluated when neurologic symptoms are present; the first step is to identify the underlying immunodeficiency.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with long-standing untreated HIV infection reports a year of insidiously worsening difficulty concentrating and forgetfulness. Over recent months she has developed a tremor and now has severe cognitive impairment. Brain MRI shows no focal enhancing or white matter lesions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder begins insidiously with concentration and memory deficits and can progress to motor signs such as tremor and severe cognitive impairment (HIV-associated dementia).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder as a spectrum of neurologic disease in which neuropsychiatric symptoms begin insidiously with deficits in concentration and memory but can progress to motor signs, such as tremor, and severe cognitive impairment, termed by some as HIV-associated dementia. It results from HIV infection of CNS cells, cytokine release, and myelin breakdown rather than from a focal opportunistic infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PML produces white matter lesions on brain imaging from JC virus demyelination; the MRI here shows none.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Toxoplasmic encephalitis presents with multiple enhancing ring-like lesions on MRI, which are absent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CMV meningoencephalitis is an infection of the leptomeninges and brain, not a slowly progressive, imaging-negative cognitive decline.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chronic neurologic changes in Lyme disease are rare and require B. burgdorferi infection, which is not suggested here.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with end-stage renal disease receives a kidney donated by his identical twin brother. Which of the following terms best describes this type of graft?

explanation.summary: An isograft is tissue transferred between genetically identical individuals of the same species, such as identical twins.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines an isograft as tissue transferred between individuals of the same species who are genetically identical. Because identical twins share the same genome, a transplant between them is an isograft, which minimizes the risk of immune rejection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An allograft is between genetically different individuals of the same species, not identical twins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An autograft transfers tissue from one body site to another on the same individual, not between two people.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A xenograft is between different species, such as animal tissue placed into a human.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Homograft is not one of the four graft types defined in this brick (autograft, isograft, allograft, xenograft).

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with cirrhosis receives a liver from a deceased, genetically unrelated human donor. Which of the following terms best describes this type of graft, which represents the most common transplant performed in medicine?

explanation.summary: An allograft is tissue transferred between genetically different individuals of the same species and is the most common transplant type.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that an allograft is tissue transferred between genetically different individuals of the same species. Because most donors and recipients are non-identical humans, allografting is the most common transplant performed in medicine.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An autograft moves tissue from one part of a patient's body to another on the same person.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An isograft is between genetically identical individuals such as identical twins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A xenograft is between different species, not two humans.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intergraft is a horticultural term for grafting plants, not a category of human transplantation.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A transplant team struggles to find a compatible donor for a patient because of the extremely high genetic variability (polymorphism) of a particular gene family. Which of the following genes is most responsible for making the donor-recipient matching process so difficult?

explanation.summary: HLA genes are highly polymorphic, which makes finding a compatible donor difficult.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that HLA genes have high genetic variability (polymorphism), which often makes it difficult to find compatible donors. HLA genes encode MHC molecules used to distinguish self from non-self, and mismatches drive rejection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ABO genes are important in matching but are not highly polymorphic like HLA genes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interleukin-1 is a circulating cytokine of inflammation; its gene is not involved in transplant compatibility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgE is an antibody notable in type 1 hypersensitivity, not transplant matching.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antinuclear antibodies are seen in autoimmune disease such as lupus and are not involved in transplant compatibility.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: The HLA gene complex is located on the short arm of chromosome 6 and is organized into three classes. Which of the following correctly pairs an HLA class with the genes it contains?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Class I contains HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DR

choices.label: B
choices.text: Class I contains HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C

choices.label: C
choices.text: Class II contains HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C

choices.label: E
choices.text: Class II encodes cytokines rather than MHC molecules

explanation.summary: Class I HLA genes are HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C; class II genes are HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DR.
explanation.whyCorrect: Per the brick, there are three class I HLA genes (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) and three class II HLA genes (HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, HLA-DR). Both class I and class II genes encode MHC molecules and are critical to transplant matching.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DR are class II genes, not class I.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C are class I genes, not class II.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Class III genes encode other molecules such as cytokines and do not contain HLA-DR.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Class II genes encode MHC molecules; it is the class III genes that encode cytokines.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: An organ procurement organization notes that a deceased donor's blood type lacks A and B antigens, allowing donation to recipients of any ABO type. Which of the following blood types did this donor most likely have?

explanation.summary: Type O individuals lack A and B antigens, making them universal donors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that people with type O blood do not have A or B antigens on their red blood cells. Because recipient anti-AB antibodies will not react against O-type cells, type O donors are considered 'universal' transplant donors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type A blood carries the A antigen, which would react with anti-A antibodies in some recipients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type B blood carries the B antigen, which would react with anti-B antibodies in some recipients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type AB carries both A and B antigens and is the least universal donor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rh status refers to a separate antigen system and does not define the universal donor concept described here for ABO.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 40-year-old kidney transplant recipient is started on an immunosuppressive medication that prevents rejection specifically by inhibiting lymphocyte proliferation. Which of the following drugs is most consistent with this mechanism of action?

explanation.summary: Mycophenolate mofetil is an immunosuppressant that inhibits lymphocyte proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick specifically states that mycophenolate mofetil inhibits lymphocyte proliferation, whereas tacrolimus inhibits T-cell responses. Blocking lymphocyte proliferation dampens the recipient immune response against the graft.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tacrolimus inhibits T-cell responses rather than acting primarily by blocking lymphocyte proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Steroids such as prednisone are broad anti-inflammatory immunosuppressants and are not described as inhibiting lymphocyte proliferation specifically.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IVIG is used to treat rejection, not as a maintenance drug that inhibits lymphocyte proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasmapheresis removes offending antibodies from the circulation and is a treatment for rejection, not a lymphocyte-proliferation inhibitor.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with cirrhosis is being ranked for a liver transplant. Her physician calculates a numeric score from her bilirubin, sodium, albumin, creatinine, and INR to determine medical urgency. Which of the following scores is being used?

explanation.summary: The MELD score ranks liver transplant urgency in patients age 12 or older using bilirubin, sodium, albumin, creatinine, and INR.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the MELD (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease) score as a numeric score used in patients age 12 or older that includes bilirubin, sodium, albumin, creatinine, and prothrombin time expressed as INR.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The PELD score is used in patients younger than 12 and includes height and weight, which are not listed here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Status 1 is a categorical highest-priority designation for fulminant failure, not a numeric score calculated from these labs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lymphocyte cross-matching detects recipient antibodies against donor lymphocytes; it is not a liver urgency score.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Extended criteria donor refers to risk features of a deceased donor, not a recipient urgency score.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man develops fulminant hepatic failure and is at the highest risk of death without immediate transplantation. He is given a listing designation that supersedes his MELD score. Which of the following best describes this designation?

explanation.summary: Status 1 designation is given to patients in fulminant hepatic failure and supersedes the MELD score.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that patients can be designated Status 1, usually those in fulminant hepatic failure, and that this designation supersedes the MELD score to prioritize them for a liver.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Extended criteria donor describes a deceased donor with certain risk factors, not a recipient priority listing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The PELD score is a numeric urgency score for children under 12, not a designation that overrides MELD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Universal donor refers to a type O blood donor, unrelated to liver listing priority.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A positive lymphocyte cross-match indicates preformed recipient antibodies and does not confer transplant priority.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A transplant surgeon requests a rapid assessment of a donor liver's viability at the time of procurement so that a decision to use the organ can be made quickly. Which of the following is the primary method used to evaluate pre-transplant organs for viability?

explanation.summary: Frozen section evaluation provides the rapid microscopic assessment needed to judge a donor organ's viability at procurement.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that frozen section, in which a portion of tissue is frozen and cut, gives a more immediate microscopic evaluation of pathology, which is what the transplant surgeon needs to quickly decide whether the organ is ready for transplant.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Routine permanent histology gives microscopic detail but takes much longer, so it cannot provide the quick assessment needed at procurement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gross evaluation may be performed but does not provide the microscopic assessment of the degree of pathology.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Electron microscopy is a slow, specialized technique not used for rapid intraoperative viability decisions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immunofluorescence is used to detect immune deposits and is not the primary rapid method for donor organ viability.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: During frozen-section evaluation of a potential donor liver, the pathologist reports 65% macrovesicular steatosis. Based on standard criteria described for donor liver assessment, this finding is best interpreted as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acceptable finding with no impact on transplant

explanation.summary: Greater than 60% macrovesicular steatosis is an absolute contraindication to using a donor liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that greater than 30% macrovesicular steatosis is a relative contraindication associated with poor early graft function, while greater than 60% macrovesicular steatosis is an absolute contraindication, meaning the organ will not be used. At 65%, this liver crosses the absolute threshold.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Steatosis of this degree is not benign; it strongly predicts poor early graft function.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A relative contraindication applies at greater than 30%; at greater than 60% the finding becomes absolute.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rejection is assessed after transplantation, not during pre-transplant donor evaluation, and steatosis is not a rejection finding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Steatosis reflects fat accumulation within hepatocytes, not viral infection of the donor liver.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: During frozen-section evaluation of a donor kidney, the pathologist identifies glomeruli showing scarring and hyalinization involving more than half of the glomerular tuft. Which of the following best describes this finding?

explanation.summary: Global glomerulosclerosis is scarring or hyalinization of more than half of the glomerulus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines global glomerulosclerosis as scarring/hyalinization of more than half of the glomerulus. It is one of the common donor kidney pathologies assessed on frozen section to determine organ viability.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Arteriolar hyalinization is thickening of arteriole walls by homogenous eosinophilic protein material, not scarring of the glomerulus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interstitial fibrosis affects the interstitium and tubules, not the glomerular tuft.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Arterial sclerosis is intimal thickening of arteries between the endothelium and internal elastic lamina.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acute tubular necrosis involves tubular epithelial injury and is not the glomerular scarring described here.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 3 years ago remains on lifelong immunosuppressive therapy. He is counseled about the long-term consequences of his medications. Which of the following is the MOST common long-term consequence of his immunosuppressive therapy?

explanation.summary: Long-term immunosuppression most commonly increases the risk of infection, which is more common than malignancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that transplant patients on long-term immunosuppressive therapy are prone to an increased risk of infection and an increased risk of malignancy, but that infections are much more common than malignancy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased malignancy risk (particularly EBV-related lymphoma) is a real consequence but is less common than infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Recurrence of the primary disease relates to the original disease process rather than to the immunosuppressive therapy itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Organ rejection is a risk that is decreased, not increased, by immunosuppressive therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Graft-versus-host disease is not described as a common long-term consequence of solid-organ immunosuppression in this brick.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with a full-thickness burn of the forearm undergoes a procedure in which a sheet of skin is harvested from his own thigh and placed over the burn wound. Which of the following terms best describes this graft?

explanation.summary: An autograft is tissue transferred from one body site to another on the same individual.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines an autograft as tissue transferred from one body site to another on the same individual. Skin harvested from the patient's own thigh and placed on his forearm is therefore an autograft, and because donor and recipient are the same person there is no genetic mismatch to drive rejection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An allograft is tissue transferred between genetically different individuals of the same species, not within one person.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An isograft is tissue transferred between genetically identical individuals of the same species, such as identical twins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A xenograft is tissue transferred between different species, such as animal tissue implanted into a human.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Heterograft is not one of the four graft types the brick defines (autograft, isograft, allograft, xenograft).

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with severe aortic stenosis undergoes valve replacement using a bioprosthetic valve manufactured from porcine (pig) tissue. Which of the following terms best describes this type of graft?

explanation.summary: A xenograft is tissue transferred between different species, such as animal tissue implanted into a human.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines a xenograft as tissue transferred between different species, giving the example of implanting animal tissue or organs into a human. A heart valve derived from pig tissue placed into a human is therefore a xenograft. Heart valves are listed among the commonly transplanted tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An autograft is tissue moved from one site to another on the same individual.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An isograft is between genetically identical individuals of the same species, such as identical twins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An allograft is between genetically different individuals of the same species, which would require a human donor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Homograft is not one of the four graft categories defined in the brick.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A medical student on a transplant surgery rotation asks the attending about the sources of organs used for transplantation in the United States. Which of the following best describes the approximate proportion of transplants that involve deceased versus living donors?

explanation.summary: Approximately 80% of transplants involve deceased donors and 20% involve living donors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that approximately 80% of transplants involve deceased donors and 20% involve living donors. It also notes that one deceased donor can save the lives of 8 people through organ donation and enhance the lives of as many as 100 people through tissue donation, which is why medical professionals are encouraged to promote organ donation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Deceased and living donors do not contribute equally; deceased donors account for the large majority of transplants.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the true proportions; living donors are the minority source.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Living donors are the minority source of transplanted organs, not 95%. (For liver transplants specifically, it is cadaveric donors that account for about 95%.)
whyWrongByChoice.E: Living donors do not account for the majority of transplants.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man who received a deceased-donor kidney develops rising creatinine several weeks after transplantation. Biopsy shows lymphocytes infiltrating and attacking the graft. This process, described as the major barrier to transplantation, is best defined as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Immune cells carried in the graft attacking recipient tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recurrence of the recipient's original renal disease in the graft

choices.label: C
choices.text: Secondary immunodeficiency caused by immunosuppressive drugs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ischemic injury sustained by the organ during procurement

choices.label: E
choices.text: The recipient's immune system recognizing the graft as foreign

explanation.summary: Rejection is the process in which the recipient's immune system recognizes the graft as foreign and attacks it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies rejection as the major barrier to transplantation and defines it as the process in which the recipient's immune system recognizes the graft as foreign and attacks it. This process involves several of the immunologic reactions covered in immunology, which is why transplantation is discussed as a component of the immune system.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rejection is directed by the recipient's immune system against the graft, not by graft cells against the recipient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Recurrence of the primary disease is a separate long-term consequence of transplantation, not the definition of rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Secondary immunodeficiency is a consequence of long-term immunosuppressive therapy, not the immune attack on the graft.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rejection is an immunologic process, not mechanical or ischemic damage from harvesting.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 45-year-old liver transplant recipient is maintained on an immunosuppressive regimen. One of her medications is described as working by inhibiting T-cell responses against the implanted foreign tissue. Which of the following drugs is most consistent with this mechanism?

explanation.summary: Tacrolimus is an immunosuppressive drug that inhibits T-cell responses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists the immunosuppressive drugs in current use as steroids, mycophenolate mofetil (which inhibits lymphocyte proliferation), and tacrolimus (which inhibits T-cell responses). These drugs block the recipient's immune response against the implanted foreign tissue and are a key reason transplant success for unrelated donor-recipient pairs now approaches that of closely matched siblings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mycophenolate mofetil is described as inhibiting lymphocyte proliferation, not specifically T-cell responses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IVIG is an additional drug used to treat rejection, not the maintenance agent described as inhibiting T-cell responses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasmapheresis removes offending antibodies from the circulation; it is a procedure used to treat rejection, not a T-cell inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Steroids are broad immunosuppressants and are not the drug the brick singles out as inhibiting T-cell responses.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 38-year-old kidney transplant recipient develops rejection attributed to circulating antibodies directed against the graft. Her team performs a procedure in which her plasma is removed to clear the offending antibodies and replaced with donor plasma lacking those antibodies. Which of the following best describes this treatment?

explanation.summary: Plasmapheresis treats rejection by removing the patient's plasma to clear offending antibodies and replacing it with donor plasma lacking those antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes plasmapheresis as a treatment for rejection in which the patient's plasma is taken out to remove offending antibodies from the circulation, and donor plasma lacking the antibodies is given. Together with IVIG, it is listed among the additional therapies used to treat rejection, as distinct from the maintenance immunosuppressants.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphocyte cross-matching is a pre-transplant test that detects recipient antibodies against donor lymphocyte antigens; it does not remove antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IVIG is also used to treat rejection, but it is an infused immunoglobulin product rather than removal and replacement of plasma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HLA antibody screening is a pre-transplant test for existing recipient antibodies, not a treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mycophenolate mofetil is a maintenance immunosuppressant that inhibits lymphocyte proliferation; it does not remove antibodies.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease is being evaluated as a potential transplant recipient. The transplant coordinator explains that the first step in donor-recipient screening involves glycoprotein antigens found on the surface of red blood cells and other tissues. Which of the following is being assessed?

explanation.summary: Matching the ABO blood type is the first step in transplant screening; blood group antigens are glycoproteins on RBCs and other tissues.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that matching the donor's and recipient's ABO blood type increases the success of transplantation, so it is the first step in screening. Blood group antigens are glycoproteins attached to the surface of red blood cells and other tissues throughout the body, and the presence of the A and B antigens determines the four major ABO blood types.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HLA gene typing is a separate, subsequent step involving MHC molecules, not the RBC surface glycoproteins described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphocyte cross-matching detects recipient antibodies against donor lymphocytes and is done in some cases, not as the universal first step.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Class III HLA genes encode cytokines and are much less important in matching.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HLA antibody screening looks for existing recipient antibodies; it does not involve the RBC surface glycoproteins.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A transplant team is discussing how far immunosuppressive therapy has advanced. A colleague notes that certain grafts can now be performed even when donor and recipient are ABO-incompatible. Which of the following is the example of such a transplant described as now being feasible?

explanation.summary: Advances in immunosuppressive medications now allow some ABO-incompatible grafts, such as fetal-infant heart transplantations.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that medications are a second reason for transplant success: immunosuppressive drugs block the recipient's immune response, so success for unrelated pairs now approaches that of closer genetic matches. It specifically states that some ABO blood type-incompatible grafts can now be transplanted, giving fetal-infant heart transplantation as the example.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adult cadaveric liver transplants are the most common type of liver transplant, but the brick does not cite them as an ABO-incompatible example.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extended criteria donors relate to expanded kidney donor acceptance criteria, not ABO incompatibility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Islets of Langerhans are listed among commonly transplanted cells, not as an ABO-incompatible example.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lung transplantation is mentioned for sarcoidosis, cystic fibrosis, or COPD, not as an ABO-incompatible graft.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A genetics student reviews HLA inheritance in preparation for a transplant immunology exam. Each parent contributes a single six-gene cluster of HLA class I and class II genes to the offspring, and all of these genes are expressed as functioning proteins. Which of the following correctly describes this inheritance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Six genes total, inherited as a recessive trait

choices.label: B
choices.text: Twelve genes total, with only the paternal haplotype expressed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Twelve genes total, with random inactivation of one haplotype

explanation.summary: Each individual has 12 HLA class I and II genes (a six-gene haplotype from each parent), all expressed codominantly.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that each individual has 12 total HLA class I and class II genes, 6 from each parent. Each parent donates a single six-gene cluster called a haplotype, and all of the genes are expressed as functioning proteins, which is known as codominant expression. Because there are 12 distinct HLA genes, achieving a good match in transplants is challenging.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The total is 12 genes, and HLA expression is codominant, not recessive.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both the maternal and paternal haplotypes are expressed; neither is silenced.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Six is the number of genes in one parental haplotype; the individual carries 12 in total.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no inactivation of one haplotype; all 12 genes are expressed as functioning proteins.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A transplant immunologist reviews the HLA typing of a kidney donor-recipient pair, which are well matched at HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DR but differ at several genes in a third region of the complex on chromosome 6. Matching at this third region is considered much less important because the genes there encode which of the following?

explanation.summary: Class III HLA genes encode other molecules such as cytokines, and matching them is much less important than matching class I and II.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the HLA complex as more than 200 genes on the short arm of chromosome 6 arranged into class I, class II, and class III regions. Class I and class II genes encode MHC molecules and their matching is critical to transplant success, whereas the class III genes encode other molecules, such as cytokines, and matching them is much less important.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ABO antigens are encoded by separate blood group genes, not by the HLA complex.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MHC molecules are encoded by the class I and class II regions, whose matching is critical, not the less important third region.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunoglobulin genes are not part of the HLA complex described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T-cell receptor genes are not part of the HLA complex described in the brick.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with a history of multiple pregnancies and prior blood transfusions is being worked up for a kidney transplant. Before any donor is identified, her serum is tested to determine whether she already has circulating antibodies that would target a donated organ. Which of the following tests is being performed?

explanation.summary: HLA antibody screening of the recipient determines whether the recipient already has antibodies that would target the donated organ or tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists three types of HLA testing generally performed: HLA gene typing of donor and recipient to identify specific alleles, HLA antibody screening of the recipient to determine if the recipient has any existing antibodies that would target the donated organ or tissue, and lymphocyte cross-matching. Screening the recipient's serum for pre-existing antibodies before a donor is identified is HLA antibody screening.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HLA gene typing identifies the specific HLA alleles of donor and recipient; it does not detect antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphocyte cross-matching tests recipient antibodies against a specific donor's lymphocytes, so it requires a donor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ABO typing identifies A and B antigens on red cells, not anti-HLA antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Frozen section is used to evaluate donor organ viability, not recipient antibodies.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A potential deceased-donor kidney has been identified for a 50-year-old recipient. Before proceeding, the laboratory mixes the recipient's serum with cells from the donor to detect recipient antibodies that would target antigens present on the donor's lymphocytes. Which of the following tests is being performed?

explanation.summary: Lymphocyte cross-matching detects recipient antibodies that would target antigens present on a specific donor's lymphocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes lymphocyte cross-matching as a test done in some cases to detect recipient antibodies that would target antigens present on donor lymphocytes. Unlike HLA antibody screening, which looks for any existing antibodies in the recipient, cross-matching tests the recipient directly against a particular donor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HLA gene typing identifies the specific HLA alleles of donor and recipient rather than testing for antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA antibody screening tests the recipient for pre-existing antibodies in general, not against a specific donor's lymphocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The MELD score is a numeric measure of medical urgency for liver allocation, not an immunologic test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Extended criteria donor assessment concerns donor risk factors such as age and hypertension, not recipient antibodies.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with end-stage renal disease is told that his transplant team will first evaluate his siblings as potential kidney donors before searching the national registry. Which of the following best explains why transplants within families generally work best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Family members are more likely to share the same ABO blood type

choices.label: B
choices.text: Family members are exempt from HLA antibody screening

choices.label: C
choices.text: Family members do not require immunosuppressive drugs after donation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Family members are more likely to have compatible HLA alleles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Family members receive priority in the UNOS ranking system

explanation.summary: Family members are more likely than unrelated donors to have compatible HLA alleles, so transplants within families generally work best.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that there is a greater chance that one or more family members will have more compatible HLA alleles than potential donors who are unrelated to the patient, which is why transplants within families generally work best. Close HLA gene matching predicts transplant success.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick attributes the advantage of related donors to HLA compatibility, not to ABO type.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HLA antibody screening of the recipient is performed regardless of the donor's relationship.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunosuppression is taken by the recipient, and the brick does not describe an exemption for related donors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The UNOS rank-order list is generated from medical data such as urgency and compatibility, not family relationship.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: In 1984, the U.S. government determined that the country needed a national system to share organs and a system to collect and store data on transplants, and that this work needed to be done by a private, non-government organization. Which of the following organizations was created as a result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease committee

choices.label: E
choices.text: The United Network for Organ Sharing

explanation.summary: The United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) was created as a private organization to run the national organ-sharing network.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that in 1984 the U.S. government decided the country needed a national system to share organs (which became the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network, OPTN), a system to collect and store transplant data (the national Scientific Registry), and that this needed to be done by a private, non-government organization. Thus, the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) was created; it matched 46,630 transplants in 2023.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Scientific Registry was one of the systems called for, but it is the data registry, not the private organization created to run the network.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CMS is a government agency and is not mentioned in the brick's account of the organ-sharing system.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MELD is a liver urgency score, not an organization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The NIH is a government body, whereas the brick specifies a private, non-government organization.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman who donated a kidney to her brother 15 years ago now develops end-stage renal disease herself and is listed for a kidney transplant. Her transplant coordinator notes that a specific factor in her history will weigh into her organ allocation. Which of the following allocation factors is specific to kidney rather than liver transplantation?

explanation.summary: Prior living donor status is a kidney-specific allocation factor, alongside waiting time, immune compatibility, survival benefit, distance, and pediatric status.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists kidney allocation factors as waiting time, donor/recipient immune system compatibility, prior living donor, distance from donor hospital, survival benefit, and pediatric status. Liver allocation factors are medical urgency (MELD and PELD scores, with Status 1 superseding MELD), distance from donor hospital, and pediatric status. Having previously been a living donor therefore applies to kidney allocation specifically.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Distance from donor hospital appears in both the liver and kidney allocation lists.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pediatric status appears in both the liver and kidney allocation lists.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The MELD score is a liver allocation factor measuring medical urgency, not a kidney factor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Status 1 designation is a liver allocation designation for fulminant hepatic failure, not a kidney factor.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl with biliary atresia and progressive liver failure is listed for liver transplantation. To rank her medical urgency, her team calculates a numeric score that incorporates her height, weight, bilirubin, albumin, INR, and creatinine. Which of the following scores is being used?

explanation.summary: The PELD score is used for liver candidates younger than 12 and includes height, weight, bilirubin, albumin, INR, and creatinine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines the PELD (Pediatric End-Stage Liver Disease) score as a numeric score used in patients younger than 12 that includes height, weight, bilirubin, albumin, INR, and creatinine. The inclusion of growth parameters (height and weight) and the patient's age distinguish it from the MELD score used in patients 12 or older.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The MELD score is used in patients age 12 or older and includes bilirubin, sodium, albumin, creatinine, and INR, not height and weight.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Status 1 is a categorical designation for fulminant hepatic failure that supersedes the numeric score; it is not calculated from labs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Extended criteria donor refers to deceased kidney donors with risk factors, not a recipient urgency score.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Survival benefit is listed as a kidney allocation factor, not a numeric liver urgency score.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A hepatology fellow is asked about the donor sources for liver transplantation. Which of the following best describes the current distribution of liver transplants between cadaveric (deceased donor) and living donor sources?

explanation.summary: Cadaveric liver transplants account for about 95% of liver transplants, with living donors making up the remaining 5%.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the most common types of liver transplants are cadaveric (deceased donor) and living donor transplants, and that cadaveric liver transplants currently account for 95% of transplants, with living donors occupying the remaining 5%. This is an even greater deceased-donor share than the roughly 80/20 split for transplants overall.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cadaveric and living donor livers are not evenly split; deceased donors dominate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the true relationship; living donors are the small minority.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Living donors account for far less than 35% of liver transplants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the true relationship; living donors provide only about 5% of liver grafts.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: During frozen-section evaluation of a donor liver, the pathologist notes hepatocytes whose cytoplasm is displaced by a single large fat droplet, and other hepatocytes containing several smaller droplets. Which of the following terms best describes this finding?

explanation.summary: Macrovesicular steatosis is a single large fat droplet or smaller droplets within the cytoplasm of a hepatocyte.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines steatosis as fat accumulation within cells and distinguishes two patterns. Macrovesicular steatosis is a single large fat droplet or smaller droplets within the cytoplasm of a cell, whereas microvesicular steatosis is when the cytoplasm is filled with tiny lipid droplets. It is the percentage of macrovesicular steatosis that determines the relative (>30%) and absolute (>60%) contraindications to using a donor liver.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Microvesicular steatosis describes cytoplasm filled with tiny lipid droplets, not a single large droplet.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coagulative necrosis is characterized by shrunken hepatocytes with loss of nuclear detail, not fat droplets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bridging fibrosis is collagen deposition highlighted by trichrome stain, not intracellular fat.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Portal inflammation is lymphocytes in the portal tract, not lipid accumulation in hepatocytes.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A frozen section of a potential donor liver shows 40% macrovesicular steatosis. Based on the criteria for donor liver evaluation, which of the following best describes the significance of this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Normal finding; the organ can be used without concern

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absolute contraindication; the organ will not be used

choices.label: C
choices.text: Indicates the donor had chronic viral hepatitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Indicates the graft is already undergoing rejection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relative contraindication; the organ may or may not be used

explanation.summary: Greater than 30% macrovesicular steatosis is a relative contraindication associated with poor early graft function; the organ may or may not be used.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that histologic confirmation of >30% macrovesicular steatosis has been associated with poor early graft function and serves as a relative contraindication to transplant, meaning the organ may or may not get used. Only when macrovesicular steatosis exceeds 60% does it become an absolute contraindication. At 40%, the liver falls in the relative-contraindication range.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Steatosis above 30% is associated with poor early graft function and is not a benign finding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The absolute contraindication threshold is >60%; 40% does not reach it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Steatosis is fat accumulation within cells and does not by itself indicate viral hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rejection is assessed after transplantation; pre-transplant evaluation of a donor organ cannot show rejection.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A pathologist reviewing a frozen section of a donor liver from a patient with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease notes numerous lymphocytes clustered in the area of the liver that contains branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct surrounded by connective tissue. Which of the following best describes this finding?

explanation.summary: The portal tract contains branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct, and portal inflammation appears as lymphocytes within it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists inflammation of the portal tract among the common pathologies assessed on donor liver frozen section and defines the portal tract as the area of the liver containing branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct surrounded by connective tissue. Its figure shows portal inflammation as numerous lymphocytes in a patient with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Microvesicular steatosis is tiny lipid droplets filling hepatocyte cytoplasm, not lymphocytes in the portal area.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulative necrosis shows shrunken hepatocytes with loss of nuclear detail rather than a lymphocytic infiltrate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bridging fibrosis is collagen deposition, highlighted by trichrome stain, not an inflammatory infiltrate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Arteriolar hyalinization is a kidney donor finding of eosinophilic protein thickening the arteriolar wall.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A frozen section of a donor liver suggests possible fibrosis, but the pathologist notes that interpretation is hindered by frozen-section artifact. A corresponding permanent section is stained with a special stain that highlights bands of collagen connecting adjacent portal areas, consistent with bridging fibrosis. Which of the following stains was most likely used?

explanation.summary: Trichrome stain highlights collagen and is used to demonstrate bridging fibrosis in donor liver biopsies.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines fibrosis as deposition of collagen that is graded based on the extent of involvement. Its figure shows a frozen section in which fibrosis is only suggested because of frozen-section artifact, with a corresponding trichrome stain that highlights bridging fibrosis (stage 3/4). Trichrome is therefore the stain that makes collagen deposition evident.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oil red O stains lipid and would highlight steatosis, not collagen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PAS stains glycogen and basement membranes, not the collagen of fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Congo red is used for amyloid, not collagen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prussian blue demonstrates iron, not collagen.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A frozen section of a potential donor liver shows regions in which hepatocytes are shrunken with loss of dark-staining nuclei, estimated to involve 15% of the parenchyma. Which of the following best describes the significance of this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reflects reversible fat accumulation and is acceptable for transplant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Represents coagulative necrosis that may disqualify the organ from transplantation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Represents portal inflammation that requires trichrome confirmation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Represents bridging fibrosis graded by extent of involvement

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reflects frozen-section artifact and has no clinical significance

explanation.summary: Hepatocyte coagulative necrosis with loss of nuclear detail exceeding 10% may disqualify a donor liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes necrosis in donor liver evaluation as hepatocytes exhibiting coagulative necrosis with loss of nuclear detail, and states that >10% necrosis may disqualify transplantation. Its figure shows dead hepatocytes that are shrunken with loss of dark-staining nuclei. At 15% involvement, this liver exceeds the threshold at which the organ may be disqualified.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fat accumulation is steatosis, which appears as lipid droplets, not shrunken cells with lost nuclei.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Portal inflammation appears as lymphocytes in the portal tract; trichrome is used for fibrosis, not inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrosis is collagen deposition highlighted by trichrome, not shrunken anucleate hepatocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Frozen-section artifact can hinder interpretation of fibrosis and glomerular morphology, but shrunken hepatocytes with lost nuclei is the described appearance of necrosis.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 56-year-old deceased donor with a history of hypertension and an elevated serum creatinine died of a cerebrovascular accident. His kidneys would typically not be accepted, but the transplant program considers using them because of the ongoing organ shortage. Which of the following best classifies this donor?

explanation.summary: Extended criteria donors are deceased donors aged 60 or older, or over 50 with at least two of hypertension, elevated creatinine, or death from stroke.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the continued shortage of donor kidneys has led to expansion of acceptance criteria. Extended criteria donors (ECD) include those aged 60 years or older and those over 50 with at least two of the following: a history of hypertension, elevated serum creatinine, and death from cerebrovascular accident (stroke). They are deceased donors with risk factors that would typically not be accepted but are used to address the organ shortage. This 56-year-old with hypertension, elevated creatinine, and death from stroke meets the definition.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Universal donor refers to type O blood donors whose cells lack A and B antigens, unrelated to donor risk factors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Status 1 is a recipient designation for fulminant hepatic failure in liver allocation, not a donor category.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This donor is deceased, and extended criteria donors are by definition deceased donors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An isograft donor is a genetically identical individual such as an identical twin, which does not apply here.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 4 years ago and remains on long-term immunosuppressive therapy develops lymphoma. His physician explains that a virus he was likely exposed to in childhood, which had remained latent, became reactivated during immunosuppression. In which of the following cells does this virus remain latent?

explanation.summary: EBV remains latent in circulating B cells and can reactivate during immunosuppression, increasing the risk of lymphoma in transplant patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the secondary immunodeficiency from long-term immunosuppressive therapy eliminates the immune system's protection against pathogens, primarily EBV, increasing the risk for malignancy, particularly lymphoma. EBV affects 90% of people worldwide in their lifetime, with primary infection most often in childhood or young adulthood, and it remains latent in circulating B cells but can become reactivated, especially during times of immunosuppression.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick describes EBV latency in B cells, not hepatocytes; hepatosplenomegaly is a symptom of mononucleosis, not the site of latency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renal tubular cells are not described as a site of EBV latency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sensory ganglia are not the site of EBV latency described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Endothelial cells are not described as a reservoir for latent EBV.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man undergoes kidney transplantation. Within minutes of vascular anastomosis, the surgeon notes that the graft becomes mottled, cyanotic, and flaccid. Biopsy shows platelet-fibrin thrombi and severe ischemic injury within glomeruli. Which of the following best explains this complication?

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD8+ T-cell-mediated destruction of graft parenchymal cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Donor T cells attacking recipient tissues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intimal smooth muscle proliferation causing vessel occlusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deposition of IgE antibodies on mast cells

explanation.summary: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to 24 hours due to pre-formed recipient antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to 24 hours after transplant when the recipient already has pre-formed antibodies that react against ABO blood group antigens or type I MHC molecules on graft endothelial cells. These antibodies trigger the complement cascade, producing thrombosis, ischemia, and necrosis, which matches the platelet-fibrin thrombi seen on biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD8+ T-cell destruction of graft cells describes acute cellular rejection, which occurs one week to several months later, not within minutes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Donor T cells attacking recipient tissue describes graft-versus-host disease, seen mainly after bone marrow transplant, not immediate kidney graft failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intimal proliferation and vessel occlusion characterize chronic rejection, which develops over months to years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgE on mast cells mediates type I hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, allergy), not antibody-mediated graft thrombosis.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man received an allogeneic bone marrow transplant for acute leukemia. Two weeks later he develops a maculopapular skin rash and watery diarrhea. Which of the following cells is most directly responsible for his symptoms?

explanation.summary: GVHD is caused by donor T cells that recognize recipient tissue as foreign.
explanation.whyCorrect: These symptoms are graft-versus-host disease after bone marrow transplant. Bone marrow transplant tissue contains many T cells, and in GVHD the donor's transplanted T cells recognize the recipient's tissues as foreign and attack organs such as the skin and gut, producing rash and diarrhea. GVHD is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction mediated by donor T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Donor B cells have not been found to cause the symptoms of GVHD; the reaction is T-cell mediated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Recipient T cells drive graft rejection, in which the recipient attacks the graft, the opposite direction of GVHD.
