explanation.whyCorrect: Both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are associated with extraintestinal manifestations, and uveitis is the characteristic ocular manifestation; a painful, red, photophobic eye in a patient with ulcerative colitis fits this diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The conjunctivitis of reactive arthritis follows an enteric infection such as Campylobacter jejuni and occurs with joint pain and painful urination, none of which is present.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytomegalovirus disease occurs in immunocompromised patients and is not the eye manifestation of ulcerative colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Herpes simplex virus causes mucosal disease with characteristic cytopathic changes; it is not an extraintestinal manifestation of IBD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Guillain-Barre syndrome is a post-Campylobacter neurologic syndrome, not an eye condition.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with Crohn's disease reports six weeks of joint pain that began in the right knee, resolved, then appeared in the left ankle, and now involves the right wrist. He has had no recent infectious diarrhea, eye symptoms, or painful urination. Which of the following best explains his joint symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reactive arthritis after Campylobacter jejuni infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Migratory polyarthritis of inflammatory bowel disease

explanation.summary: Joint pain that moves from one peripheral joint to another in an IBD patient is migratory polyarthritis, an extraintestinal manifestation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are known for extraintestinal manifestations that include migratory polyarthritis; the shifting involvement of knee, ankle, and wrist without an antecedent enteric infection fits this manifestation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reactive arthritis is an immune-mediated triad of joint pain, conjunctivitis, and urethritis that follows Campylobacter jejuni infection; there was no preceding infection, eye symptom, or painful urination.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ankylosing spondylitis involves the spine and sacroiliac joints rather than migrating peripheral joints.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Guillain-Barre syndrome is a neurologic complication of Campylobacter infection, not an arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dermatitis herpetiformis is a blistering skin disease associated with celiac disease and does not cause arthritis.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A physician reviews the systemic conditions that can accompany immune-related causes of diarrhea. Which of the following is associated with celiac disease rather than with inflammatory bowel disease?

explanation.summary: Dermatitis herpetiformis is the IgA-mediated skin condition associated with celiac disease; the other listed conditions are extraintestinal manifestations of IBD.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dermatitis herpetiformis is an IgA-mediated blistering disease seen in association with celiac disease when the patient develops IgA antibodies that cross-react with reticulin, whereas primary sclerosing cholangitis, ankylosing spondylitis, migratory polyarthritis, and uveitis are the extraintestinal manifestations of Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ankylosing spondylitis is an extraintestinal manifestation of Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Uveitis is an extraintestinal manifestation of IBD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Migratory polyarthritis is an extraintestinal manifestation of IBD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is an extraintestinal manifestation of IBD.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with celiac disease develops an intensely pruritic blistering eruption. Skin biopsy confirms dermatitis herpetiformis. The IgA antibodies responsible for her skin disease cross-react with which of the following?

explanation.summary: Dermatitis herpetiformis arises when celiac patients develop IgA antibodies that cross-react with reticulin, a connective tissue protein.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dermatitis herpetiformis, a blistering disease, may be seen in association with celiac disease if the patient develops IgA antibodies that cross-react with reticulin, an important connective tissue protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gliadin, a constituent of gluten, is the dietary trigger of the intestinal immune response in celiac disease; the skin disease is explained by cross-reactivity with reticulin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The villous epithelium is damaged in celiac disease, but the skin lesions of dermatitis herpetiformis are attributed to antibodies cross-reacting with reticulin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophil collections in colonic crypts are a feature of inflammatory bowel disease, not the target of the antibodies in dermatitis herpetiformis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granuloma histiocytes are a feature of Crohn's disease and are unrelated to dermatitis herpetiformis.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with chronic diarrhea and bloating has a duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, and celiac disease is diagnosed. Which of the following is the mainstay of treatment?

explanation.summary: Avoidance of dietary gluten is the mainstay of celiac disease treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Celiac disease results from an immune response to gliadin, a constituent of the grain protein gluten, so removing gluten from the diet removes the trigger and is the mainstay of treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibiotics treat bacterial enterocolitis; celiac disease is an immune reaction to a dietary protein, not an infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antiviral therapy is relevant to cytomegalovirus or herpes simplex virus disease in immunocompromised patients, not celiac disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dairy avoidance does not address the gliadin-driven immune injury of celiac disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Celiac disease is treated by dietary gluten avoidance, not by resecting the duodenum.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man has chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and bloating that worsen after eating bread and pasta. Celiac disease is suspected. Endoscopic biopsy of which of the following sites is most likely to demonstrate the characteristic villous atrophy?

explanation.summary: Celiac disease produces duodenal villous atrophy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Celiac disease results from intestinal inflammation triggered by an immune response to gliadin, resulting in tissue damage and duodenal villous atrophy; the duodenum is therefore the site to biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The esophagus has no villi and is not the site of celiac injury.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The sigmoid colon is a site of ulcerative colitis or Crohn's colitis, not celiac villous atrophy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The rectum is involved in ulcerative colitis; it has no villi to become atrophic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The cecum is colonic and not the site of celiac villous atrophy.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with chronic diarrhea and weight loss undergoes upper and lower endoscopy. The duodenal biopsy report states a villous height-to-crypt ratio of 3:1. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this duodenal finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Villous atrophy consistent with celiac disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Crypt abscesses consistent with ulcerative colitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal villous architecture arguing against celiac disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Granulomatous inflammation consistent with Crohn's disease

explanation.summary: A duodenal villous height-to-crypt ratio of 3:1 is normal and argues against celiac disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Celiac disease causes villous atrophy and flattening with a reduced villous height-to-crypt ratio; a 3:1 ratio indicates normal villous height, so this biopsy does not support celiac disease and the diarrhea must be explained by another process.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Villous atrophy would lower the villous height-to-crypt ratio; 3:1 is normal, not atrophic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Crypt abscesses are collections of neutrophils in colonic crypts; a villous ratio is a small-bowel measurement and says nothing about crypt abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granulomas are nodular aggregates of histiocytes; a normal villous ratio does not indicate granulomatous inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytomegalovirus is recognized by owl's eye inclusions, not by villous architecture.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with celiac disease has bulky, foul-smelling stools and has lost weight despite a normal appetite. Which of the following histologic changes best accounts for her malabsorption?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Owl's eye inclusions in the colon

explanation.summary: Duodenal villous atrophy in celiac disease results in malabsorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: In celiac disease, the immune response to gliadin causes tissue damage and duodenal villous atrophy, which results in malabsorption and the associated steatorrhea and weight loss.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crypt abscesses are a colonic feature of inflammatory bowel disease and do not cause small-bowel malabsorption.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Non-caseating granulomas are a feature of Crohn's disease, not celiac disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transmural colonic inflammation characterizes Crohn's disease and is not the lesion of celiac disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Owl's eye inclusions indicate cytomegalovirus infection in immunocompromised patients.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man returns from a hiking trip with two weeks of bloating and greasy, foul-smelling stools. Stool examination identifies Giardia lamblia. The clinical picture of this infection most closely resembles which of the following immune-related causes of diarrhea?

explanation.summary: Both Giardia lamblia infection and celiac disease present with malabsorption and greasy stools.
explanation.whyCorrect: Giardia lamblia infections result in malabsorption and greasy stools, and celiac disease likewise produces malabsorption through duodenal villous atrophy; the two therefore overlap clinically even though one is infectious and the other immune-mediated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ulcerative colitis is a continuous mucosal colitis of the colon and rectum, not a malabsorptive small-bowel process.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Crohn's disease is a transmural granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease rather than a primarily malabsorptive steatorrheal illness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dermatitis herpetiformis is a blistering skin disease, not a diarrheal presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reactive arthritis is a post-infectious triad of joint pain, conjunctivitis, and urethritis, not a malabsorptive diarrhea.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A public health student is classifying causes of diarrhea as immune-related or infectious. Which of the following is an infectious cause of enterocolitis?

explanation.summary: Shigella is one of the bacterial pathogens that cause infectious enterocolitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infectious enterocolitis can result in diarrhea and can be caused by many pathogens including Escherichia coli, Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, and cytomegalovirus in immunocompromised patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Crohn's disease is an inflammatory bowel disease of complex immune, microbial, and genetic pathogenesis, not an infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ulcerative colitis is an immune-related inflammatory bowel disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Celiac disease is an immune response to dietary gliadin, not an infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dermatitis herpetiformis is an IgA-mediated skin disease associated with celiac disease.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man develops pain in several joints and red, light-sensitive eyes three weeks after a diarrheal illness caused by Campylobacter jejuni. Which of the following additional symptoms would complete the classic triad of his post-infectious syndrome?

explanation.summary: Reactive arthritis after Campylobacter infection is the triad of joint pain, conjunctivitis, and urethritis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Campylobacter jejuni infections are associated with reactive arthritis, an immune-mediated triad of joint pain, conjunctivitis (producing light sensitivity), and urethritis (producing painful urination).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ascending weakness describes Guillain-Barre syndrome, a separate consequence of Campylobacter infection, not part of the reactive arthritis triad.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A pruritic vesicular rash describes dermatitis herpetiformis, which is associated with celiac disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Greasy stools indicate malabsorption, as in Giardia lamblia infection or celiac disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Jaundice suggests hepatobiliary disease such as primary sclerosing cholangitis in IBD, not reactive arthritis.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman develops knee and ankle pain, conjunctivitis, and dysuria two weeks after recovering from Campylobacter jejuni enteritis. Aspiration of the knee yields sterile fluid. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of her joint disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct bacterial invasion of the synovium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Viral cytopathic injury of synovial cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune-mediated reaction following the enteric infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Non-caseating granulomatous inflammation of the joint

explanation.summary: Reactive arthritis is an immune-mediated post-infectious syndrome rather than a joint infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Campylobacter jejuni infections are associated with reactive arthritis, an immune-mediated triad of joint pain, conjunctivitis, and urethritis that develops after the enteric infection; the sterile joint fluid supports an immune rather than directly infectious process.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Direct bacterial invasion would produce an infected joint with organisms in the fluid, which is not the mechanism of reactive arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Viral cytopathic changes such as owl's eye inclusions or nuclear molding belong to cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus disease, not reactive arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgA antibodies cross-reacting with reticulin explain dermatitis herpetiformis in celiac disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Non-caseating granulomas are the hallmark of Crohn's disease, not reactive arthritis.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy develops bloody diarrhea four days after eating an undercooked hamburger at a picnic. Stool culture grows Escherichia coli O157:H7. Over the following week, which of the following complications should be most closely monitored for?

explanation.summary: Escherichia coli O157:H7 dysentery may be followed by hemolytic uremic syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Escherichia coli O157:H7 is an important cause of bloody diarrhea (dysentery) and may trigger hemolytic uremic syndrome, so a child with confirmed infection should be watched for this complication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reactive arthritis is a post-infectious complication of Campylobacter jejuni, not E. coli O157:H7.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Guillain-Barre syndrome follows Campylobacter jejuni infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is an extraintestinal manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin disease associated with celiac disease.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with long-standing ulcerative colitis treated with immunosuppressive therapy develops worsening bloody diarrhea and fever. Colonic biopsy shows enlarged cells containing large intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flare of ulcerative colitis with crypt abscesses

explanation.summary: Owl's eye inclusions in an immunosuppressed IBD patient are a clue to a superimposed cytomegalovirus infection rather than a simple disease flare.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytomegalovirus causes colitis in immunocompromised patients, and viral cytopathic inclusions such as owl's eye inclusions are an important clue to an infectious etiology in immunocompromised patients with gastrointestinal disease; this patient's immunosuppression makes CMV colitis the correct interpretation of the inclusions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An ulcerative colitis flare would show crypt abscesses and mucosal inflammation without viral inclusions; the inclusions indicate infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Crohn's disease is recognized by skip lesions, transmural inflammation, and non-caseating granulomas, none of which is described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Herpes simplex virus produces multinucleation, nuclear molding, and chromatin margination rather than a single large intranuclear inclusion with a halo.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Campylobacter jejuni is a bacterial pathogen and does not produce intranuclear viral inclusions.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: Cytomegalovirus is listed among the causes of infectious enterocolitis. In which of the following patient groups does cytomegalovirus characteristically cause diarrheal disease?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hikers who drink untreated stream water

choices.label: C
choices.text: Children who eat undercooked ground beef

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients who consume wheat, barley, and rye

explanation.summary: Cytomegalovirus causes enterocolitis in immunocompromised patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infectious enterocolitis can be caused by many pathogens, and cytomegalovirus is specifically a cause in immunocompromised patients, in whom its owl's eye inclusions serve as a clue to an infectious etiology.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Untreated freshwater exposure is the classic setting for Giardia lamblia infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Undercooked beef is the classic source of Escherichia coli O157:H7 infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Wheat, barley, and rye contain gluten, the trigger of celiac disease, not a viral infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antibiotic exposure is the setting for Clostridioides difficile infection, a bacterial enterocolitis.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A pathologist reviews an esophageal ulcer biopsy from a bone marrow transplant recipient and identifies a single enlarged cell with a large intranuclear inclusion and a surrounding clear halo, consistent with cytomegalovirus. Which of the following findings, if present instead, would indicate herpes simplex virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nodular aggregates of histiocytes in the lamina propria

choices.label: B
choices.text: Multinucleated cells with nuclear molding and margination

choices.label: C
choices.text: Collections of neutrophils within epithelial crypts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Flattened villi with a reduced villous-to-crypt ratio

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transmural inflammation with intervening skip areas

explanation.summary: Herpes simplex virus is recognized by multinucleation, nuclear molding, and chromatin margination, in contrast to the single owl's eye inclusion of cytomegalovirus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Viral cytopathic inclusions are important clues to an infectious etiology in immunocompromised patients: cytomegalovirus produces owl's eye inclusions, whereas herpes simplex virus produces multinucleation, nuclear molding, and chromatin margination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Non-caseating granulomas are a feature of Crohn's disease, not a viral cytopathic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils in crypts (crypt abscesses) are a feature of inflammatory bowel disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Flattened villi indicate the villous atrophy of celiac disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transmural inflammation with skip lesions characterizes Crohn's disease.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A pathology report on a colonic biopsy from a patient with chronic diarrhea describes a nodular aggregation of histiocytes within the bowel wall. Which of the following terms best describes this finding?

explanation.summary: A nodular aggregate of histiocytes is a non-caseating granuloma, the classic histologic feature of Crohn's disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Crohn's disease classically features nodular aggregates of histiocytes, which are non-caseating granulomas; recognizing this description is key to distinguishing Crohn's disease from ulcerative colitis, which lacks granulomas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A crypt abscess is a collection of neutrophils within a colonic crypt, not an aggregate of histiocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Villous atrophy is the flattening of duodenal villi in celiac disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An owl's eye inclusion is an intranuclear viral inclusion of cytomegalovirus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A skip lesion describes the gross distribution of Crohn's disease (diseased segments separated by normal bowel), not a microscopic histiocyte aggregate.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman is being evaluated for chronic bloody diarrhea, and ulcerative colitis is the leading diagnosis. Inflammatory involvement of which of the following sites would argue most strongly against this diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Ulcerative colitis is limited to the colon and rectum, so small-bowel involvement argues against it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ulcerative colitis is limited to the colon and rectum with continuous involvement of the mucosa and superficial submucosa; disease in the jejunum, a segment of small bowel, would instead suggest Crohn's disease, which can affect any portion of the GI tract.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The rectum is a characteristic site of ulcerative colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The sigmoid colon is part of the colon and is commonly involved in ulcerative colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The transverse colon lies within the colonic extent of ulcerative colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The cecum is colonic and can be involved in extensive ulcerative colitis.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman reports several months of fatigue and generalized itching. Physical exam is unremarkable except for mild scratch marks. Laboratory studies show a markedly elevated serum alkaline phosphatase with only mild transaminase elevation. Serologic testing is positive for anti-mitochondrial antibodies. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Anti-mitochondrial antibodies with a cholestatic (high alkaline phosphatase) picture in a middle-aged woman indicate primary biliary cholangitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is an autoimmune destruction of small and medium intrahepatic bile ducts with a 9:1 female predominance peaking at 40-50 years. Diagnosis rests on elevated alkaline phosphatase, supportive histology, and anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA), which are present in about 95% of cases. Early symptoms are fatigue and pruritus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune hepatitis is associated with ANA, anti-smooth muscle actin, and anti-LKM-1 antibodies, not AMA, and produces a hepatitic (high transaminase) rather than a purely cholestatic pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is associated with p-ANCA and predominantly affects men with ulcerative colitis, not AMA-positive women.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic hepatitis C produces anti-HCV antibodies and detectable HCV RNA, not anti-mitochondrial antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia is a laboratory classification of elevated bilirubin, not a specific antibody-associated disease.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with a 5-year history of ulcerative colitis develops fatigue, pruritus, and intermittent jaundice. Alkaline phosphatase is elevated. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography shows a characteristic beaded appearance of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts with strictures alternating with dilated segments. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A man with ulcerative colitis and beaded bile ducts on cholangiography has primary sclerosing cholangitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) causes inflammation and obliterative fibrosis of extrahepatic and large intrahepatic bile ducts, producing strictures with dilation of preserved segments. It occurs mostly in men in the 3rd to 5th decades and has a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease (70%), particularly ulcerative colitis. The gold-standard finding is beading of the ducts on ERCP/MRCP.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Primary biliary cholangitis attacks small intrahepatic ducts, has a 9:1 female predominance, and is diagnosed with AMA rather than by ductal beading on cholangiography.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autoimmune hepatitis is a hepatocellular disease with interface hepatitis, not an obliterative fibrosing disease of the bile ducts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic hepatitis C causes portal lymphoplasmacytic inflammation of the parenchyma and is diagnosed by HCV RNA PCR, not by biliary beading.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Choledocholithiasis produces a discrete obstructing stone, not diffuse multifocal strictures and beading throughout the biliary tree, and is not linked to ulcerative colitis.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is evaluated for fatigue and anorexia. She has a history of autoimmune thyroiditis. Laboratory studies show markedly elevated AST and ALT and an elevated serum IgG. Liver biopsy shows inflammation and hepatocellular injury at the interface between the portal tract and parenchyma with numerous plasma cells in clusters. Which of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be positive?

explanation.summary: Interface hepatitis with plasma cells and high IgG in a young woman with another autoimmune disease is autoimmune hepatitis, associated with anti-smooth muscle actin antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is a chronic progressive hepatitis with female predominance, elevated serum IgG, and histologic interface inflammation with clusters of plasma cells. Its typical autoantibodies are ANA, anti-smooth muscle actin (SMA, type I), and anti-LKM-1 (type II). Anti-SMA is more specific for AIH than the nonspecific ANA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-mitochondrial antibody characterizes primary biliary cholangitis, a cholestatic bile duct disease, not the interface hepatitis described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: p-ANCA is associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis and vasculitis, not with plasma-cell-rich interface hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-HCV antibody indicates hepatitis C, which classically shows portal lymphoplasmacytic inflammation rather than the interface pattern with high IgG and autoimmune associations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited systemic sclerosis (CREST), not autoimmune hepatitis.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use has fatigue and persistently elevated transaminases documented over the past 8 months. You suspect chronic viral hepatitis. Which of the following is the best test to demonstrate active infection?

choices.label: C
choices.text: HCV RNA by polymerase chain reaction

explanation.summary: HCV RNA by PCR is the best early test to confirm active hepatitis C infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatitis C virus usually presents as a chronic infection with persistently elevated transaminases for more than 6 months and is spread parenterally, including via IV drug use. Diagnosis involves PCR testing for HCV RNA, which is the best early test demonstrating active infection, along with serologic testing for anti-HCV antibodies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-HCV IgG indicates exposure but cannot distinguish active from past infection; a positive antibody with negative PCR reflects prior, cleared infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alkaline phosphatase is a marker of cholestatic bile duct disease such as PBC or PSC, not a test for active HCV replication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-mitochondrial antibody is a marker of primary biliary cholangitis and has no role in diagnosing hepatitis C.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum IgG supports autoimmune hepatitis and does not demonstrate active viral replication.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A liver biopsy from a 50-year-old woman with cholestatic liver disease shows a portal tract markedly expanded by lymphocytes and plasma cells surrounding a destructive granulomatous reaction centered on a bile duct. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A granulomatous reaction destroying a bile duct (the florid duct lesion) is characteristic of primary biliary cholangitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The characteristic histology of PBC is lymphocytic and/or granulomatous destruction of small and medium intrahepatic bile ducts. The classic florid duct lesion is a portal tract expanded by lymphocytes and plasma cells around a destructive granulomatous reaction centered on a bile duct, matching this biopsy in a middle-aged woman.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune hepatitis shows interface hepatitis with plasma cells attacking hepatocytes, not a granulomatous reaction centered on a bile duct.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary sclerosing cholangitis shows periductal onion-skin concentric fibrosis, not a granulomatous florid duct lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic hepatitis C shows portal lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with fibrosis of the parenchyma, without bile-duct-centered granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alcoholic hepatitis shows steatosis, Mallory-Denk bodies, and neutrophilic infiltration, not granulomatous bile duct destruction.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A liver biopsy from a patient with a cholestatic bile duct disorder shows a degenerating bile duct entrapped within a dense concentric layer of fibrosis described as an onion-skin pattern. Which of the following diseases does this finding most strongly suggest?

explanation.summary: The onion-skin concentric periductal fibrosis is the hallmark histology of primary sclerosing cholangitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In primary sclerosing cholangitis there is periductal inflammation in the portal tracts that leads to fibrosis (sclerosis) of the smaller bile ducts. The classic histologic finding is a degenerating bile duct entrapped in a dense onion-skin concentric scar, which progresses to stenosis of biliary ducts with dilation of segments behind the obstruction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Primary biliary cholangitis shows a granulomatous florid duct lesion, not concentric onion-skin periductal fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autoimmune hepatitis shows interface inflammation with plasma cells, not periductal onion-skin scarring.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic hepatitis C shows portal lymphoplasmacytic inflammation and bridging fibrosis on trichrome, not onion-skin duct scarring.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepatic amyloidosis shows amorphous eosinophilic deposits that stain with Congo red, not periductal concentric fibrosis.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl presents with acute hepatitis and is found to have autoimmune hepatitis. Testing reveals a specific autoantibody more commonly seen in the pediatric form of this disease. Which of the following autoantibodies was most likely detected?

explanation.summary: Anti-LKM-1 defines type II autoimmune hepatitis, which is more common in children.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoimmune hepatitis autoantibodies include ANA, anti-smooth muscle actin (type I), and anti-LKM-1 (anti-liver kidney microsome-1). Anti-LKM-1 antibodies mark type II AIH and are noted to be more common in children, making them the expected finding in this pediatric case.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-mitochondrial antibody characterizes primary biliary cholangitis, a disease of middle-aged women, not pediatric autoimmune hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: p-ANCA is associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis and vasculitis, not type II AIH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-HCV antibody indicates hepatitis C infection, not autoimmune hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-dsDNA antibody is specific for systemic lupus erythematosus, not for autoimmune hepatitis subtypes.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: During evaluation of a patient with suspected primary biliary cholangitis, anti-mitochondrial antibodies are found to be positive. Which of the following statements best describes the diagnostic value of this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: AMA is present in only a small subset of PBC cases and is usually absent

choices.label: B
choices.text: AMA is elevated in about 95% of PBC patients

choices.label: C
choices.text: AMA is entirely specific for PBC and never appears in other conditions

choices.label: D
choices.text: AMA titer correlates directly with the severity of bile duct destruction

choices.label: E
choices.text: AMA is the confirmatory test for primary sclerosing cholangitis

explanation.summary: AMA is highly sensitive for PBC (about 95%) but is not perfectly specific, appearing in lupus and autoimmune hepatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A diagnosis of PBC combines elevated serum alkaline phosphatase, characteristic histology, and anti-mitochondrial antibodies. AMA are elevated in 95% of patients with PBC but can also be seen in lupus and autoimmune hepatitis, so the diagnosis rests on the overall clinical, biochemical, and histologic picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AMA is present in the large majority (about 95%) of PBC cases, not a small subset.
whyWrongByChoice.C: AMA is not entirely specific; it can appear in lupus and autoimmune hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick does not describe AMA titer as a direct measure of severity; diagnosis relies on the combined clinical picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The confirmatory approach for PSC is cholangiography (ERCP/MRCP), not AMA testing.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A patient with primary sclerosing cholangitis is being discussed at a conference. A proposed mechanism of bile duct injury in this disease is described. Which of the following best represents this mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-mitochondrial antibodies directly lyse biliary epithelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of immune complexes within hepatocyte cytoplasm

choices.label: C
choices.text: T cells activated in the damaged colonic mucosa migrate to the liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: Direct viral cytopathic destruction of bile ducts by hepatitis C

choices.label: E
choices.text: Copper accumulation causing oxidative bile duct injury

explanation.summary: In PSC, T cells activated in inflamed ulcerative colitis mucosa are proposed to migrate to the liver and cross-react with a bile duct antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: PSC has a genetic component (first-degree relatives at increased risk, association with HLA-B8) and a strong link to inflammatory bowel disease. A proposed mechanism is that T cells activated in the damaged mucosa of patients with ulcerative colitis migrate to the liver and cross-react with a bile duct antigen, driving the biliary injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are the marker of primary biliary cholangitis, and the brick does not describe them causing direct lysis in PSC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune complex deposition in hepatocytes is not the described mechanism of PSC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PSC is not caused by direct hepatitis C viral cytopathic destruction; that describes a different, viral process.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Copper accumulation describes Wilson disease, not the T-cell cross-reactivity mechanism proposed for PSC.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is found to have positive anti-HCV IgG antibodies on routine screening. Follow-up HCV RNA polymerase chain reaction testing is negative. Which of the following best explains these results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Active, actively replicating hepatitis C infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Past hepatitis C infection that has resolved

choices.label: D
choices.text: A false-positive requiring anti-mitochondrial antibody testing

explanation.summary: Positive anti-HCV IgG with negative HCV RNA PCR indicates a past, resolved hepatitis C infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diagnosis of HCV uses PCR for HCV RNA to demonstrate active infection and serologic testing for anti-HCV antibodies. Positive anti-HCV IgG antibodies with a negative HCV PCR indicate past infection, because antibodies persist after the virus has been cleared.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Active replication would show a positive HCV RNA PCR, but the PCR here is negative.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary biliary cholangitis is diagnosed by AMA and cholestatic labs and is unrelated to anti-HCV serology.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pattern is the expected serologic signature of resolved infection, not a false positive needing AMA testing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Autoimmune hepatitis is diagnosed by autoantibodies and elevated IgG, not by anti-HCV antibodies.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with acute onset nausea, vomiting, and jaundice progressing to confusion. Laboratory studies show markedly elevated liver transaminases consistent with acute liver failure. Autoimmune hepatitis is suspected. According to the diagnostic approach for this disease, which combination of features best establishes the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated alkaline phosphatase plus positive anti-mitochondrial antibody

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beading of the bile ducts on cholangiography plus p-ANCA positivity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autoantibodies, elevated serum IgG, exclusion of other causes, and supportive biopsy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Positive HCV RNA PCR plus anti-HCV antibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal transaminases

explanation.summary: AIH is diagnosed by combining autoantibodies, elevated serum IgG, exclusion of other etiologies, and supportive histology.
explanation.whyCorrect: A diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis rests on the combination of four features: the presence of autoantibodies, elevation of serum IgG, exclusion of other etiologies such as viral hepatitis and drugs, and supportive histologic findings on liver biopsy. AIH can present acutely with life-threatening liver failure and markedly elevated transaminases, as in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Elevated alkaline phosphatase and AMA define primary biliary cholangitis, a cholestatic disease, not autoimmune hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ductal beading and p-ANCA point to primary sclerosing cholangitis, not autoimmune hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HCV RNA PCR and anti-HCV antibodies diagnose hepatitis C, which must actually be excluded to diagnose AIH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal transaminases is not the hepatitic picture of autoimmune hepatitis.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing why jaundice is an important physical finding. Which of the following statements best describes the pathophysiologic basis of jaundice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yellow discoloration of skin caused by elevated bilirubin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blue discoloration of the extremities caused by deoxygenated hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bronze skin pigmentation caused by iron overload

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pallor caused by reduced red blood cell mass

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reddening of the palms caused by elevated estrogen

explanation.summary: Jaundice is yellow discoloration of skin, sclera, and mucous membranes due to elevated bilirubin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Jaundice is a yellow discoloration of the skin, sclera, and mucous membranes caused by elevated bilirubin, and it may indicate serious underlying pathology. Hyperbilirubinemia can be classified into unconjugated and conjugated types, each with different causes, including the infectious and inflammatory liver diseases covered in this brick.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Blue discoloration from deoxygenated hemoglobin describes cyanosis, not jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bronze pigmentation from iron overload describes hemochromatosis, not the bilirubin-driven yellowing of jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pallor from reduced red cell mass describes anemia, not jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Palmar erythema from elevated estrogen is a sign of chronic liver disease but is not the definition of jaundice.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman of Northern European ancestry is diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis after evaluation of elevated transaminases, a positive anti-smooth muscle actin antibody, and interface hepatitis on biopsy. Her physician explains that the disease has a known genetic predisposition. Which of the following HLA associations is most strongly linked to autoimmune hepatitis in her population?

explanation.summary: Autoimmune hepatitis in Caucasian populations is strongly associated with HLA-DR3.
explanation.whyCorrect: AIH has a known genetic predisposition with strong HLA associations that differ by population: HLA-DR3 in the Caucasian population, HLA-DR4 in the Japanese population, and HLA-DRB1 in the South American population. In a patient of Northern European ancestry, HLA-DR3 is the expected association.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HLA-B8 is the antigen associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis, not autoimmune hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA-DR4 is the AIH association described in the Japanese population, not the Caucasian population.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HLA-B27 is not among the HLA associations described for autoimmune hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HLA-DRB1 is the AIH association described in the South American population, not the Caucasian population.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman is diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis after a work-up for fatigue and elevated transaminases. She asks what will happen if she declines treatment. Which of the following best describes the expected natural history of untreated disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spontaneous remission in the majority of patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stable mild transaminase elevation without fibrosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progression to end-stage liver disease or death in most patients

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conversion to a cholestatic pattern with bile duct loss

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resolution once the inciting viral trigger clears

explanation.summary: Untreated autoimmune hepatitis leads to death or progresses to cirrhosis in the majority of cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic, progressive hepatitis. The degree of fibrosis increases with disease progression, and untreated disease leads to death or progresses to end-stage liver disease (cirrhosis) in a majority of cases. This is why the disease, although rare, accounts for 3-5% of liver transplants and why a therapeutic response to immunosuppression is a defining feature.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AIH does not remit spontaneously in most patients; it is described as chronic and progressive.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrosis increases with disease progression rather than remaining stable and absent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: AIH is a hepatocellular disease with interface inflammation; conversion to a bile-duct-destroying cholestatic disease is not its natural history.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Triggers such as viral infections are proposed initiators, but the disease is a self-sustaining chronic progressive process rather than one that resolves when a trigger clears.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus is found to have elevated AST and ALT, elevated serum IgG, positive antinuclear and anti-smooth muscle actin antibodies, and interface hepatitis on liver biopsy. Viral hepatitis and drug causes have been excluded. Which of the following therapeutic responses is characteristic of her disease?

explanation.summary: Autoimmune hepatitis is defined in part by a therapeutic response to immunosuppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient meets the four diagnostic features of autoimmune hepatitis (autoantibodies, elevated IgG, exclusion of other etiologies, supportive histology), and her coexisting type 1 diabetes fits the association of AIH with other autoimmune conditions. AIH is described as a chronic, progressive hepatitis associated with genetic predisposition, autoantibodies, and a therapeutic response to immunosuppression.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antiviral therapy addresses viral hepatitis, which has already been excluded in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Biliary stenting addresses obstructive duct disease such as the strictures of primary sclerosing cholangitis, not hepatocellular autoimmune inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Copper chelation treats Wilson disease, not autoimmune hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phlebotomy treats iron overload, not an autoimmune hepatocellular disease.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has routine laboratory testing the morning after completing his first marathon. Serum AST is markedly elevated, while ALT is only minimally elevated. He has no jaundice, abdominal pain, or history of liver disease. Which of the following best explains the elevated AST?

explanation.summary: AST is not liver-specific; an isolated AST elevation may reflect muscle damage rather than liver disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALT (alanine transaminase) is an enzyme found in the liver that is released into the bloodstream when the liver is damaged. AST (aspartate transaminase) helps the body break down amino acids, and an increase in AST may mean liver damage, liver disease, or muscle damage. A marked AST rise with only minimal ALT change after strenuous exercise points to muscle as the source.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune hepatitis produces elevation of both AST and ALT (elevated transaminases) along with autoantibodies and elevated IgG, not an isolated AST rise after exertion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholestatic bile duct disease such as PBC or PSC is marked by elevated alkaline phosphatase, not an isolated AST elevation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic hepatitis C causes persistent elevation of serum transaminases over months, not a sudden isolated AST rise in a healthy man after a race.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Impaired bilirubin conjugation causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which would not explain an elevated transaminase.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis has persistently elevated transaminases and an elevated serum IgG. Viral hepatitis serologies are negative and she takes no medications. Liver biopsy shows interface hepatitis with clusters of plasma cells. ANA, anti-smooth muscle actin, and anti-LKM-1 antibodies are all negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune hepatitis is excluded because autoantibodies are absent

choices.label: B
choices.text: The biopsy findings indicate steatohepatitis rather than autoimmune disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Primary biliary cholangitis is the most likely diagnosis given her thyroiditis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seronegative autoimmune hepatitis remains likely based on the overall picture

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat viral testing is required because negative serology cannot exclude hepatitis C

explanation.summary: Autoantibodies may be absent in a small subset of AIH cases (seronegative autoimmune hepatitis), so diagnosis rests on overall clinical, serologic, and histologic features.
explanation.whyCorrect: Typical AIH autoantibodies (ANA, anti-SMA, anti-LKM-1) may not be present in a small subset of cases, termed seronegative autoimmune hepatitis. Because titers do not correlate well with severity or outcome and antibodies can be absent, it is important to make the diagnosis based on the overall clinical, serologic, and histologic features. This woman has elevated IgG, an associated autoimmune condition, exclusion of viral and drug causes, and classic interface hepatitis with plasma cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absent autoantibodies do not exclude AIH; a small subset of cases are seronegative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Interface hepatitis with clusters of plasma cells is the typical pathology of autoimmune hepatitis, not steatohepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PBC is a cholestatic bile duct disease diagnosed by elevated alkaline phosphatase, anti-mitochondrial antibodies, and granulomatous duct destruction, none of which is present here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral hepatitis has already been excluded by negative serologies; the negative autoantibodies do not create a need to re-test for HCV.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with a remote history of intravenous drug use has chronically elevated transaminases. HCV RNA PCR is positive. As part of the evaluation, antinuclear antibodies and anti-smooth muscle actin antibodies are also found to be positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He has autoimmune hepatitis, and the HCV finding is incidental

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoantibodies can occur in chronic viral hepatitis and do not establish autoimmune hepatitis here

choices.label: C
choices.text: The positive PCR is a false positive caused by cross-reacting autoantibodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Combined positivity confirms overlap of primary biliary cholangitis and hepatitis C

choices.label: E
choices.text: The autoantibody titers indicate severe disease requiring urgent transplant listing

explanation.summary: AIH autoantibodies may appear in other disease processes such as chronic viral hepatitis, so they cannot make the diagnosis of AIH when viral hepatitis is present.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoantibodies such as ANA and anti-SMA also may be present in other disease processes such as steatohepatitis and chronic viral hepatitis (e.g., with HBV and HCV). A diagnosis of AIH requires exclusion of other etiologies including viral hepatitis, and this patient has active hepatitis C demonstrated by positive HCV RNA PCR. The autoantibodies therefore do not establish AIH.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AIH cannot be diagnosed without excluding viral hepatitis, and this patient has active HCV infection with a compatible parenteral exposure history.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HCV RNA PCR detects viral RNA and is the best early test demonstrating active infection; autoantibodies do not cause a false-positive PCR.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary biliary cholangitis is associated with anti-mitochondrial antibodies and a cholestatic picture, neither of which is described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Autoantibody titers do not correlate well with disease severity or outcome.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with long-standing dry eyes and dry mouth attributed to Sjogren syndrome develops fatigue and generalized itching. Laboratory studies show an elevated serum alkaline phosphatase with mildly elevated transaminases. Which of the following liver diseases is most strongly associated with her underlying condition?

explanation.summary: Primary biliary cholangitis is associated with other autoimmune conditions including Sjogren syndrome, thyroiditis, systemic sclerosis, and celiac disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: PBC is an autoimmune disease with a 9:1 female predominance peaking at 40-50 years, and it is associated with other autoimmune conditions including Sjogren syndrome, thyroiditis, systemic sclerosis, and celiac disease. This woman's early symptoms of fatigue and pruritus with elevated alkaline phosphatase fit the early presentation of PBC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PSC is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (70% of patients), especially ulcerative colitis, and occurs mostly in men.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatitis C is spread parenterally or sexually and is not an autoimmune association of Sjogren syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: AIH is associated with type 1 diabetes, thyroiditis, and celiac sprue and presents with a hepatitic (transaminase-predominant) rather than cholestatic (alkaline phosphatase-predominant) picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alcoholic hepatitis is a toxic injury, not an autoimmune disease associated with Sjogren syndrome.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman with primary biliary cholangitis asks how her immune system damages her liver. Which of the following best describes the pathogenic mechanism of bile duct injury in this disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neutrophil-mediated suppurative destruction of large bile ducts

choices.label: B
choices.text: T-lymphocyte-mediated attack on small interlobular bile ducts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct viral cytopathic injury to biliary epithelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eosinophil-mediated injury of the extrahepatic bile duct

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immune complex deposition in the hepatic sinusoids

explanation.summary: PBC is a T-lymphocyte-mediated attack on small interlobular bile ducts.
explanation.whyCorrect: As with other autoimmune conditions, a combination of genetic predisposition and an environmental trigger (infections, toxic chemical exposure) contributes to the development of PBC, which is a T-lymphocyte-mediated attack on small interlobular bile ducts. This produces the characteristic lymphocytic and/or granulomatous destruction of small and medium-sized intrahepatic bile ducts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PBC targets small and medium intrahepatic ducts via lymphocytes and granulomas, not large ducts via neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PBC is autoimmune, not a viral cytopathic process.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The extrahepatic bile duct is the territory of PSC, and PBC injury is lymphocytic rather than eosinophilic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immune complex deposition in sinusoids is not the described mechanism of PBC.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 53-year-old woman was diagnosed with primary biliary cholangitis 8 years ago after presenting with fatigue and pruritus. At a follow-up visit she now has scleral icterus and a palpable spleen tip. Which of the following best characterizes these new findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Expected early manifestations that precede pruritus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Findings unrelated to her liver disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Evidence that the diagnosis was actually primary sclerosing cholangitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Manifestations of a superimposed acute viral hepatitis

explanation.summary: In PBC, fatigue, pruritus, and right upper quadrant pain are early symptoms, whereas splenomegaly and jaundice are seen with advanced disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Early on, patients with PBC present with fatigue, pruritus, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Splenomegaly and jaundice are seen with advanced disease, and later stages can progress to liver cirrhosis (chronic liver scarring and poor function). The appearance of jaundice and splenomegaly years after an early presentation therefore signals progression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Jaundice and splenomegaly are late findings; the early manifestations are fatigue, pruritus, and right upper quadrant pain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Splenomegaly and jaundice are specifically listed as features of advanced PBC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PSC and PBC share overlapping symptoms; jaundice and splenomegaly indicate advanced disease in either and do not change the diagnosis of an AMA-established PBC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nothing in the scenario suggests a new viral exposure; these findings are the described progression of PBC itself.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with no symptoms is found on routine screening labs to have an elevated serum alkaline phosphatase. Transaminases and bilirubin are normal. She takes no medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate next test to evaluate for the likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: An increasing number of PBC cases are detected in asymptomatic patients with elevated alkaline phosphatase; anti-mitochondrial antibody testing is the key serologic step.
explanation.whyCorrect: An increasing number of PBC cases are being detected in asymptomatic patients with elevated serum alkaline phosphatase levels. The diagnosis of PBC is established by a combination of elevated serum alkaline phosphatase, characteristic histology, and the presence of anti-mitochondrial antibodies, which are elevated in 95% of patients. In a middle-aged woman (peak incidence 40-50 years, 9:1 female predominance), AMA testing is the appropriate next step.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HCV RNA PCR evaluates viral hepatitis, which presents with persistently elevated transaminases rather than an isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Serum IgG supports autoimmune hepatitis, a hepatocellular disease with elevated transaminases, not an isolated cholestatic enzyme elevation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-LKM-1 is a marker of type II autoimmune hepatitis, which is more common in children and produces a hepatitic picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ceruloplasmin evaluates Wilson disease, not the cholestatic autoimmune duct disease suggested here.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with primary biliary cholangitis confirmed by anti-mitochondrial antibodies and a florid duct lesion on biopsy is found to also have a positive antinuclear antibody. Which of the following best describes the significance of this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ANA is elevated in about half of PBC patients and does not change the diagnosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: ANA positivity indicates the patient has autoimmune hepatitis instead of PBC

choices.label: C
choices.text: ANA is never found in PBC and indicates a laboratory error

choices.label: D
choices.text: ANA positivity indicates coexisting primary sclerosing cholangitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: ANA positivity means the AMA result was a false positive

explanation.summary: In addition to AMA (95%), antinuclear antibodies are also elevated in about 50% of PBC cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: AMA are elevated in 95% of patients with PBC, and in 50% of cases antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are also elevated. ANA is a nonspecific autoantibody seen in a variety of autoimmune conditions, so its presence in a patient with established PBC is expected in roughly half of cases and does not alter the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: ANA is not specific for AIH and is found in about half of PBC patients; this patient's AMA, cholestatic picture, and florid duct lesion establish PBC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ANA is elevated in about 50% of PBC cases, so it is a common rather than impossible finding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PSC patients may have elevated ANA, but ANA positivity does not diagnose PSC; PSC requires characteristic beading of the bile ducts on ERCP/MRCP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A positive ANA does not invalidate AMA; both antibodies commonly coexist in PBC.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A pathologist is comparing two autoimmune cholestatic diseases. In primary biliary cholangitis, which portion of the biliary tree is the target of inflammatory destruction?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Large intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Small and medium-sized intrahepatic bile ducts

explanation.summary: PBC destroys small and medium-sized intrahepatic bile ducts, whereas PSC affects extrahepatic and large intrahepatic ducts.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary biliary cholangitis is an autoimmune disease characterized by inflammatory destruction of small and medium-sized intrahepatic bile ducts, mediated by a T-lymphocyte attack on small interlobular bile ducts. This contrasts with PSC, which is characterized by inflammation and obliterative fibrosis of extrahepatic and large intrahepatic bile ducts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Extrahepatic duct involvement characterizes PSC, not PBC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The gallbladder and cystic duct are not the target of PBC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Large intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts are the territory of primary sclerosing cholangitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The ampulla is not the site of PBC's inflammatory destruction.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with ulcerative colitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis diagnosed 10 years ago presents with hematemesis, abdominal distension with a fluid wave, and new confusion. Which of the following best describes his current status?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An acute ulcerative colitis flare requiring urgent colectomy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cirrhosis from PSC progression, which requires liver transplant

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acute autoimmune hepatitis superimposed on the underlying PSC

choices.label: D
choices.text: The typical early presentation of primary sclerosing cholangitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Choledocholithiasis obstructing the common bile duct

explanation.summary: With progression, 15-25% of PSC patients develop cirrhosis with esophageal bleeding, ascites, and confusion, and these patients require a liver transplant.
explanation.whyCorrect: The most common presenting symptoms of PSC are fatigue, pruritus, and jaundice, and nearly half of patients are asymptomatic with elevated alkaline phosphatase. With progression, 15%-25% of those with PSC develop liver cirrhosis, with accompanying esophageal bleeding, ascites, and confusion. These patients require a liver transplant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hematemesis, ascites, and confusion are manifestations of liver cirrhosis, not of a colitis flare.
whyWrongByChoice.C: AIH presents with markedly elevated transaminases and autoantibodies; this triad reflects decompensated cirrhosis from PSC progression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Early PSC presents with fatigue, pruritus, and jaundice, or is asymptomatic with elevated alkaline phosphatase; esophageal bleeding, ascites, and confusion are late.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A common duct stone would cause obstructive jaundice and pain, not the ascites and confusion of cirrhosis.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man whose father has primary sclerosing cholangitis asks whether he is at risk. Which of the following best reflects what is known about the etiology of this disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: First-degree relatives have an increased risk, and there is an association with HLA-B8

choices.label: B
choices.text: The disease is caused by chronic hepatitis C infection acquired within families

choices.label: C
choices.text: The disease has no genetic component and arises purely from bile duct stones

choices.label: D
choices.text: The disease is transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion with full penetrance

choices.label: E
choices.text: First-degree relatives are protected because of shared HLA-DR3 alleles

explanation.summary: PSC has a genetic component: first-degree relatives are at increased risk and there is an association with HLA-B8.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-degree relatives of patients with PSC have an increased risk of developing the disease, suggesting a genetic component, and there is an association with certain HLA antigens (HLA-B8). A proposed mechanism of injury is that T cells activated in the damaged mucosa of ulcerative colitis migrate to the liver and cross-react with a bile duct antigen.

whyWrongByChoice.B: PSC is an autoimmune cholestatic disease, not a consequence of hepatitis C infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The increased risk in first-degree relatives and the HLA-B8 association indicate a genetic component.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick describes increased familial risk and an HLA association, not a fully penetrant autosomal dominant inheritance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HLA-DR3 is the autoimmune hepatitis association in Caucasians; PSC is linked to HLA-B8, and relatives are at increased rather than decreased risk.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with ulcerative colitis and an elevated alkaline phosphatase is scheduled for magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography to evaluate for primary sclerosing cholangitis. Which of the following best describes this study?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A nuclear medicine scan of hepatocyte excretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: A specialized MRI that visualizes fine details of the biliary tract

choices.label: C
choices.text: An endoscopic injection of contrast into the bile ducts

choices.label: D
choices.text: A contrast-enhanced CT of the liver parenchyma

choices.label: E
choices.text: A transabdominal ultrasound of the gallbladder

explanation.summary: MRCP is a specialized type of MRI scan that visualizes fine details of the biliary tract.
explanation.whyCorrect: The gold standard for the diagnosis of PSC is the characteristic beading of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts by endoscopic/magnetic retrograde cholangiopancreaticography (ERCP/MRCP). MRCP is a specialized type of MRI scan that visualizes fine details of the biliary tract, showing focal dilation in some ducts and strictures (thinning or absence) in others.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MRCP is an MRI-based study, not a nuclear medicine scan.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endoscopic contrast injection describes ERCP, which can be done in unclear cases; MRCP is noninvasive MRI.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MRCP is MRI of the biliary tract, not CT of the liver parenchyma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ultrasound of the gallbladder is not the modality described.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man with ulcerative colitis has a mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase. Serologic testing shows a positive perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (pANCA). His gastroenterologist wonders whether this establishes a diagnosis of primary sclerosing cholangitis. Which of the following is the most accurate statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: pANCA is diagnostic of PSC because it is present in nearly all cases

choices.label: B
choices.text: pANCA positivity excludes PSC and instead points to autoimmune hepatitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: pANCA is found in only a small minority of PSC cases and is rarely helpful

choices.label: D
choices.text: pANCA is nonspecific in this setting, so cholangiography is needed

choices.label: E
choices.text: pANCA positivity indicates primary biliary cholangitis rather than PSC

explanation.summary: pANCA is elevated in 30-80% of PSC cases but is not specific, also appearing in vasculitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and inflammatory bowel disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA) are elevated in 30-80% of PSC cases, but this elevation is also seen in some types of vasculitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and inflammatory bowel disease. Because this patient already has ulcerative colitis, pANCA cannot confirm PSC; the gold standard is the characteristic beading of the bile ducts on ERCP/MRCP.

whyWrongByChoice.A: pANCA is present in 30-80% of PSC cases, not nearly all, and is nonspecific.
whyWrongByChoice.B: pANCA is common in PSC and does not exclude it; it can also occur in AIH but does not point away from PSC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: pANCA is found in a substantial proportion (30-80%) of PSC patients, not a small minority, so it is far from rare.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PBC is marked by anti-mitochondrial antibodies, not pANCA.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 27-year-old nurse sustains a needle-stick injury from a patient known to have hepatitis C. Two weeks later she has no symptoms and asks what illness she should watch for. Which of the following best describes the typical clinical course of hepatitis C virus infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A dramatic symptomatic acute hepatitis followed by complete clearance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fulminant liver failure within days of exposure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rarely symptomatic acute hepatitis, usually presenting as chronic infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: An obstructive cholestatic illness with pruritus and pale stools

choices.label: E
choices.text: Self-limited infection that never persists beyond a few weeks

explanation.summary: HCV rarely causes symptomatic acute hepatitis and instead presents as a chronic infection (chronic active hepatitis).
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatitis C virus rarely causes symptomatic acute hepatitis but instead presents as a chronic infection, marked by symptomatic (fatigue, malaise, loss of appetite, occasional bouts of jaundice), biochemical, or serologic evidence of continuing or relapsing hepatic disease for more than 6 months. In some patients, persistent elevation of serum transaminases is the only sign. HCV is spread by parenteral transmission such as needle-stick injuries and IV drug use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Symptomatic acute hepatitis is rare with HCV, and the infection typically persists rather than clearing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HCV does not typically cause fulminant failure within days; its hallmark is chronic, often silent infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HCV is a hepatocellular infection, not an obstructive cholestatic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HCV characteristically persists for more than 6 months as a chronic infection rather than resolving within weeks.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with no history of transfusion, needle-stick injury, or intravenous drug use tests positive for hepatitis C. Her long-term partner has chronic hepatitis C. Which of the following routes most likely explains her infection?

explanation.summary: HCV is spread through parenteral transmission (needle-stick injuries, IV drug use) or sexual transmission.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatitis C virus is spread through parenteral transmission, meaning blood transmission through needle-stick injuries or IV drug use, or through sexual transmission. In a woman with no parenteral exposures whose partner has chronic HCV, sexual transmission is the most likely route.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fecal-oral spread is not a described route of HCV transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HCV is not spread by respiratory droplets.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HCV is not vector-borne.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Soil contact is not a route of HCV transmission.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use is found to have a positive HCV RNA PCR. His physician wants to determine whether the infection meets the definition of chronic hepatitis. Evidence of continuing or relapsing hepatic disease must be present for at least which of the following durations?

explanation.summary: Chronic hepatitis is defined by symptomatic, biochemical, or serologic evidence of continuing or relapsing hepatic disease for more than 6 months.
explanation.whyCorrect: HCV presents as a chronic infection (chronic active hepatitis), which is marked by symptomatic (fatigue, malaise, loss of appetite, occasional bouts of jaundice), biochemical, or serologic evidence of continuing or relapsing hepatic disease for more than 6 months. In some patients, persistent elevation of serum transaminases is the only sign of chronic disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two weeks is far shorter than the threshold that defines chronic hepatic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Six weeks does not meet the more-than-6-month definition of chronic hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Three months is below the 6-month threshold that defines chronicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chronicity is established after 6 months; 2 years is not the defining threshold.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A liver biopsy from a 50-year-old man with long-standing chronic hepatitis C is stained with trichrome. The stain highlights delicate blue bands extending between portal tracts. Which of the following best describes the significance of this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bridging fibrosis that appears later in the disease course

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute lymphocytic infiltration seen at initial infection

explanation.summary: Trichrome stain highlights delicate bridging fibrosis (blue) in chronic viral hepatitis, seen later in the disease course.
explanation.whyCorrect: The defining histologic feature of chronic viral hepatitis is portal lymphocytic or lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with fibrosis. A trichrome stain highlights delicate bridging fibrosis in blue, which is seen later in the disease course. Untreated chronic inflammation can lead to cirrhosis and liver failure that requires transplantation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Trichrome stains collagen (fibrosis), not lymphocytes, and bridging fibrosis is a late rather than initial finding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Granulomatous bile duct destruction is the florid duct lesion of primary biliary cholangitis, not a trichrome finding in hepatitis C.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Onion-skin concentric periductal fibrosis is the hallmark of primary sclerosing cholangitis, not the bridging fibrosis of chronic viral hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Steatosis and Mallory-Denk bodies characterize alcoholic hepatitis, not the fibrosis highlighted here.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use and persistently elevated transaminases undergoes liver biopsy. The portal tracts are expanded by a lymphocytic infiltrate surrounding the bile duct, hepatic artery, and portal vein, with early fibrosis. There is no granulomatous reaction and no concentric periductal scarring. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Portal lymphocytic or lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with fibrosis is the defining histologic feature of chronic viral hepatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The defining histologic feature of chronic viral hepatitis is portal lymphocytic or lymphoplasmacytic (lymphocytes plus plasma cells) inflammation with fibrosis. In an IV drug user with persistently elevated transaminases, a portal lymphocytic infiltrate without bile-duct-centered granulomas or onion-skin scarring fits chronic hepatitis C, which is spread parenterally and typically presents as a chronic infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PBC shows lymphocytic and/or granulomatous destruction of bile ducts (the florid duct lesion), which is specifically absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PSC shows a degenerating bile duct entrapped in dense onion-skin concentric scar, which is absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alcoholic hepatitis features steatosis, Mallory-Denk bodies, and neutrophils rather than a portal lymphocytic infiltrate in a parenterally exposed patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Amyloidosis shows amorphous eosinophilic deposits, not portal lymphocytic inflammation.

questions.topicName: Infectious/Inflammatory Causes of Jaundice

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with yellow discoloration of the skin and sclera. His physician explains that the first step in evaluating jaundice is to classify the elevated bilirubin. Hyperbilirubinemia is classified into which of the following two categories, each with different causes?

explanation.summary: Hyperbilirubinemia is classified into unconjugated and conjugated types, each with different causes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Jaundice is a yellow discoloration of the skin, sclera, and mucous membranes caused by elevated bilirubin and may indicate serious pathology. Hyperbilirubinemia, or elevated bilirubin, can be classified into unconjugated and conjugated types, each with different causes. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia is a type of elevated bilirubin that can have different causes, distinct from the inflammatory and infectious liver diseases covered in this brick.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bilirubin is classified by its conjugation state, not by hepatic versus renal origin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemolysis is one possible cause, but the classification framework is unconjugated versus conjugated bilirubin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Infectious and inflammatory describe categories of liver disease that cause jaundice, not the classification of hyperbilirubinemia itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acute versus chronic describes disease duration, not the biochemical classification of bilirubin.

questions.stem: A hepatologist is discussing the burden of autoimmune hepatitis with a group of trainees. The disease is overall rare, with an incidence of about 1 case per 100,000. Despite this rarity, approximately what proportion of all liver transplants does autoimmune hepatitis account for?

explanation.summary: Autoimmune hepatitis is rare (1 per 100,000) but accounts for 3-5% of all liver transplants.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoimmune hepatitis is an autoimmune condition with a female predominance (78%). It is overall a rare condition (1 case per 100,000) but accounts for 3-5% of all liver transplants, reflecting the fact that untreated disease leads to death or progresses to end-stage liver disease in a majority of cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Despite its rarity, AIH contributes a disproportionate 3-5% of transplants, far more than 0.1%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 15-25% is the proportion of PSC patients who develop cirrhosis, not the AIH share of transplants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 30-80% is the range of pANCA positivity in PSC, not a transplant statistic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 50% is the proportion of PBC patients with elevated ANA and of PSC patients who are asymptomatic, not the AIH transplant share.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman develops fatigue, anorexia, and abdominal pain, and is diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis. She asks what could have set off the disease. Which of the following is among the proposed triggers that, combined with genetic predisposition, contribute to the development of this condition?

explanation.summary: AIH is thought to arise from genetic predisposition combined with proposed triggers such as viral infections, drugs/toxins, and vaccination.
explanation.whyCorrect: Though the exact mechanism of AIH is unknown, it is suggested that a combination of genetic predisposition (HLA-DR3, HLA-DR4, HLA-DRB1 depending on population) with proposed triggers such as viral infections, drugs/toxins, and vaccination contributes to development of the disease. This patient's insidious presentation with fatigue, anorexia, and abdominal pain is one of the described presentations of AIH.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron excess is not among the proposed triggers of autoimmune hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Biliary obstruction by stones is not a described trigger of this autoimmune hepatocellular disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fasting is not a proposed trigger of AIH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Copper excess is not among the proposed triggers of AIH.
